dossiers.title: The Rigged Compass: Panel Banks Bent the World's Reference Rate to Profit Their Own Swap Books

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Daily basis-point shifts in LIBOR fixings, requested by derivatives traders at panel banks, moved payouts on interest-rate-swap and other positions priced off the benchmark — a continuous skim across hundreds of trillions in notional instruments.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: LIBOR was set not from actual transactions but from submissions by the very banks that traded against it, administered by the British Bankers' Association — a self-polled benchmark with no independent verification, constructed for capture.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Rigging ran through chat rooms, broker intermediaries and oral requests off any transaction record; the absence of an observable market rate meant the manipulation left no direct pricing trail for counterparties to detect.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Panel banks held privileged knowledge of their own submissions and positions, harvesting gains on swap books and — during 2008 — lower perceived funding costs by lowballing submissions to appear healthier.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Regulators collected fines (Barclays ~£290m, UBS $1.5bn, RBS ~$612m), a single trader (Tom Hayes) was convicted, and the consolidated private antitrust suit was dismissed at the pleading stage with the Second Circuit affirming in May 2016 — no bank-level criminal conviction on the rate rigging, and the benchmark was quietly re-homed to ICE in 2014.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Thatcher-era Big Bang architecture left benchmark construction to the British Bankers' Association and a submission panel of the same banks that traded on the rate — self-regulation inherited from the 1986 settlement of LIBOR administration.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Financial Services (Banking Reform) Act 2013 criminalised benchmark manipulation and transferred LIBOR to ICE Benchmark Administration — formalising the benchmark while leaving the dealer-panel structure and derivative pricing power intact.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Fines and settlement payments flowed to treasuries and regulators, not to the counterparties, municipalities, and borrowers whose student loans, mortgages and municipal swaps were priced off the rigged rate; the derivative gains stayed on bank books.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The dismissal of antitrust injury claims pushed benchmark-rigging claims into commodity and fraud theories, narrowing private enforcement and hardening the pleading-stage shield later deployed across FX-rigging and other benchmark scandals.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: Regulators (the Fed / Bank of England) ordered the low submissions in 2008, so the whole scandal was official policy and no one was defrauded.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The pre-2008 profit-driven rigging is documented independently in DOJ settlement statements and the court record; regulator awareness of crisis-period lowballing is a separate, narrower fact that cannot explain seven years of trader-directed fixings.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Extraction ran through the derivative books — panel banks moved the world's reference rate to win their own swaps, with UBS, RBS and Barclays settlements and the Tom Hayes conviction on the record.

dossiers.title: Grief as Leverage: The Firm That Died on 9/11 Patented the Treasury Market's Pipes
participants: U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware
U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Cantor Fitzgerald spun off eSpeed in a 1999 Nasdaq IPO, monetizing its dominant Treasury brokerage position by attaching patent claims to the basic act of electronic matching of financial instruments.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Patent law was converted from protection of invention into a toll booth over market infrastructure: whoever owned matching patents owned the electronic plumbing of the deepest bond market on earth.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The 9/11 catastrophe — 658 Cantor employees killed in the North Tower — enveloped the firm in an aura of pure victimhood that rendered its aggressive IP enforcement and infrastructure claims socially and judicially unassailable.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: eSpeed litigated BrokerTec through the Delaware courts from 2004 into the Federal Circuit's 2007 ruling, contesting infringement and validity of matching patents while collecting positional rents on Treasury trading's electronic migration.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The Cantor Fitzgerald v. American Airlines negligence suit (S.D.N.Y. 2011) and the firm's canonization as 9/11's greatest corporate martyr sealed the record on loss, while the patent choke point over Treasury plumbing receded from public accounting.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: eSpeed inherited Cantor Fitzgerald's decades-old interdealer dominance in US Treasury trading and the 1990s patent regime governing software-era business methods.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The litigation established patent licensing as a durable control layer over electronic fixed-income markets, outliving eSpeed's absorption into BGC Partners.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Patent enforcement revenue and licensing leverage over rivals like BrokerTec flowed back to the Cantor/BGC complex, funding further acquisition of trading infrastructure.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The model — proprietary control of matching engines for sovereign-debt cash markets — prefigured the exchange and platform monopolies that structured the 2008-era derivatives and Treasury clearing landscape.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: Cantor Fitzgerald made billions from 9/11 compensation or traded on insider foreknowledge of the attacks.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The firm's human, physical, and business losses on 9/11 are exhaustively documented, and its post-attack recoveries came through open-court litigation such as the American Airlines negligence suit, not hidden windfalls.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The real ledger is the patent portfolio over electronic matching — a choke point on the Treasury market's infrastructure enforced in court from 2004 to 2007, monetizing the pipes of bond trading regardless of who died defending the building.

dossiers.title: BCCI: The Licensed Criminal Bank That Chartered Fraud Offshore and Bought Washington Through Front Men
participants: Bank of Credit and Commerce International
Financial General Bankshares / First American Bankshares

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: BCCI charged deposits and fees across 70+ countries while routing drug, arms, and dictator funds through layered offshore accounts, skimming a spread on money no legitimate bank would touch.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: A Luxembourg charter with London management and Gulf ownership meant no single regulator could see the whole; BCCI then secretly acquired licensed U.S. banks through fronts, installing Clark Clifford as chairman and Robert Altman as president to conceal foreign control in violation of U.S. banking law.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Front-men governance, offshore bookkeeping, and manufactured audits obscured the ledger for nearly two decades; the Tampa undercover probe ('Operation C-Chase') only cracked the fog after years of moving money through mainstream clearing banks.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: As the unregulated clearinghouse for the Medellín cartel, Noriega, Saddam Hussein's agricultural schemes, and Abu Nidal's accounts, BCCI captured the monopoly rent on unbankable money — roughly $10-13 billion ultimately vanished against roughly $20 billion in declared assets.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The July 5, 1991 coordinated seizure by the Bank of England and seven regulators was framed as an outlier bust; a guilty plea to racketeering and money laundering, decades of liquidation paying depositors cents on the dollar, the acquittal of Altman and the dismissal of Clifford's indictment on health grounds closed the file while the respectable-Washington architecture that fronted the bank escaped structural reform.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: BCCI inherited the post-colonial offshore chartering system — Luxembourg incorporation, City of London operations, Gulf capital — and the Cold War tolerance for opaque conduits useful to intelligence services, as mapped in the 1992 Senate Kerry-Brown report 'The BCCI Affair'.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The collapse produced a permanent forfeiture-and-victim-distribution apparatus in U.S. federal court (United States v. BCCI Holdings, 1996-1999), institutionalizing cross-border asset recovery as the successor remedy of choice for global bank fraud.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Recoveries flowed back through liquidation proceedings and settlements rather than prosecution of enablers; the major clearing banks, blue-blood directors, and chartering jurisdictions that made the conduit operable retained their fees and their licenses.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The offshore-charter-plus-front-man template survived the seizure intact, seeding the next generation of transnational laundering vehicles and structurally compromised correspondent-banking networks of the late 1990s.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: BCCI was a rogue outlier, a 'bank of crooks and criminals' that says nothing about respectable finance.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: BCCI did not operate in the shadows — it operated through First American's blue-blood Washington board and moved its money through the world's major clearing banks; the respectable letterhead was the mechanism, and its front men beat the criminal charges.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The record shows extraction ran through offshore chartering plus front-man acquisition of licensed U.S. banks, with the criminality adjudicated in federal court: the black ledger was franchised through the front door.

dossiers.title: The Bank Nobody Could Kill: Basel's Reparations Machine Outlives Its Mandate and Captures Its Founders

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The Hague Agreements of January 1930 chartered the BIS to collect and administer Germany's Young Plan reparation payments — a perpetual toll on a sovereign's output, extracted via intergovernmental debt schedules inherited from the Dawes Plan.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The victors' central banks seated the institution in Basel, outside any single nation's jurisdiction, with constituent charters granting legal immunity to its assets and archives — an extraction instrument built constitutionally beyond audit, seizure, or subpoena.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Charter-level archive immunity meant the BIS's ledgers were closed to national parliaments and courts; during WWII it operated gold and foreign-exchange channels with all belligerents while its American president Thomas H. McKittrick kept lines open to both Allied and Axis central banks, all under diplomatic darkness.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: After the Hoover Moratorium (1931) and Lausanne (1932) killed the reparations flow it existed to manage, the BIS did not dissolve — it repurposed into the monopoly clearinghouse and club of central bankers, a wartime intermediary whose neutrality charter was itself the market.

dossiers.title: Famine as Fiscal Policy: How the East India Company Taxed Bengal's Dead to Repay Parliament

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Company inherited the joint-stock monopoly charter east of the Cape and, via Plassey, the Mughal revenue-farming apparatus of Bengal, fusing corporate trade privilege with sovereign tax power.

closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Bengal land tax serviced the parliamentary loan and Company dividends, recirculating colonial extraction upward to British creditors and shareholders at the direct cost of the taxed famine population.

dossiers.title: Coffin Ships: How British Shipowners Monetized Drowned Crews Until One MP Drew the Line

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Shipowners pocketed freight revenue from vessels loaded past any safe draught, knowing that over-insured hulls would pay out on loss — the freight skim was underwritten by the coffins the crews sailed in.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The law of the sea put no load-line duty on owners: freeboard was a matter of contract and custom, and the marine insurance market priced the practice in rather than refusing it, structurally normalizing the coffin-ship economy.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Casualty statistics were scattered across registries and Lloyd's listings, and wreck inquests were local and brief; the systematic pattern — overloaded, over-insured, lost with all hands — was invisible until Plimsoll assembled it in Parliament.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was the freight-and-payout duality: owners whose ships sank often collected more than owners whose ships arrived, making mass death a rational business model sustained by the insurance market's pricing.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The shipowners' bloc in Parliament fought every load-line bill to a compromise, and the Merchant Shipping (Load Line) Act 1876 passed only softened — owner-empowered enforcement, diluted penalties, and Plimsoll briefly suspended from the Commons for refusing to accept the watering-down.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Plimsoll's campaign inherited the Victorian liberal-reform machinery of Royal Commissions and Commons select committees, and ran it against an owners' interest seated in both Houses.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The 1876 Act created the load-line obligation itself — the state marking on every hull of the maximum safe draught — a permanent, visible, inspection-based safety framework where none had existed.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The diluted enforcement left owners collecting on pre-load-line losses while the new marking re-valued survivors' freight rates upward; the industry absorbed the reform as a cost, not a forfeiture, with no liability reopened for the drowned.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The load line became universal standard practice in merchant shipping, and the pattern — a safety marking fought to a compromised first law — stands behind every later maritime safety regime, including the SOLAS convention after the Titanic.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The cozy Victorian image of Plimsoll the saintly MP versus a few wicked greedy owners — a morality tale with one hero and some villains.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The decoy personalizes a structural machine: the profits flowed from the insurance market's pricing of loss, from Parliamentary representation of the owning class, and from the absence of any marking duty at all — not from a handful of rogue characters.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The ledger is the coffin-ship economics: overload, heavy overinsurance, payout on sinking, and a legislative fight recorded in Hansard against owners who profited when crews drowned; the 1876 Merchant Shipping (Load Line) Act and its load line are the surviving framework, and Plimsoll's Commons suspension for disorderly protest is on the record.

closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The 1893-95 wave institutionalized the banker-dominated reorganization committee — deposit agreements, foreclosure sale, and recapitalization by the incumbents — as the standard template for American railroad receivership.

extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Third-class passengers, many of them immigrants with limited English, were left without guidance or accessible routes upward as the ship foundered; the ship's navigation at speed through a known ice field was normalized in company testimony as routine seamanship.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The transatlantic emigrant trade's dominant carriers captured fares on the promise of speed and grandeur while externalizing death risk onto the cheapest-fare class; Ismay's survival preserved the managing director who embodied that cost-transfer model.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The Mersey inquiry focused its findings on crew conduct and seamanship rather than company policy, declined to censure Ismay, and closed the liability loop for the parent company; the US Smith Committee pressed harder but the British verdict became the operative record.

closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The 1913-1914 SOLAS convention created the first binding international maritime safety framework, mandating lifeboat capacity for all aboard and institutionalizing state enforcement of carrier obligations.

dossiers.title: All Passengers Saved: The Night a Private Wire Outran Every Official Channel and Printed a Lie
participants: press associations of the North Atlantic ports

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Wireless telegraphy was a private commercial service — Marconi Company operators aboard ships, paid by message and by contract, whose bulletins were the product sold to a hungry press within hours of the disaster.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: No government or company channel existed to verify or suppress wireless traffic; the Marconi operators' relayed dispatches moved directly from the ether to front pages, and the press associations ran them without source discipline.

extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The wireless companies' monopoly on fast news was the windfall: speed sold papers and messages, and the error was corrected only when slower official channels caught up — when the Carpathia docked in New York on April 18 and the first accurate lists replaced the fiction.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The fog closed as a story of technology's teething pains rather than a structural account of a private information infrastructure printing unverified disaster news; the falsified casualty reports were left to folklore, not to any accounting.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The fog inherited the Marconi Company's monopoly on ship-to-shore traffic and the press associations' competitive wire economy, both built on speed as the salable product.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The April 1912 fog established the standard crisis-information pattern of the twentieth century: private infrastructure first, official confirmation last, with the gap between filled by whoever owns the fastest channel.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The error cost the press nothing that mattered to the wire companies: the same channels that printed the false safety of the morning sold the corrected horror of the evening, and speed — not accuracy — remained the priced good.

dossiers.title: Senator Aldrich and Wall Street Bankers Draft a National Reserve Association in Secret at Jekyll Island

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The Panic of 1907 left the banking system without a lender of last resort, and the bankers who had privately organized the rescue stood to profit from institutionalizing that role. A legislated national reserve mechanism, with banker-dominated district boards as proposed in the Aldrich Plan, would give the large New York banks standing access to emergency liquidity and a central clearing of credit.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The Aldrich–Vreeland Act of May 1908 created the National Monetary Commission, chaired by Senator Nelson W. Aldrich, putting the writing of banking reform in the hands of the very interests to be regulated. The commission's tour of Europe and its 1910–1912 reports produced the Aldrich Plan for a National Reserve Association with 15 district associations under banker-dominated boards, embedding private control in the institutional architecture.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: In November 1910 Aldrich met a small group of banking figures at the Jekyll Island Club, Georgia, to draft the reserve plan — established by later accounts of participants, and only later itself framed by conspiracy writing as a secret cabal. The drafting was removed from public view, and the mechanism of who would control the new liquidity spigot was buried inside technical commission reports issued between 1910 and 1912.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was structural rather than a one-time sum: the drafters of the plan stood to hold the governance boards of the proposed National Reserve Association, the institutional heart of national credit allocation. Banker-dominated district associations would have given the drafters a durable grip on liquidity creation.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The Aldrich Plan was rejected in Congress and attacked in the 1912 campaign as a 'money trust' instrument, with Woodrow Wilson running against it. Yet the Federal Reserve Act of December 1913 adopted the reserve-association architecture as a compromise, placing a presidentially appointed public Board over it — normalizing the Jekyll Island design while the original secret drafting was absorbed into founding mythology, later distorted further by conspiracy framing that obscured the documented mechanism.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Panic of 1907 response and the Aldrich–Vreeland Act of May 1908, which created the National Monetary Commission as the official vehicle for banking reform.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Aldrich Plan's National Reserve Association with 15 district associations under banker-dominated boards — the architectural template later carried into the Federal Reserve System.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The commission's 1910–1912 findings and the Jekyll Island draft circulated as an official reform blueprint, converting private banking priorities into legislative text despite the plan's rejection in Congress.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The Federal Reserve Act of December 1913, which adopted the reserve-association architecture under a public Board, establishes the central-bank liquidity machinery that subsequent dossiers in this lineage trace through the twentieth century.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The pop-culture version is the secret cabal myth: a shadowy cabal of bankers scheming in total secrecy at a private island club to seize the nation's money, as later conspiracy writing framed the Jekyll Island meeting.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The cabal frame erases the documented mechanism: a legally constituted body, the National Monetary Commission chaired by Senator Nelson W. Aldrich under the Aldrich–Vreeland Act of May 1908, openly touring Europe and issuing reports from 1910 to 1912, whose plan was in fact rejected in Congress and attacked by Woodrow Wilson in 1912. The capture attempt was contested and partially defeated — a fact the conspiracy story flattens into inevitability.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: After the Panic of 1907, the Aldrich–Vreeland Act of May 1908 created the National Monetary Commission chaired by Senator Nelson W. Aldrich of Rhode Island, which toured Europe and issued reports in 1910–1912. In November 1910, Aldrich met a small group of banking figures at the Jekyll Island Club, Georgia, to draft what became the Aldrich Plan for a National Reserve Association with 15 district associations under banker-dominated boards, as established by later accounts of participants. The plan was rejected in Congress and attacked in the 1912 campaign as a 'money trust' instrument, with Woodrow Wilson running against it. The Federal Reserve Act of December 1913 then created the Federal Reserve System as a compromise, adopting the reserve-association architecture while placing a presidentially appointed public Board over it.

dossiers.title: Strong, Norman, and the Call-Money Machine: How a Transatlantic Gold Pact Fueled Wall Street's Margin Bubble
participants: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Before the fog, the profit sat in the New York call-loan market, where lenders charged call rates on collateralized broker loans financing stock margin purchases. Non-bank lenders — "others" in the Federal Reserve data — supplied most of the growth as broker loans roughly doubled between 1927 and 1929, standing to collect interest on an expanding leveraged book.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The structural arrangement was transatlantic and personal: Benjamin Strong at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, from the bank's founding in November 1914 until his death in October 1928, maintained a working partnership with Bank of England Governor Montagu Norman (1920–1944), including shared views on gold-sterilisation and market management. The July 1927 Long Island conference — Strong, Norman, Rist, Schacht — produced an agreement to ease.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The mechanism stayed invisible because the easing decision was made privately among central-bank chiefs, not through any public legislative or regulatory channel, and its transmission ran through the call-rate structure of the NYSE rather than through visible policy announcements. That the 1927 ease fed the late-1920s speculation was identified only later, and even then contested.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall accrued to holders of the call-loan book and to leveraged equity positions financed on margin: broker loans roughly doubled 1927–1929, with non-bank lenders capturing most of that growth in interest income while stock collateral kept rising. The rate structure sat atop a market the Fed managed rather than constrained.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Strong's death in October 1928 removed the transatlantic coordination, and the story was subsequently framed around whether the NY Fed alone could manage the call-rate structure — a technical question that launders the prior arrangement. The 1927 ease's role in feeding speculation remains contested in the historiography rather than plainly accounted for.

extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: After the June 1954 coup, Carlos Castillo Armas became president and UFC lands were largely returned. The windfall — restoration of the company's Guatemalan land monopoly and the cheap-declaration tax baseline — was captured by United Fruit and its shareholders.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The operation was laundered as a Cold War victory against communist penetration rather than a corporate land recovery. The CIA's own declassified history (Nick Cullather, 1994) eventually documented the operation, but the decades of civil conflict that followed were never truly accounted for by the beneficiaries.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: It inherited the early Cold War national-security state framework, in which anti-communist framing justified covert intervention anywhere perceived Soviet influence appeared.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: It created the template for CIA-directed covert regime change under a communist-penetration justification, formally documented only decades later in declassified histories.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: United Fruit's restored lands and protected low tax valuations rolled into continued extraction from Guatemala, while the Dulles-era fusion of corporate counsel and intelligence power carried into subsequent interventions.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: By demonstrating that a private land dispute could be converted into a covert state operation, PBSuccess established the playbook of corporate-captured foreign policy that subsequent dossiers in this lineage trace.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The pop-culture version: a thrilling Cold War spy story of brave American agents stopping a communist beachhead in Latin America, with Árbenz as a Soviet pawn and the coup as a regrettable necessity.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: That frame erases the documented mechanism: the dispute's core was compensation pegged to United Fruit's own understated tax valuations, and the Dulles brothers' UFC-linked interests and Sullivan & Cromwell's representation of the company are documented in scholarship. The Cold War framing was the fog, not the motive.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: In 1952, Árbenz's Decree 900 redistributed unused land including United Fruit Company holdings, with compensation pegged to UFC's own declared tax valuations, far below market. After Guatemala's March 1953 arms purchase from Czechoslovakia supplied the 'communist penetration' framing, the CIA planned PBSuccess in 1952–53 and directed the operation that overthrew Árbenz in June 1954, as documented in the CIA's declassified history by Nick Cullather (1994). Carlos Castillo Armas became president; UFC lands were largely returned, and decades of civil conflict followed. The Dulles brothers' UFC-linked interests and Sullivan & Cromwell's representation of the company are documented in scholarship.

dossiers.title: Simon's Secret Saudi Deal: OPEC Surpluses Become a Standing Bid Under US Debt
participants: US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: When the 1973–74 embargo roughly quadrupled oil prices, Saudi Arabia and other OPEC members accumulated large dollar surpluses with no established outlet. The US fiscal apparatus, running deficits and needing buyers for Treasury debt, stood to profit up front from capturing those surpluses as a standing bid under its debt issuance.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Treasury Secretary William E. Simon led the 1974 Saudi negotiations that opened US Treasury purchases to the Saudis, with oil priced in dollars generating the surplus in the first place. The June 1974 US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation institutionalised the financial and military relationship, binding surplus recycling to security guarantees.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The arrangement was secret at the time; it was only reconstructed decades later from released official files and Simon's own memoirs. Because the recycling ran through routine Treasury purchases rather than any announced treaty, the mechanism stayed invisible to the public and regulators — and must be carefully separated from the unsupported 'secret treaty binding oil to the dollar' version.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was structural US fiscal capacity: OPEC surpluses became a standing bid under US debt, locking in the government's ability to finance itself through the decade. The Saudis and OPEC held the recycled assets; the US Treasury held the guaranteed demand for its paper.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The arrangement was laundered through the bland institutional form of the Joint Commission and normalized as ordinary Treasury market operations. Because the strong 'secret treaty' claim is unsupported, public debate fixates on the conspiracy version — while the documented recycling ledger line is never truly accounted for as a policy choice with distributional consequences.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The post-1971 end-of-Bretton-Woods dollar and the prior US-Saudi security relationship formed the inheritance; oil was already priced in dollars when the embargo struck.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A new framework of petrodollar surplus recycling — OPEC surpluses channeled into US Treasuries — institutionalised via the June 1974 US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Dollar payments for oil flowed to OPEC, and the surpluses rolled back into US Treasury debt, financing the deficits of the decade and sustaining the dollar's reserve role — proceeds and positions feeding the next round of issuance.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The standing foreign bid under US debt established the fiscal capacity and secrecy precedent that later dossiers on deficit finance and conduit structures build upon.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The pop-culture version holds that a secret 1974 treaty bound Saudi oil to the dollar by explicit pact, a hidden cabal deal engineered by Simon and the Saudis, often styled as the origin of the 'petrodollar conspiracy.'
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The secret-treaty frame erases the documented mechanism: routine, secret-at-the-time Treasury purchases negotiated by Simon and institutionalised through the Joint Commission. By chasing a nonexistent treaty, the decoy hides the real ledger — surplus recycling through Treasuries that locked in structural US fiscal capacity through the decade.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: In 1974, following the 1973–74 oil embargo that roughly quadrupled prices, Saudi Arabia and other OPEC members held large dollar surpluses with nowhere established to put them. Treasury Secretary William E. Simon led secret Saudi negotiations opening US Treasury purchases to the Saudis — an arrangement reconstructed decades later from released official files and Simon's memoirs. The US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation (June 1974) institutionalised the financial and military relationship. The documented mechanism was surplus recycling through Treasuries with oil priced in dollars; OPEC surpluses became a standing bid under US debt, locking in structural US fiscal capacity through the decade. The strong 'secret treaty binding oil to the dollar' version is unsupported.

dossiers.title: Cheney's Old Firm Wins Cost-Plus War Logistics: Halliburton's LOGCAP III Rakes Fees From Iraq Occupancy

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Before any fog settled, Brown & Root — the Halliburton subsidiary later operating as KBR — stood to profit directly from a pre-awarded contingency logistics contract. LOGCAP III, won in December 2001 to cover Kuwait, Afghanistan and Iraq, guaranteed revenue on a cost-plus award-fee basis: every dollar of cost incurred generated fee on top. The revenue asset was war itself, locked in before the wars fully began.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The structural arrangement was LOGCAP itself, launched by the US Army in 1985 to pre-award contingency logistics so military operations would not require new wartime procurement. By 2001 the incumbent from LOGCAP I (1992, Balkans support) was the same firm, giving it an entrenched position no competitor could dislodge once troops deployed. Dick Cheney had been Halliburton CEO from 1995 to 2000, and his deferred compensation from the company continued into his vice presidency — publicly documented, and publicly attacked as a conflict of interest, the framing this node keeps exact.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Cost-plus award-fee structure meant the public could not see what a 'fair' price for fuel or a meal was; every cost was reimbursed, so scrutiny had to come after the fact through GAO and DoD-IG reports and congressional hearings. KBR fuel-import pricing (2003–04) and dining-facility cost claims (2004–05) only surfaced through those investigations, not through contract oversight at the point of spending.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall accrued to KBR/Halliburton as sole incumbent across Kuwait, Afghanistan and Iraq simultaneously, with fees scaled to costs rather than outcomes. Congressional investigators later scrutinised the fee structure itself. The positions — and the liabilities, including the electrocution deaths of US soldiers in KBR-built showers documented by DoD-IG in 2009 — stayed with the contractor while the fees flowed the other way.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The arrangement was normalized as procurement policy: LOGCAP was a 1985 program, the award was lawful, and the conflict-of-interest attack on Cheney was public and openly litigated rather than hidden. GAO and DoD-IG findings on fuel pricing, dining facilities, and shower electrocutions were published, but the cost-plus structure that generated them was never dismantled — KBR separated as KBR Inc in 2007 and carried the model forward.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: LOGCAP, the US Army's 1985 contingency logistics program, and Brown & Root's incumbent position from LOGCAP I (1992, Balkans).
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: LOGCAP III (December 2001) as a rolling cost-plus award-fee occupation-logistics contract spanning Kuwait, Afghanistan and Iraq.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Fees proportional to costs meant higher wartime spending directly enlarged contractor revenue, incentivizing cost expansion rather than restraint, and insulating the incumbent across successive task orders.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The entrenched cost-plus occupation-logistics position establishes the template of fee-on-spend war contracting that later reconstruction and contingency dossiers inherit.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The pop-culture version is 'Cheney got rich off the Iraq War' — a personal-corruption story about deferred compensation and one man's greed.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: That frame erases the documented mechanism: the deferred compensation was publicly documented and publicly attacked, but the extraction ran through LOGCAP III's cost-plus award-fee structure — a pre-awarded 1985 program that guaranteed fees on every cost incurred, regardless of who held office.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The US Army launched LOGCAP in 1985 to pre-award contingency logistics contracts. Brown & Root — later a Halliburton subsidiary operating as KBR, separated as KBR Inc in 2007 — won LOGCAP I in 1992 for Balkans support and LOGCAP III in December 2001, covering Kuwait, Afghanistan and Iraq, on a cost-plus award-fee basis. Dick Cheney, Halliburton CEO from 1995 to 2000, retained deferred compensation into his vice presidency — publicly documented and publicly attacked as a conflict of interest. GAO and DoD-IG reports and congressional hearings documented KBR fuel-import pricing (2003–04), dining-facility cost claims (2004–05), and the electrocution deaths of US soldiers in KBR-built showers (DoD-IG 2009).

dossiers.title: Famine-Price Land: The Encumbered Estates Court Liquidates Ireland for Its London Creditors
participants: London and Irish encumbrance holders (mortgage and judgement creditors)
UK Parliament (1858 Commons and Lords record; Landed Estates Court Acts 1861 and 1866)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The up-front profit sat with two parties: the encumbrance holders — largely English and London lenders whose mortgages and judgement debts against Irish land were fixed while famine collapsed the rents that serviced them — and the new buyers waiting to acquire estates at famine-depression prices. Only a forced sale could turn those frozen claims into cash.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The Encumbered Estates Act 1849, passed in August 1849, built the machine: a statutory court empowered to sell encumbered Irish estates quickly, overriding prior judicial and settlement constraints on sale, and to pay proceeds to creditors ahead of other interests. Generations of lending against land had built the claim structure; the Act made it executable at depression prices.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was legal by design: the sales ran through a specialized court whose overriding of prior constraints was exactly its mandate, so no rule was visibly broken. The parliamentary record shows the machinery as routine business — an 1858 Commons supply debate budgeting accommodation for the new commissioners of the Encumbered Estates Court and a Land Transfer Office, and the same session's committee debate on the Sale and Transfer of Land (Ireland) Bill arguing the parliamentary-title principle for encumbered estates sold under the machinery. The mortgagees who collected stayed offstage in the record.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Estates fetched famine-depression prices far below pre-famine values; on the order of three thousand estates had been sold by the time the court was superseded. The windfall was split between the creditors cleared — paid ahead of other interests out of Irish land — and the new commercial buyers who acquired land cheap under titles the court had made unchallengeable.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The liquidation was laundered as reform: 'inefficient' indebted landlords replaced by 'improving' solvent owners, a free-market upgrade rather than a creditors' execution. The 1858 bill was presented to the Lords as the fruit of the Royal Commission on the Irish encumbered estates courts — with Lord St Leonards recalling on the record that Sir Robert Peel had authored the original measure — and the Landed Estates Court (Ireland) Act 1858 retained and extended the same machinery under a neutral name; the Lords Commissioners' prorogation speech announced the Transfer of Land Bill as extending the powers hitherto exercised by the Incumbered Estates Commissioners. The court's jurisdiction passed quietly to the High Court of Justice in Ireland in the late 1870s. What was never accounted for was the term left untouched: tenancy.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The post-famine debt structure: fixed mortgages and judgement debts against Irish land whose rental income had collapsed in the Great Irish Famine of 1845-52.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The statutory liquidation court — quick-sale machinery overriding prior judicial and settlement constraints, created by the Encumbered Estates Act 1849 and retained and extended by the Landed Estates Court (Ireland) Act 1858.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Creditor claims paid out of Irish land at depression prices flowed back to English and London lenders, while the new commercial owners' capital rolled into further estate purchase in the same depressed market.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The post-liquidation structure — solvent commercial landlords over unchanged and insecure tenancies — is the arrangement that presages the land-question politics of the 1870s-80s, from the Land League of 1879 onward.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The pop-culture version is the Victorian melodrama of the idle absentee landlord — and its modern descendant, the framing of the famine period as simple villainy or deliberate intent — a morality tale of bad masters and suffering tenants.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The melodrama erases the mechanism: a creditors' liquidation court that sold the land to clear mortgage debts, welcomed at the time as reform. The decoy names no creditors, no court, no statute, and misses the term that mattered to millions — tenancy — which was never for sale.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The Great Irish Famine of 1845-52 killed on the order of a million people, drove mass emigration, and collapsed the rents that serviced landlords' fixed mortgages and judgement debts, owed largely to English and London lenders. The Encumbered Estates Act 1849, passed August 1849, established the Encumbered Estates Court with power to sell encumbered estates quickly, overriding prior judicial and settlement constraints, paying proceeds to creditors ahead of other interests. The court sat from 1849-50; sales began in 1850 at famine-depression prices, and on the order of three thousand estates — a widely cited figure — had been sold by supersession. The Landed Estates Court (Ireland) Act 1858 (21 & 22 Vict. c. 72) replaced the court, retaining and extending the machinery; further acts in 1861 and 1866 amended it, and its jurisdiction passed to the High Court of Justice in Ireland in the late 1870s. Tenant farmers gained no security from any of it; the creditors' liquidation that sold the land while leaving tenancy untouched is documented in scholarship as presaging the land-question politics of the 1870s-80s. The transfer ran through the parliamentary record as routine business: an 1858 Commons supply debate budgeted accommodation for the court's new commissioners and a Land Transfer Office, and the Lords Commissioners' prorogation speech announced the Transfer of Land Bill as extending the powers hitherto exercised by the Incumbered Estates Commissioners.

dossiers.title: Twenty-One Million Dollars for Burnt Contraband: The Opium Traders’ Loss Becomes China’s Sovereign Debt

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The Bengal opium monopoly the East India Company built after the Diwani is sold at Calcutta auction and carried to Canton by private firms — Jardine, Matheson & Co. and Dent & Co. the largest — who take the margin on a trade Chinese law prohibits and British law does not reach.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: When Commissioner Lin Zexu confiscates the 20,283 chests at Canton in March 1839, Superintendent Charles Elliot takes them into Crown hands first and promises the holders that the British government will make the loss good. A private stock of contraband becomes, in a single administrative act, a claim on the Treasury.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The claim is argued in London as a question of national honour and the liberty of British subjects, not as compensation for a drug cargo. Sir James Graham’s censure motion of 7 April 1840 keeps the Commons three nights on the imprudence of ministers; the expedition sails either way.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The Treaty of Nanking charges the whole bill to the Chinese state: six million dollars for the destroyed opium, three million for Hong-merchant debts, twelve million for the expedition itself, twenty-one million in all on a schedule to 1845, plus Hong Kong in perpetuity and five ports opened to British trade.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: No British party pays. The indemnity is settled on China as sovereign debt, the traders are made whole for a cargo their own government had surrendered, and the treaty-port system becomes the template for the next century of forced-trade settlements.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The East India Company’s Bengal revenue and opium monoculture, and the Crown’s habit of standing behind chartered traders’ losses.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The gunboat indemnity: a state-to-state treaty that converts a private trading loss into sovereign debt with a payment schedule, secured by ceded territory and treaty ports.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The firms whose stock was surrendered are paid out of the indemnity; the indemnity is collected from Chinese customs revenue; the ports opened to collect it carry the next decade of the same trade.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: A clash of civilisations over free trade and diplomatic protocol — an arrogant empire refusing to open its ports, met by a Britain defending the rights of its merchants abroad.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The treaty itself names the consideration. Article IV pays six million dollars ‘as the value of the Opium which was delivered up at Canton in the month of March, 1839’ — the destroyed contraband is written into the settlement as a priced item, before the war costs in Article VI.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Elliot took the traders’ opium into government hands against a promise of compensation; the Commons debated and narrowly declined to censure the ministry on 7 April 1840; and the Treaty of Nanking recovered the whole sum — twenty-one million dollars under Articles IV to VII — from the Chinese state, with Hong Kong and five treaty ports attached.

Art. V adds three millions for insolvent Hong-merchants’ debts, Art. VI twelve millions for the expedition’s expenses, and Art. VII fixes the total at "Twenty-one Millions of Dollars" payable by the end of 1845. dossiers.title: Ten Dollars a Head: The Bounty That Filled the Sultana and the Verdict That Was Annulled
participants: Released prisoners of Cahaba and Andersonville

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The War Department pays steamboat operators by the body to move released prisoners north from Vicksburg in the spring of 1865 — five dollars an officer, ten dollars an enlisted man — so a boat’s earnings rise with every man crowded onto her deck.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The Sultana is licensed for 376 passengers. She leaves Vicksburg with roughly 2,100 to 2,400 aboard — a survivor’s count puts it at 2,141, "over six times her capacity" — and with a bulged boiler sheet patched rather than replaced, because the days a proper repair would take would hand the payload to a rival boat.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The explosion above Memphis on 27 April 1865 lands in a news cycle already filled: Lincoln had been shot on 14 April and Booth killed on 26 April. The deadliest maritime disaster in American history is reported and then dropped.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The contract value had already been captured at Vicksburg, where the payload was assigned. The boat is gone, her master is dead, and the bounty has been earned.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Captain Frederic Speed is court-martialled and convicted; the Judge Advocate General disapproves the finding and it is annulled. Reuben Hatch, the quartermaster suspected of taking a share, is never brought to account. Nobody is punished for a loss of roughly 1,100 to 1,800 lives.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Wartime transport contracting by the head, and the practice of settling military transport disasters inside the army’s own disciplinary machinery rather than in court.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A per-capita bounty that prices human cargo above the vessel’s rated capacity, paired with a court-martial record that convicts an officer and then annuls the conviction.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The bounty money stays with the operators and the officers who assigned the payload; the loss falls on parolees already held one to twenty-three months in Confederate prisons, and their families receive effectively nothing.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: A tragic accident of early steam engineering — a bad boiler on a crowded river in a chaotic month — and a disaster the public simply forgot because the war had exhausted it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The overloading was not an accident of the river: it followed a bounty paid by the head, and the boiler was patched rather than re-sheeted while the boat held the contract. The contemporaneous engineers’ statement reprinted by Berry is careful on causation — "nothing has been discovered to show that the disaster was attributable to the imperfect patching" — and the loading and the patch are documented independently of it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A boat rated for 376 carried roughly six times that number under a War Department bounty of ten dollars an enlisted man; her boiler was patched at Vicksburg while she held the payload; she exploded on 27 April 1865; the one conviction that followed was annulled, and no one was held to account.

Its introduction records that the Sultana reached Vicksburg with about two hundred passengers and crew and "remained here little more than one day; among other things repairing one of her boilers, at the same time receiving on board 1,965 federal soldiers and 35 officers just released from the rebel prisons at Cahaba, Ala., Macon and Andersonville, Ga."; a survivor’s account in the same volume puts the number aboard at 2,141, "over six times her capacity". A contemporaneous engineers’ statement reprinted there also says that, pending examination of the boilers, "nothing has been discovered to show that the disaster was attributable to the imperfect patching". dossiers.title: A Private Army by Barge: Homestead, Three Congressional Inquiries, and a Statute That Bound Only the Government
participants: Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers
Senate Committee on Education and Labor

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Carnegie Steel’s chairman Henry Clay Frick moves to break the Amalgamated Association’s contract at Homestead in 1892; the wage scale the lockout replaces is the standing cost the company means to remove.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Rather than municipal or state police, the company contracts a private firm. About three hundred armed Pinkerton men are brought up the Monongahela by barge on 6 July 1892, and the landing becomes a gun battle that kills men on both sides.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fight is argued as a riot by workmen rather than as a corporation deploying a private armed force, and the Pennsylvania militia occupies the town, which settles the plant’s operation long before any inquiry reports.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The union is driven out of Homestead and out of the steel industry for a generation; the labour cost the lockout targeted stays removed.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Three congressional investigations take evidence — the House Judiciary Committee’s hearings, its report of 7 February 1893, and a Senate select committee resolution — and the statutory answer, the Anti-Pinkerton proviso of 3 March 1893, forbids the federal government from employing such an agency. It says nothing about a corporation hiring one against its own workforce. Prosecutions on both sides, including treason charges against strike leaders, end in no convictions.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The nineteenth-century practice of corporations retaining private detective agencies as guards, strikebreakers and informants, with no statute addressing the arrangement.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The congressional-inquiry-plus-narrow-statute pattern: a public investigation of a private armed force, answered by a rule that binds only federal hiring and leaves the private market for armed contractors intact.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The agency keeps the contract market; the company keeps the wage reduction; the record of the inquiry becomes the public settlement of the matter, and the next corporation hires guards under the same law.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: Homestead as a spontaneous riot — a mob of armed strikers attacking watchmen hired to protect a mill — or, in the other telling, as a one-off outrage already answered by the Anti-Pinkerton Act.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Congress investigated the arrangement itself, three times in seven months: a House Judiciary hearing volume, a House report, and a Senate resolution for a select committee on the employment of "Pinkerton men". The statute that followed reaches federal hiring only, so the practice it is said to have ended continued in private hands.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A corporation contracted roughly three hundred armed men and landed them by barge at its own plant; the state then supplied the militia; three congressional records (H. Misc. Doc. 52-335, H. Rept. 52-2447, S. Rept. 52-1105) document the employment of the agency; and the resulting proviso of 3 March 1893 restricted only the government’s own use of it.

dossiers.title: The Tent Colony and the Company Union: Ludlow, and the Plan That Answered It

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Colorado Fuel & Iron runs closed camps — company housing, company stores, company scrip, company-appointed officials — so the wage is recaptured on the way out of the miner’s hand, and the September 1913 strike threatens that whole arrangement at once.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Evicted families move into tent colonies on leased ground. Company-paid guards and, from October 1913, the Colorado National Guard surround them through the winter; the armoured car and the searchlight at Ludlow are part of the siege.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Ivy Lee’s bulletins carry the operators’ account of the strike to the national press. The Commission on Industrial Relations later takes evidence on their accuracy, and the ownership question — who was directing the refusal to meet the miners — is argued as a local Colorado dispute.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The strike is broken and the union kept out; the camps and their scrip economy continue.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Militia officers tried by court-martial are acquitted and no one is convicted over the deaths. The company’s answer is the Colorado Industrial Plan — an employee-representation scheme drafted with W. L. Mackenzie King — which replaces the union with a body the company itself convenes.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The private-force arrangement left intact after Homestead: guards on the corporate payroll, state militia at the operators’ call, and inquiry as the public settlement.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The company union plus the professional publicity bureau — a structure that answers a massacre with representation the employer controls and a narrative the employer supplies.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The costs of the siege are borne by the company and recovered through the broken strike; the Commission’s findings carry no penalty; the industrial-relations plan becomes a model exported to other Rockefeller properties.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: A distant absentee owner who knew nothing of Colorado — a local quarrel between a state militia and an armed camp of strikers, in which a stray fire destroyed the tents.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Commission on Industrial Relations’ own Report on the Colorado Strike places the ownership and the policy together: the executives’ acts "had the hearty support and endorsement of the greatest and most powerful financial interest in America, that of John D. Rockefeller, and his son, John D. Rockefeller, Jr., who controlled the company through ownership of approximately 40 per cent of its stocks and bonds", with letters from Rockefeller Jr. "heartily approving" the refusal to meet the miners’ representatives.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A strike against a company held through roughly 40 per cent of its stocks and bonds; tent colonies besieged by company guards and state militia; about twenty dead at Ludlow on 20 April 1914, including two women and eleven children; two federal inquiries, including the Commission whose final report was filed as H. Rept. 64-31 on 11 January 1916; no convictions; and a company-convened representation plan in place of the union.

citations.title: George P. West, Report on the Colorado Strike (United States Commission on Industrial Relations, 1915)
citations.quoteOrFact: The Commission’s own report on the strike. Its text states that the acts of the executive officials of the Colorado Fuel & Iron Company "had the hearty support and endorsement of the greatest and most powerful financial interest in America, that of John D. Rockefeller, and his son, John D. Rockefeller, Jr., who controlled the company through ownership of approximately 40 per cent of its stocks and bonds", with "Letters from Mr. Rockefeller, Jr., heartily approving of his company’s refusal to meet representatives of" the miners, and that his support "contributed largely to the unyielding and lawless policy that finally resulted in the horrors of the Ludlow massacre and the intervention of the federal government". Read from the Internet Archive full text.

The page is the catalogue record for the Commission’s final report; the Colorado testimony is in the Commission’s separate testimony volumes.

dossiers.title: Good Offices: The State Department’s Standing Brief for United Fruit and the Ciénaga Station Square
participants: U.S. Department of State (Secretary Frank B. Kellogg)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: United Fruit holds the Magdalena banana zone on terms that keep the workforce off the company’s books: men engaged through contractors rather than hired, paid in scrip spendable at company stores, housed and doctored at the company’s discretion.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The arrangement runs on a host state that will not test it. Months before the strike, Washington is already intervening on the company’s behalf: the Foreign Relations volume for 1928 carries a chapter of telegrams titled "Good offices of the Department of State to protect the interests of the United Fruit Company in Colombia", in which the Secretary of State instructs the Minister in Bogotá to press the Colombian government to hold off until a company dispute can be judicially determined.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: When roughly 25,000 workers strike in November 1928 for written contracts, a six-day week and an end to scrip, the demands are recast as subversion rather than contract terms, and the foreign-interest framing is already in place in Bogotá.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Colombian troops under General Carlos Cortés Vargas fire on a crowd at the railway station square in Ciénaga on 6 December 1928. The strike ends; the labour terms do not change; the company’s position in the zone is restored without the company firing a shot.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The death toll is never settled — official Colombian figures in the dozens, legation dispatches far higher, estimates from under fifty to more than a thousand. Jorge Eliécer Gaitán’s 1929 debates in the Chamber of Representatives are the principal public reckoning; no company or United States officer faces any proceeding.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The private-force template of Homestead and Ludlow, carried abroad: by 1928 the armed force is the host nation’s army, and the corporation’s part is the diplomatic brief.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: Proxy suppression through good offices — the lobbying of a foreign ministry becomes the mechanism, the host state supplies the troops, and the company keeps clean hands and an unchanged payroll.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The zone’s export revenue continues to flow north; the diplomatic relationship that protected it is unaffected; the company faces no liability in either country.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: A purely Colombian affair — a communist-led strike put down by a nervous government — or, in the other direction, a massacre ordered outright from Washington on the company’s instruction.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Neither survives the record. The published telegrams show the State Department acting as the company’s standing advocate in Bogotá months before the strike, which disposes of the purely local account; and those same telegrams carry no instruction to use force, which is why this dossier does not claim one.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Foreign Relations of the United States 1928, volume II, chapter "Good offices of the Department of State to protect the interests of the United Fruit Company in Colombia": four telegrams, March to June 1928, in which Washington presses Colombia on the company’s behalf. In November 1928 some 25,000 workers struck over contracts, hours and scrip; on 6 December Colombian troops fired on the crowd at Ciénaga; the toll remains disputed and no one was prosecuted.

citations.title: The Secretary of State (Kellogg) to the Minister in Colombia (Piles), telegram, 12 March 1928, file 321.1154 United Fruit Company/1 — Foreign Relations of the United States 1928, Volume II, Document 655
citations.quoteOrFact: Published State Department telegram instructing the Minister in Colombia to take the United Fruit Company’s complaint up informally with the Colombian authorities and, if the facts are as the company states, to request formally that the Colombian Government "postpone further action in the matter until the controversy can be judicially determined". It sits in the volume’s chapter "Good offices of the Department of State to protect the interests of the United Fruit Company in Colombia" (documents 655–658, March–June 1928). The chapter concerns an irrigation and land dispute; it does not cover the December 1928 strike.

citations.title: The Washington Daily News (Washington, D.C.), 14 December 1928 — Chronicling America issue page
citations.quoteOrFact: Issue returned by a Library of Congress newspaper full-text search for the phrase "banana strike" limited to 1928–1929, which returns nineteen United States newspaper issues from December 1928 onward. The citation is the issue page: loc.gov serves the page OCR only to browsers (403 to scripts), so the text itself was not read here.

dossiers.title: Immunity by Order 17: Nisour Square, a Dismissed Indictment, and a Pardon
participants: Blackwater USA / Blackwater Lodge & Training Center
U.S. Department of State (Worldwide Personal Protective Services)
House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia
Families of the Nisour Square dead

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Diplomatic protection in Iraq is bought as a service under the State Department’s Worldwide Personal Protective Services contract, a cost-reimbursement vehicle whose task orders run into the hundreds of millions, with the per-guard day rate billed through the contractor.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The force that results is armed, foreign and outside both military discipline and Iraqi process: Coalition Provisional Authority Order 17 had placed contractors beyond Iraqi legal reach, leaving no local forum at all.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: On 16 September 2007 Blackwater guards fire into traffic at Nisour Square in Baghdad, killing seventeen civilians. The incident is first handled as a protective-detail shooting and investigated by the agency that employed the detail, and the guards’ compelled statements become the evidentiary problem that later sinks the prosecution.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The contract work continues through the hearing cycle and beyond under successor arrangements; the company is restructured and renamed rather than excluded.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Congress holds a hearing on 2 October 2007; the criminal case is dismissed on 31 December 2009 over the use of the compelled statements; the D.C. Circuit revives it and convictions follow years later; the civil suits by victims’ families settle; and in December 2020 the four convicted men are pardoned.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The cost-plus war-logistics vehicle of LOGCAP III and the post-9/11 liability shields — contractor immunity by occupation order rather than by statute.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A private armed force operating under a civilian agency’s contract with no host-state jurisdiction, where the accountability path runs only through a distant criminal court and ends at the pardon power.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The protective-services market keeps the revenue through the litigation; the principals move on to successor entities and new contracts; the families’ claims are settled privately and the convictions are erased.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: Rogue contractors — a few trigger-happy men who disgraced an otherwise ordinary security company, dealt with by the courts in the end.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The structure, not the men, is what the record documents: an occupation order that removed Iraqi jurisdiction, a hearing that examined the contract and the company rather than the shooters, a dismissal in 2009 on the handling of compelled statements, and a pardon in 2020 that undid the convictions the system eventually produced.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A State Department protective-services contract; seventeen civilians killed at Nisour Square on 16 September 2007; a House Oversight hearing titled "Blackwater USA" on 2 October 2007; United States v. Slough dismissed in the District of Columbia on 31 December 2009; Estate of Abtan v. Blackwater Lodge & Training Center litigated and settled; convictions in United States v. Slatten; presidential pardons in December 2020.

The record is the docketed opinion entry.

dossiers.title: Exclusive Standing: The Bhopal Act, the Forum Moved to India, and the Settlement That Closed Every Claim
participants: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Union Carbide Corporation holds 50.9 percent of Union Carbide India Limited, with 22 percent owned or controlled by the government of India and the rest spread across some 23,500 Indian shareholders. The parent takes the return on a majority holding in a company that is, in the Second Circuit's words, "managed and operated entirely by Indians in India" — ownership in New York, operation in Madhya Pradesh.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The Bhopal plant opens in 1969 converting imported pesticides, and from 1979 or 1980 manufactures them on site, producing hazardous waste held in tanks, pits and three solar evaporation ponds on leased land. UCIL's own documents record the consequences early: in March 1982 the company is aware of leakage from one pond with another showing signs of it, and in April 1982 a UCIL document notes that "continued leakage from [an] evaporation pond [was] causing great concern".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: After the gas escapes on the night of 2-3 December 1984, the record itself is held at a distance from the claims. India's Central Bureau of Investigation seizes some 78,000 pages, of which about 36,000 are plant operation records and 1,700 pages relate to plant maintenance in 1983 and 1984. In the United States, discovery is confined to the forum question alone: Union Carbide briefs only forum non conveniens and suggests the court need not reach its other grounds, so the merits are never developed in the forum that has the parent.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Two instruments close the exposure. India's Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act of 29 March 1985 makes the Union of India the only party that may represent the victims "in India or elsewhere"; and the forum non conveniens dismissal sends every US action to the courts of that same government. The defendant now negotiates once, with a counterparty that is also a 22 percent owner of the subsidiary and a co-defendant in the Indian suits. In February 1989 the Supreme Court of India approves $470 million for "all litigations, claims, rights and liabilities related to and arising out of the [Bhopal] disaster".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The conditions that would have bound the parent are removed on appeal. The Second Circuit deletes the requirement that Union Carbide consent to enforcement of a final Indian judgment, holding it rested on an erroneous assumption and that its "minimal requirements of due process" language was ambiguous, and deletes the requirement that it submit to broad discovery under the Federal Rules while confined to narrower Indian discovery — then affirms as modified. In December 1989 the Supreme Court of India upholds the Act and the government's exclusive authority to compromise every claim; in 1993 the Second Circuit holds that the individual victims have no standing to attack the settlement made on their behalf.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Forum non conveniens as the Supreme Court had lately restated it in Gulf Oil Corp. v. Gilbert (1947) and Piper Aircraft Co. v. Reyno (1981): a plaintiff who is not a resident of the United States gets no deference for choosing a United States court, and the receiving forum need only be adequate rather than equal.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: Sovereign exclusive representation. A host state grants itself, by statute, the sole right to speak for every victim of a disaster on its soil, in its courts or anyone else's. The defendant then settles once, with a government, and that settlement is approved by that government's own highest court and held in New York to bar the people it was made for.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The parent keeps the return on a majority-owned subsidiary, answers in the forum with the lower damages, and is released by a settlement negotiated with a counterparty that is simultaneously the victims' sole representative, a 22 percent owner of the subsidiary and a defendant in the Indian actions. The objectors are told in the United States that they lack standing to question it.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the account turns on one fugitive executive — that Warren Anderson slipped out of India and that a single arrest, or extradition, would have settled it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The closure was structural, not personal. The Bhopal Act of 1985 made the Union of India the only party able to sue or compromise the civil claims, and the Supreme Court of India approved a settlement covering "all litigations, claims, rights and liabilities" arising out of the disaster. A criminal proceeding against any individual would not have reopened the civil claims that settlement discharged, which is why the Second Circuit could tell the victims in 1993 that they had no standing to challenge it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: In re Union Carbide Corp. Gas Plant Disaster at Bhopal, 809 F.2d 195 (2d Cir. 1987), affirming the forum non conveniens dismissal to India after deleting two of the district court's three conditions; the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act of 29 March 1985, granting the Union of India the exclusive right to represent the victims "in India or elsewhere"; the Supreme Court of India's orders of 14-15 February 1989 approving $470 million in settlement of all claims, and its decision of 22 December 1989 in Charan Lal Sahu upholding the Act and that exclusive authority; and Bi v. Union Carbide Chemicals & Plastics Co., 984 F.2d 582 (2d Cir. 1993), holding that the individual victims lacked standing to challenge the settlement.

citations.title: In re Union Carbide Corporation Gas Plant Disaster at Bhopal, India in December, 1984, 809 F.2d 195 (2d Cir. 1987)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full. Argued 24 November 1986, decided 14 January 1987. Opens by framing the appeal as whether claims arising from "the most devastating industrial disaster in history--the deaths of over 2,000 persons and injuries of over 200,000" should be tried in the United States or in India. States that UCIL was 50.9% owned by UCC, 22% owned or controlled by the government of India, with the balance held by about 23,500 Indian citizens, and was "managed and operated entirely by Indians in India". Records that India enacted the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act on 29 March 1985 "granting to its government, the UOI, the exclusive right to represent the victims in India or elsewhere", and that Judge Keenan dismissed on forum non conveniens on 12 May 1986 (634 F. Supp. 842) on three conditions. The court deletes two: the condition that UCC consent to enforcement of a final Indian judgment (held "predicated on an erroneous legal assumption" with ambiguous "due process" language) and the condition that UCC submit to broad discovery under the Federal Rules while confined to narrower Indian discovery. Concludes "As so modified the district court's order is affirmed." A footnote records that of 78,000 pages of documents seized by India's Central Bureau of Investigation some 36,000 are plant operation records, of which 1,700 pages relate to plant maintenance in 1983 and 1984. The opinion does not state a settlement figure — there was none yet — and does not decide any question of liability.

citations.title: Bano Bi v. Union Carbide Chemicals and Plastics Company Inc., 984 F.2d 582 (2d Cir. 1993)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full. Argued 10 November 1992, decided 26 January 1993. Frames the issue as "whether the federal and state courts of this country should defer to the judgment of a democratic foreign government that disputes arising from a mass tort occurring within its borders can be best resolved by according the foreign government exclusive standing to represent the victims of the disaster in the courts of the world", and holds: "We conclude that the plaintiffs lack standing and on that ground affirm." Records that by orders dated 14 and 15 February 1989 the Supreme Court of India approved a settlement of "all litigations, claims, rights and liabilities related to and arising out of the [Bhopal] disaster" (Union Carbide Corp. v. Union of India, 1989 [Supp.] S.C.A.L.E. 89, 90), under which "Union Carbide and UCIL agreed to pay $470 million to the Indian Government for the benefit of all victims"; that on 4 May 1989 that Court set out its reasons, being "concerned primarily that the victims of the disaster receive immediate relief"; and that on 22 December 1989, in Charan Lal Sahu v. Union of India, it "upheld the constitutional validity of the Bhopal Act and confirmed the Indian Government's exclusive authority to compromise all claims arising out of the Bhopal disaster". The appellants' grounds — that the Indian Government had a conflict of interest as part owner of UCIL, that most victims opposed the settlement as grossly inadequate, and that they had inadequate notice, inadequate representation and no opportunity to opt out — are recorded as the appellants' contentions, not as findings of the court. No per-victim distribution figure appears.

citations.title: Bano v. Union Carbide Corporation, 361 F.3d 696 (2d Cir. 2004)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full. Argued 30 October 2003, decided 17 March 2004. Confirms that the claims arising out of the gas release itself had already been dismissed as "barred by a settlement between Union Carbide and the government of India that had been approved by the Supreme Court of India", citing Bano I, 273 F.3d 120, 122 (2d Cir. 2001). The claims at issue here are the separate common-law claims for environmental injury from the plant site: the court affirms except as to Bi's claims for injury to her property, which it vacates and remands. Records that the plant opened in 1969 on two noncontiguous tracts totalling 88 acres leased from the State of Madhya Pradesh, that UCIL began manufacturing on site in 1979 or 1980, and that a UCIL document of March 1982 shows awareness of leakage from one solar evaporation pond with another showing signs of leakage, while an April 1982 UCIL document notes "continued leakage from [an] evaporation pond [was] causing great concern". It also records that a 1990 report by India's National Environmental Engineering Research Institute concluded that "no contamination of soils and ground water was observed due to the impoundment of wastewater in solar evaporation ponds" while recommending remediation — a finding against the plaintiffs on pond contamination, recorded here rather than omitted. This opinion concerns the water claims; it is not authority on the gas-release settlement beyond noting that it barred those claims.

dossiers.title: War Is a Racket: The Profit Cap of 1934 and the Senate Committee That Reported It Unenforceable
participants: Senate Special Committee on Investigation of the Munitions Industry (Nye Committee)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Naval construction is let to private yards on bids the Navy is in no position to price. The evidence before the Senate munitions committee covers 1933 contracts worth $130,000,000 to the private shipbuilders, awarded by a department that takes the low bid and, in the committee's phrase, leaves the taxpayers "to hope and pray that the low one is somewhere within a few million dollars of being reasonable and proper".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The one instrument that could have priced the work is left unused. The committee finds that the Navy's failure "to turn the navy yards into effective yardsticks by which the charges of private shipyards could be measured and kept down has resulted in leaving the profits of the shipbuilders practically uncontrolled". The government yard that would have shown what a destroyer costs is not made to do it.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The buyer cannot see the price.
