Investors relied on them, often blindly. In some cases, they were obligated to use them, or regulatory capital standards were hinged on them ... This crisis could not have happened without the rating agencies." Its conclusion on them is that their failures "were essential cogs in the wheel of financial destruction".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: What the arrangement bought was regulatory room, and the Commission names who gave it: "the Federal Reserve neglected its mission ‘to ensure the safety and soundness of the nation’s banking and financial system and to protect the credit rights of consumers.’ It failed to build the retaining wall before it was too late. And the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Office of Thrift Supervision, caught up in turf wars, preempted state regulators from reining in abuses." The preemption is the windfall: it removed the one layer of supervision that was trying to act.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The Commission refuses the exculpatory account in its first conclusion — "We conclude this financial crisis was avoidable ... Theirs was a big miss, not a stumble" — and refuses the claim that nobody could have seen it: "Despite the expressed view of many on Wall Street and in Washington that the crisis could not have been foreseen or avoided, there were warning signs." But it was a divided body. Its report carries dissenting views by Keith Hennessey, Douglas Holtz-Eakin and Bill Thomas, and a separate dissent by Peter J. Wallison; the conclusions above are the majority’s. It determined no liability and brought no proceedings.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Originate-to-distribute mortgage finance, nationally chartered lenders able to preempt state consumer-protection enforcement, and capital rules that deferred to private credit ratings.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-crisis supervisory architecture — a consolidated consumer regulator, the abolition of the Office of Thrift Supervision, and rating-agency provisions — built on the Commission’s diagnosis but not on any finding of liability.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Loose underwriting produced volume; volume produced securities; ratings made the securities saleable and capital rules made them attractive to hold; demand for securities fed back as demand for loans, which pushed underwriting looser still. The supervisor that might have interrupted it had preempted the supervisors who were trying.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the crisis was a hundred-year storm nobody could have predicted — or, from the other direction, that it was a single conspiracy run from a few desks in New York.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Commission’s first conclusion rejects the storm: "We conclude this financial crisis was avoidable. The crisis was the result of human action and inaction, not of Mother Nature or computer models gone haywire ... Theirs was a big miss, not a stumble." And it rejects the idea that the signals were absent: "These trends were not secret." But its own account is not a conspiracy either; it is a list of systems failing in parallel — regulation, corporate governance, leverage, ethics, origination, derivatives, ratings — each with its own conclusion. The dossier should also carry what the report itself carries: the Commission split, and two sets of dissenting commissioners rejected the majority’s framing. A reader who takes "avoidable" as a settled national verdict is quoting a majority, not a unanimity.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A congressionally chartered commission concluding that the crisis was avoidable and that the warning signs existed. That collapsing mortgage-lending standards and the securitization pipeline "lit and spread the flame of contagion and crisis", with lenders taking borrowers’ qualifications "on faith, often with a willful disregard for a borrower’s ability to pay". That the Federal Reserve "neglected its mission" and "failed to build the retaining wall", and that the OCC and OTS, "caught up in turf wars, preempted state regulators from reining in abuses". That the rating agencies’ failures were "essential cogs in the wheel of financial destruction" and that the crisis "could not have happened without" them. And that the Commission reached these conclusions over the dissent of Hennessey, Holtz-Eakin and Thomas, and of Wallison separately.

citations.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, The Financial Crisis Inquiry Report: Final Report of the National Commission on the Causes of the Financial and Economic Crisis in the United States (January 2011)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. A TEXT CAUTION: the extraction drops numerals in a number of sentences in the conclusions (for example "nearly , mortgage-related securities"), so no figure is quoted from this document here and only sentences that survive extraction intact are reproduced. THE COMMISSION’S CONCLUSIONS, in its own enumerated form: "We conclude this financial crisis was avoidable. The crisis was the result of human action and inaction, not of Mother Nature or computer models gone haywire. The captains of finance and the public stewards of our financial system ignored warnings and failed to question, understand, and manage evolving risks within a system essential to the well-being of the American public. Theirs was a big miss, not a stumble. While the business cycle cannot be repealed, a crisis of this magnitude need not have occurred." It adds: "Despite the expressed view of many on Wall Street and in Washington that the crisis could not have been foreseen or avoided, there were warning signs." Further conclusions, each stated in the same form: "We conclude widespread failures in financial regulation and supervision"; "We conclude dramatic failures of corporate governance and risk management"; "We conclude a combination of excessive borrowing, risky investments, and lack" of transparency; "We conclude the government was ill prepared for the crisis, and its inconsistent" response added to uncertainty; "We conclude there was a systemic breakdown in accountability and ethics"; "We conclude collapsing mortgage-lending standards and the mortgage securitization pipeline lit and spread the flame of contagion and crisis"; "We conclude over-the-counter derivatives contributed significantly to this" crisis; and "We conclude the failures of credit rating agencies were essential cogs in the wheel of financial destruction." On origination: "Many mortgage lenders set the bar so low that lenders simply took eager borrowers’ qualifications on faith, often with a willful disregard for a borrower’s ability to pay." On whether this was visible at the time: "These trends were not secret. As irresponsible lending, including predatory and fraudulent practices, became more prevalent, the Federal Reserve and other regulators and authorities heard warnings from many quarters. Yet the Federal Reserve neglected its mission ‘to ensure the safety and soundness of the nation’s banking and financial system and to protect the credit rights of consumers.’ It failed to build the retaining wall before it was too late. And the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Office of Thrift Supervision, caught up in turf wars, preempted state regulators from reining in abuses." On ratings: "The mortgage-related securities at the heart of the crisis could not have been marketed and sold without their seal of approval ... This crisis could not have happened without the rating agencies." THE COMMISSION WAS DIVIDED, and the report says so on its own contents page: it carries DISSENTING VIEWS "By Keith Hennessey, Douglas Holtz-Eakin, and Bill Thomas" and, separately, "By Peter J. Wallison". The conclusions above are the majority’s. The Commission determined no liability and brought no proceedings.

crash-conduits.title: Six Complaints, Five Examinations, One Phone Call Never Made: the SEC’s Own Report on Missing Madoff
participants: Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities LLC
SEC Office of Compliance Inspections and Examinations

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was the fiction of a trade. The scheme required only that statements be produced; the OIG establishes the gap between the paper and the holdings with a single comparison it ran itself — one feeder-fund statement claiming "approximately $2.5 billion of S&P 100 equities as of January 31, 2005" against DTC records showing Madoff held "less than $18 million worth of S&P 100 equities in his DTC account" on that date.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What was compromised was the examination function, repeatedly and on the record. "Despite three examinations and two investigations being conducted, a thorough and competent investigation or examination was never performed." The information to trigger a real one was not lacking: "the SEC received more than ample information in the form of detailed and substantive complaints over the years", six of them between June 1992 and December 2008, each raising "significant red flags concerning Madoff’s hedge fund operations".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was not that nobody could see; it was that nobody checked. The OIG names the omission exactly: "This was perhaps the most egregious failure in the Enforcement investigation of Madoff; that they never verified Madoff’s purported trading with any independent third parties." A senior SEC examiner is quoted on why that mattered: someone running a Ponzi "is not going to hesitate to lie or create records", so the "only way to verify" is "independent third-party verification" like DTC.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was continuation. Madoff’s own account, recorded by the OIG, is of a man who believed the scheme was finished and found that it was not: he "thought he was caught after his testimony about the DTC account", and said of the moment he gave the account number, "I thought it was the end game, over. Monday morning they'll call DTC and this will be over . . . and it never happened." He "was astonished" when Enforcement did not follow up.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment here is the one that did not happen, and that is why the dossier exists. The SEC’s own Inspector General investigated the agency and published a public version naming the failures in its own words. It is an internal review with the limits of one: it examines the conduct of a regulator, makes no finding about any investor’s losses, and determines no liability.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A disclosure-and-examination regime in which a registered broker-dealer’s own books are the first and often the only evidence of what it holds.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-Madoff examination reforms and the custody-rule tightening that followed — and this report itself, an agency publishing a forensic account of its own failure.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Each examination that closed without independent verification became part of the record that the firm had been examined; the fact of having been examined reassured the next complainant’s audience; and the complaints kept arriving at an agency that had, in its own words, never performed a competent one.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the SEC was bought: that Madoff’s family connection inside the agency — his niece’s relationship with an SEC assistant director — is why five separate encounters with the regulator produced nothing.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The SEC’s own Inspector General investigated precisely that theory and rejected it on the evidence. It "did not find evidence that any SEC personnel who worked on an SEC examination or investigation of" the firm "had any financial or other inappropriate connection with Bernard Madoff or the Madoff family that influenced the conduct of their examination or investigatory work"; it "did not find that former SEC Assistant Director Eric Swanson’s romantic relationship with Bernard Madoff’s niece, Shana Madoff, influenced the conduct of the SEC examinations", finding that the relationship "did not begin until March of 2006, nearly a year after the OCIE examination he had conducted had been completed in June of 2005"; and it found no evidence of senior officials attempting to influence or interfering with the staff’s work. The documented failure is worse than the rumour in one specific way: corruption would at least imply someone understood what they were covering up. What the OIG describes is an agency that had the account number and never rang the custodian.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Six substantive complaints to the SEC between June 1992 and December 2008, each raising significant red flags, plus two articles in reputable publications in 2001 questioning the returns. Three examinations and two investigations, and "a thorough and competent investigation or examination was never performed". No independent third-party verification of the trading at any point, which the OIG calls perhaps the most egregious failure of the Enforcement investigation. A feeder-fund statement claiming about $2.5 billion in S&P 100 equities on 31 January 2005 against DTC records showing under $18 million held that day. And Madoff’s own statement that he expected the DTC call to end it, and was astonished when it never came.

citations.title: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Office of Investigations, Investigation of Failure of the SEC to Uncover Bernard Madoff’s Ponzi Scheme — Report of Investigation, Case No. OIG-509, Public Version, 31 August 2009
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from sec.gov and read as extracted text. (sec.gov returns 403 to a generic browser user-agent; it serves the file to a request that declares an identity and contact address, which is what the agency asks for.) WHAT THE OIG LOOKED FOR AND DID NOT FIND, from the Executive Summary: "The OIG investigation did not find evidence that any SEC personnel who worked on an SEC examination or investigation of Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities, LLC (BMIS) had any financial or other inappropriate connection with Bernard Madoff or the Madoff family that influenced the conduct of their examination or investigatory work. The OIG also did not find that former SEC Assistant Director Eric Swanson’s romantic relationship with Bernard Madoff’s niece, Shana Madoff, influenced the conduct of the SEC examinations of Madoff and his firm. We also did not find that senior officials at the SEC directly attempted to influence examinations or investigations of Madoff or the Madoff firm, nor was there evidence any senior SEC official interfered with the staff’s ability to perform its work." On the relationship specifically, it found the romance "did not begin until March of 2006, nearly a year after the OCIE examination he had conducted had been completed in June of 2005", and "no evidence that Swanson shared information regarding SEC examinations or investigations of Madoff with Shana while Swanson was at the SEC." WHAT IT DID FIND, in the same summary: "The OIG investigation did find, however, that the SEC received more than ample information in the form of detailed and substantive complaints over the years to warrant a thorough and comprehensive examination and/or investigation of Bernard Madoff and BMIS for operating a Ponzi scheme, and that despite three examinations and two investigations being conducted, a thorough and competent investigation or examination was never performed. The OIG found that between June 1992 and December 2008 when Madoff confessed, the SEC received six substantive complaints that raised significant red flags concerning Madoff’s hedge fund operations and should have led to questions about whether Madoff was actually engaged in trading." THE SINGLE MOST DAMNING PASSAGE, on verification: "This was perhaps the most egregious failure in the Enforcement investigation of Madoff; that they never verified Madoff’s purported trading with any independent third parties." The OIG made the check itself: "We reviewed a January 2005 statement for one Madoff feeder fund account, which alone indicated that it held approximately $2.5 billion of S&P 100 equities as of January 31, 2005. On the contrary, on January 31, 2005, DTC records show that Madoff held less than $18 million worth of S&P 100 equities in his DTC account." And Madoff’s own account of the moment: he "stated that he had thought he was caught after his testimony about the DTC account, noting that when they asked for the DTC account number, 'I thought it was the end game, over. Monday morning they'll call DTC and this will be over . . . and it never happened'", and that when Enforcement did not follow up he "was astonished". This is an inspector-general report on the conduct of a regulator. It makes no finding about any investor’s losses and determines no liability.

crash-conduits.title: Knowingly Allowed: Six Findings Against a Board That Witnessed and Chose to Ignore

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was taken at the top and the Subcommittee counts it as its own finding: the Board "approved excessive compensation for company executives, failed to monitor the cumulative cash drain caused by Enron’s 2000 annual bonus and performance unit plans, and failed to monitor or halt abuse by Board Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Kenneth Lay of a company-financed, multi-million dollar, personal credit line."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What was compromised was the balance sheet, with the Board’s knowledge. Finding (4): the Board "knowingly allowed Enron to conduct billions of dollars in off-the-books activity to make its financial condition appear better than it was and failed to ensure adequate public disclosure of material off-the-books liabilities that contributed to Enron’s collapse." Finding (2) is one sentence long and does the same work: the Board "knowingly allowed Enron to engage in high risk accounting practices."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was aimed outward while the Board could see in. The Subcommittee’s first finding records that "The Board witnessed numerous indications of questionable practices by Enron management over several years, but chose to ignore them to the detriment of Enron shareholders, employees and business associates." The public disclosure that would have shown the liabilities was, on finding (4), not made.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall ran through a vehicle the Board itself authorised. Finding (3): "Despite clear conflicts of interest, the Enron Board of Directors approved an unprecedented arrangement allowing Enron’s Chief Financial Officer to establish and operate the LJM private equity funds which transacted business with Enron and profited at Enron’s expense. The Board exercised inadequate oversight of LJM transaction and compensation controls and failed to protect Enron shareholders from unfair dealing."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The check that should have been independent was not. Finding (6): "The independence of the Enron Board of Directors was compromised by financial ties between the company and certain Board members." The Subcommittee reached its findings on "over one million pages of subpoenaed documents, interviews of 13 Enron Board members, and the Subcommittee hearing on May 7, 2002" — and it is a congressional report, which determines no liability and adjudicates nothing against any individual director.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A board model in which the audit and compensation committees rely on management’s own presentation of the numbers, and in which directors may hold financial relationships with the company they oversee.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-Enron governance regime — audit committee independence requirements, certification of financial statements, and restrictions on auditor conflicts — built directly on findings of this kind.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The off-books structures improved the reported condition; the improved condition supported the compensation the Board approved; the Board that approved it was, on the Subcommittee’s finding, compromised by financial ties to the company whose numbers it was signing off.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Enron was a handful of rogue executives running a scheme nobody upstairs understood — a conjuring trick too clever for its own directors to see.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Senate Subcommittee found the opposite, twice, in the same word. The Board "knowingly allowed Enron to engage in high risk accounting practices", and "knowingly allowed Enron to conduct billions of dollars in off-the-books activity to make its financial condition appear better than it was". It also found that the Board "witnessed numerous indications of questionable practices by Enron management over several years, but chose to ignore them", and that it approved — "Despite clear conflicts of interest" — the arrangement under which the chief financial officer ran private funds that "transacted business with Enron and profited at Enron’s expense". What should not be drawn from this document is any individual’s liability: it is a congressional subcommittee report, not an adjudication, and it determines none.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Six findings of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, reached on over one million pages of subpoenaed documents and interviews with 13 directors: fiduciary failure; high risk accounting knowingly allowed; inappropriate conflicts of interest in the LJM arrangement approved despite clear conflicts; extensive undisclosed off-the-books activity knowingly allowed, with inadequate public disclosure of material off-the-books liabilities; excessive compensation, including a failure to monitor or halt abuse of a company-financed multi-million dollar personal credit line by the chairman and chief executive; and a board whose independence was compromised by financial ties between the company and certain of its members.

citations.title: U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Committee on Governmental Affairs, The Role of the Board of Directors in Enron’s Collapse, S. Prt. 107-70, 8 July 2002
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. The report states its own evidentiary basis: "Based upon the evidence before it, including over one million pages of subpoenaed documents, interviews of 13 Enron Board members, and the Subcommittee hearing on May 7, 2002", it makes six numbered findings, reproduced here in its own words. "(1) Fiduciary Failure. The Enron Board of Directors failed to safeguard Enron shareholders and contributed to the collapse of the seventh largest public company in the United States, by allowing Enron to engage in high risk accounting, inappropriate conflict of interest transactions, extensive undisclosed off-the-books activities, and excessive executive compensation. The Board witnessed numerous indications of questionable practices by Enron management over several years, but chose to ignore them to the detriment of Enron shareholders, employees and business associates." "(2) High Risk Accounting. The Enron Board of Directors knowingly allowed Enron to engage in high risk accounting practices." "(3) Inappropriate Conflicts of Interest. Despite clear conflicts of interest, the Enron Board of Directors approved an unprecedented arrangement allowing Enron’s Chief Financial Officer to establish and operate the LJM private equity funds which transacted business with Enron and profited at Enron’s expense. The Board exercised inadequate oversight of LJM transaction and compensation controls and failed to protect Enron shareholders from unfair dealing." "(4) Extensive Undisclosed Off-The-Books Activity. The Enron Board of Directors knowingly allowed Enron to conduct billions of dollars in off-the-books activity to make its financial condition appear better than it was and failed to ensure adequate public disclosure of material off-the-books liabilities that contributed to Enron’s collapse." "(5) Excessive Compensation. The Enron Board of Directors approved excessive compensation for company executives, failed to monitor the cumulative cash drain caused by Enron’s 2000 annual bonus and performance unit plans, and failed to monitor or halt abuse by Board Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Kenneth Lay of a company-financed, multi-million dollar, personal credit line." "(6) Lack of Independence. The independence of the Enron Board of Directors was compromised by financial ties between the company and certain Board members." The phrase "knowingly allowed" is the report's own, used in findings (2) and (4). This is a congressional subcommittee report about the conduct of a board. It determines no liability, and it is not a criminal or civil adjudication of any individual director.

crash-conduits.title: Never Deployed, $100,000 Earned: What the SEC Alleged, and What Was Neither Admitted Nor Denied
participants: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, San Francisco Regional Office

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The raise is the number that matters and the Commission states it plainly: the charge concerns "raising more than $700 million from investors through an elaborate, years-long fraud in which they exaggerated or made false statements about the company’s technology, business, and financial performance." Against that, the operating business the same year the company was said to be approaching nine figures of revenue: "a little more than $100,000 in revenue from operations in 2014".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What was compromised, on the Commission’s allegation, was the product claim itself. The complaints allege investors were deceived "into believing that its key product – a portable blood analyzer – could conduct comprehensive blood tests from finger drops of blood", whereas "Theranos’ proprietary analyzer could complete only a small number of tests, and the company conducted the vast majority of patient tests on modified and industry-standard commercial analyzers manufactured by others."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was manufactured in the places investors look: the Commission alleges "numerous false and misleading statements in investor presentations, product demonstrations, and media articles". The media article is listed alongside the investor deck as an instrument of the alleged fraud, which is the detail most worth carrying out of this document.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall sought was credibility by association with the state, and it is the allegation that bears directly on this node’s old framing. The complaints charge that the defendants "claimed that Theranos’ products were deployed by the U.S. Department of Defense on the battlefield in Afghanistan and on medevac helicopters" — and that "In truth, Theranos’ technology was never deployed by the U.S. Department of Defense."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The resolution was a settlement, and its terms are the only part of this that is more than allegation: a $500,000 penalty, a ten-year bar from serving as an officer or director of a public company, the return of 18.9 million shares, and the conversion of super-majority Class B shares to Class A, surrendering voting control — all "subject to court approval". And the sentence that governs how this dossier reads everything above it: "Theranos and Holmes neither admitted nor denied the allegations in the SEC’s complaint."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Private-company capital raising, where the disclosure obligations that bind public issuers do not apply and the investor’s information comes from the founder’s own presentation.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Commission’s own stated principle in this matter: "there is no exemption from the anti-fraud provisions of the federal securities laws simply because a company is non-public, development-stage, or the subject of exuberant media attention."
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The claimed deployment lent the technology credibility; the credibility supported the valuation; the valuation attracted the coverage; and the coverage, on the Commission’s allegation, became one of the instruments by which investors were deceived.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Theranos was shielded by its board of generals, cabinet secretaries and statesmen — that national-security connections kept regulators off a company everyone inside knew was empty.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: No document read for this dossier supports a shield. What the record shows is the opposite relationship with the state: the Commission alleges that the Department of Defense connection was itself one of the false claims — that the defendants "claimed that Theranos’ products were deployed by the U.S. Department of Defense on the battlefield in Afghanistan and on medevac helicopters" when "In truth, Theranos’ technology was never deployed by the U.S. Department of Defense." And the company was charged by a federal regulator, which obtained a penalty, a ten-year officer-and-director bar and the surrender of voting control. The dossier’s former title asserted a shield; the document asserts a fabricated endorsement. Equally, nothing here should be read as proof of what happened: "Theranos and Holmes neither admitted nor denied the allegations in the SEC’s complaint", and the criminal proceedings that followed were not sourced for this dossier, so no verdict or sentence is asserted in it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: An SEC charge, in March 2018, concerning the raising of more than $700 million through what the Commission called an elaborate, years-long fraud. Allegations that the portable analyser could complete only a small number of tests while most patient testing ran on modified commercial analysers made by others; that false and misleading statements were made in investor presentations, product demonstrations and media articles; and that claims of Department of Defense battlefield deployment were untrue, against operating revenue in 2014 of a little more than $100,000. A settlement by Theranos and Holmes comprising a $500,000 penalty, a ten-year public-company officer and director bar, the return of 18.9 million shares and the surrender of voting control, subject to court approval — entered while neither admitting nor denying the allegations. And separate claims against Balwani that the Commission said it would litigate in the Northern District of California.

citations.title: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, "Theranos, CEO Holmes, and Former President Balwani Charged With Massive Fraud", Press Release 2018-41, 14 March 2018
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from sec.gov. (sec.gov serves the page to a request declaring an identity and contact address; a generic browser user-agent is refused, which is why automated link checks report sec.gov URLs as blocked.) THE CHARGE, as the Commission describes it: the SEC "charged Silicon Valley-based private company Theranos Inc., its founder and CEO Elizabeth Holmes, and its former President Ramesh 'Sunny' Balwani with raising more than $700 million from investors through an elaborate, years-long fraud in which they exaggerated or made false statements about the company's technology, business, and financial performance." THE SPECIFIC ALLEGATIONS: "The complaints allege that Theranos, Holmes, and Balwani made numerous false and misleading statements in investor presentations, product demonstrations, and media articles by which they deceived investors into believing that its key product – a portable blood analyzer – could conduct comprehensive blood tests from finger drops of blood, revolutionizing the blood testing industry. In truth, according to the SEC's complaint, Theranos' proprietary analyzer could complete only a small number of tests, and the company conducted the vast majority of patient tests on modified and industry-standard commercial analyzers manufactured by others." And, on the claim most relevant to any national-security framing of this company: "The complaints further charge that Theranos, Holmes, and Balwani claimed that Theranos' products were deployed by the U.S. Department of Defense on the battlefield in Afghanistan and on medevac helicopters and that the company would generate more than $100 million in revenue in 2014. In truth, Theranos' technology was never deployed by the U.S. Department of Defense and generated a little more than $100,000 in revenue from operations in 2014." THE RESOLUTION: "Holmes agreed to pay a $500,000 penalty, be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for 10 years, return the remaining 18.9 million shares that she obtained during the fraud, and relinquish her voting control of Theranos by converting her super-majority Theranos Class B Common shares to Class A Common shares", with the settlements "subject to court approval". CRUCIALLY, AND THE REASON THIS DOSSIER TREATS THE ABOVE AS ALLEGATION RATHER THAN FINDING: "Theranos and Holmes neither admitted nor denied the allegations in the SEC's complaint." The release records that the Commission "will litigate its claims against Balwani in federal district court in the Northern District of California". The criminal proceedings that followed in the Northern District of California were NOT sourced here: no Department of Justice document was read for this dossier, because the justice.gov pages for them return a not-found page, and nothing about any criminal verdict or sentence is asserted anywhere in it.

crash-conduits.title: A Virtually Unlimited Line of Credit, Funded by the Customers: What the SEC Alleged About FTX and Alameda

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The equity raise is the figure the Commission puts first: more than $1.8 billion from investors "who bought an equity stake in FTX believing that FTX had appropriate controls and risk management measures". The customer float is the larger pool, and the complaint alleges it was moving out from the beginning: "from the start, Bankman-Fried improperly diverted customer assets to his privately-held crypto hedge fund".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise alleged is an exemption written into the platform itself. Investors were told "that FTX had top-notch, sophisticated automated risk measures in place to protect customer assets, that those assets were safe and secure, and that Alameda was just another platform customer with no special privileges." The complaint alleges the opposite was true: Alameda was exempted from the risk mitigation measures and given "significant special treatment on the FTX platform, including a virtually unlimited 'line of credit' funded by the platform's customers."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was a public persona maintained while the diversion ran. "Throughout this period, Bankman-Fried portrayed himself as a responsible leader of the crypto community. He touted the importance of regulation and accountability. He told the public, including investors, that FTX was both innovative and responsible." The complaint alleges the customer funds went to "undisclosed venture investments, lavish real estate purchases, and large political donations" — the undisclosed venture book and the political giving both being, in effect, reputational spend financed from the float.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was time. When crypto prices fell in May 2022 and Alameda's lenders called their loans, the complaint alleges Bankman-Fried "directed FTX to divert billions more in customer assets to Alameda to ensure that Alameda maintained its lending relationships, and that money could continue to flow in from lenders and other investors." Through that summer he is alleged to have directed hundreds of millions more, used for further venture investments and for "loans" to himself and other executives.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: There is no commission and no liability shield in this one; it ended in a filing. FTX, Alameda "and their tangled web of affiliated entities filed for bankruptcy on November 11, 2022", and the Commission sued a month later, charging violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5. A complaint is an accusation: this dossier records it as one.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: An offshore crypto exchange holding customer assets in commingled form, with an affiliated proprietary trading firm on the other side of the platform and no regulator examining either.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-FTX enforcement posture and custody debate; and, as precedent, the Commission's use of the ordinary anti-fraud provisions — Section 17(a), Section 10(b), Rule 10b-5 — against the operator of a crypto platform.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Customer deposits funded the affiliate's positions; the affiliate's apparent strength supported the platform's reputation; the reputation attracted the next round of deposits and the next equity raise, which were needed because the earlier deposits were no longer there.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That FTX was a sound exchange brought down by a bank run — bad luck, a liquidity crunch, a crypto winter — or alternatively that the whole thing was obvious to anyone paying attention and the investors were simply greedy.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The run account is not what the Commission alleges. Its complaint puts the diversion of customer assets "from the start", years before November 2022, and describes the May 2022 price fall as the moment an existing hole became unservable rather than its cause. The blame-the-investors account fails on the complaint's own description of what they were told: that FTX had "top-notch, sophisticated automated risk measures", that customer assets were "safe and secure", and that Alameda was "just another platform customer with no special privileges" — statements the Commission alleges were false, concealing an exemption from the risk engine and a virtually unlimited line of credit funded by customers. What this dossier does not do is treat any of that as established: it is a civil complaint, and the criminal case that followed was not sourced here, so no verdict is asserted.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A complaint filed by the Securities and Exchange Commission in the Southern District of New York on 13 December 2022, alleging a scheme running from at least May 2019 to November 2022; more than $1.8 billion raised from equity investors; customer assets diverted to Alameda Research from the start and used for undisclosed venture investments, real estate and political donations; Alameda exempted from the platform's risk measures and given a virtually unlimited line of credit funded by customers; billions more diverted after May 2022 to keep Alameda's lenders in place; and charges under Section 17(a) of the Securities Act and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 of the Exchange Act. The bankruptcy filing of 11 November 2022 is recorded in the same document. Everything else about this matter — including anything decided in a courtroom afterwards — is outside what was read for this dossier.

citations.title: Securities and Exchange Commission v. Samuel Bankman-Fried, Complaint, No. 1:22-cv-10501 (S.D.N.Y., filed 13 December 2022)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from sec.gov and read as extracted text. (sec.gov refuses a generic browser user-agent and serves the file to a request declaring an identity and contact address, so automated link checks report sec.gov URLs as blocked.) EVERYTHING BELOW IS AN ALLEGATION IN A CIVIL COMPLAINT, NOT A FINDING. The Summary alleges: "From at least May 2019 through November 2022, Bankman-Fried engaged in a scheme to defraud equity investors in FTX Trading Ltd. ('FTX'), the crypto asset trading platform of which he was CEO and co-founder, at the same time that he was also defrauding the platform's customers. Bankman-Fried raised more than $1.8 billion from investors, including U.S. investors, who bought an equity stake in FTX believing that FTX had appropriate controls and risk management measures. Unbeknownst to those investors (and to FTX's trading customers), Bankman-Fried was orchestrating a massive, years-long fraud, diverting billions of dollars of the trading platform's customer funds for his own personal benefit and to help grow his crypto empire." On the public posture: "Throughout this period, Bankman-Fried portrayed himself as a responsible leader of the crypto community. He touted the importance of regulation and accountability." On the mechanism alleged: "from the start, Bankman-Fried improperly diverted customer assets to his privately-held crypto hedge fund, Alameda Research LLC ('Alameda'), and then used those customer funds to make undisclosed venture investments, lavish real estate purchases, and large political donations." On what investors were told: "He told investors and prospective investors that FTX had top-notch, sophisticated automated risk measures in place to protect customer assets, that those assets were safe and secure, and that Alameda was just another platform customer with no special privileges. These statements were false and misleading. In truth, Bankman-Fried had exempted Alameda from the risk mitigation measures and had provided Alameda with significant special treatment on the FTX platform, including a virtually unlimited 'line of credit' funded by the platform's customers." On the collapse: when crypto prices fell in May 2022 and Alameda's lenders demanded repayment, "Bankman-Fried directed FTX to divert billions more in customer assets to Alameda"; through the summer of 2022 he "directed hundreds of millions more in FTX customer funds to Alameda, which he then used for additional venture investments and for 'loans' to himself and other FTX executives"; and the scheme ended when "FTX, Alameda, and their tangled web of affiliated entities filed for bankruptcy on November 11, 2022." The complaint charges violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5. The criminal proceedings in the Southern District of New York were NOT sourced for this dossier — justice.gov serves a not-found page for the press releases and nothing from it was read — so no verdict or sentence is asserted anywhere in it.

crash-conduits.title: $4 Billion to $36 Billion in Six Months: Swaps, "Marking the Close", and Counterparties Who Had Started Asking
participants: Prime brokers and security-based swap counterparties
Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The growth figure is the Commission's headline and it is the whole shape of the case: the scheme alleged "increased Archegos's assets under management from around $4 billion to over $36 billion in just under six months", achieved "largely through the entry into SBSs with about a dozen Counterparties".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What the instrument did was hold the exposure off anyone's view but the counterparty's. Security-based swaps gave Archegos "significant exposure to rising and falling share prices of the issuers referenced in its SBSs" without the firm appearing as the holder, and with about a dozen counterparties each seeing only their own slice of a book none of them saw whole.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is alleged to have been deliberate and specific. Archegos "knowingly provided these Counterparties with false assurances concerning its portfolio composition, its concentrated exposure, and its liquidity profile", which "fraudulently convinced its Counterparties that Archegos's overall positioning was less concentrated and more liquid than it actually was". The point of the deception was capacity: it "induced Archegos's Counterparties to continue to transact with it and extend leverage beyond what the Counterparties' risk tolerance would have otherwise permitted had they known the truth".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was a price the firm set for itself. The Commission alleges Archegos "chose not to rely on ordinary market forces" and instead manipulated the market in its top ten holdings "by dominating the market" for them, by "setting the tone" with large pre-market trading, "by bidding up prices by entering incrementally higher limit orders throughout the trading day", and by "marking the close" with large trading in the final thirty minutes — "all with the goal of artificially inflating the share prices of its Top 10 Holdings". The inflated marks then supported the margin that funded the next round.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment came two years later, and it fell on the bank rather than the fund. On 24 July 2023 the Federal Reserve announced a consent order and a $268.5 million fine with UBS for misconduct by Credit Suisse, finding "unsafe and unsound counterparty credit risk management practices" and stating that "During Credit Suisse’s relationship with Archegos, Credit Suisse failed to adequately manage the risk posed by Archegos despite repeated warnings." FINMA, acting the same day, "found that Credit Suisse had seriously and systematically violated financial market law in the context of its business relationship with the Archegos family office", ordered corrective measures from UBS as legal successor, and opened proceedings against a former Credit Suisse manager. The Federal Reserve and Prudential Regulation Authority penalties totalled approximately $387 million — against a Credit Suisse loss the Board puts at approximately $5.5 billion.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Security-based swaps as a route to equity exposure that does not appear in the holder's own disclosure, and prime brokerage relationships in which each counterparty prices the risk of a client whose total book it cannot see.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-Archegos tightening of security-based swap position reporting and of prime-broker counterparty risk practice, and a set of concluded enforcement actions — a Federal Reserve consent order, a FINMA finding, a Prudential Regulation Authority penalty — directed at the counterparties’ risk management rather than at the fund.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Margin extended by the counterparties funded the trading that inflated the prices; the inflated prices raised the value of the collateral; the richer collateral justified more margin. The loop ran until a price it did not set moved against it.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Archegos was a freak event — one secretive family office that fooled a dozen of the most sophisticated banks in the world, who were its victims.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The complaint does allege deception of the counterparties, and that half stands. But the banks-as-victims reading does not survive the regulators. The Federal Reserve’s July 2023 consent order found Credit Suisse’s counterparty credit risk management "unsafe and unsound" and stated that it "failed to adequately manage the risk posed by Archegos despite repeated warnings" — "despite repeated warnings" being the Board’s phrase, not an inference drawn here. FINMA found that in the same relationship Credit Suisse had "seriously and systematically violated financial market law". The SEC’s own complaint says the deception worked "despite varying degrees and quality of risk management and proactive questioning of Archegos by its Counterparties", and that "certain of Archegos’s Counterparties already had begun asking Archegos questions to evaluate its risk profile" before the relevant period began. Nor was the fund merely secretive: it is alleged to have been setting the prices of its own collateral by pre-market trading, incremental limit orders and marking the close. What remains allegation is what the SEC alleges against the individuals; the findings against the bank are concluded regulatory actions. The dossier keeps the two apart.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: An SEC complaint filed in the Southern District of New York on 27 April 2022 alleging that between March 2020 and March 2021 Archegos grew from around $4 billion to over $36 billion in assets under management — the Commission’s press release putting it as "approximately $1.5 billion with $10 billion in exposure in March 2020 to a value of more than $36 billion with $160 billion in exposure at its peak" — largely through security-based swaps with about a dozen counterparties; that it manipulated the market in its top ten holdings by dominating trading, setting the tone pre-market, entering incrementally higher limit orders and marking the close; and that it gave counterparties false assurances about exposure, concentration and liquidity to obtain trading capacity. Those are allegations. What is concluded, by consent and by finding: the Federal Reserve’s $268.5 million fine on UBS for Credit Suisse’s "unsafe and unsound counterparty credit risk management practices", its statement that Credit Suisse "failed to adequately manage the risk posed by Archegos despite repeated warnings", and approximately $5.5 billion of Credit Suisse losses from the default; FINMA’s finding that Credit Suisse "seriously and systematically violated financial market law" in the relationship, with corrective measures ordered against UBS and proceedings opened against a former manager; and combined Federal Reserve and Prudential Regulation Authority penalties of approximately $387 million.

citations.title: Securities and Exchange Commission v. Sung Kook (Bill) Hwang, Patrick Halligan, William Tomita and Scott Becker, Complaint, No. 1:22-cv-03402 (S.D.N.Y., filed 27 April 2022)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from sec.gov and read as extracted text. EVERYTHING BELOW IS AN ALLEGATION IN A CIVIL COMPLAINT, NOT A FINDING. The Summary alleges "a fraudulent scheme by Defendants that included interlocking deceptive acts and misconduct, through false and misleading statements to security-based swap ('SBS') counterparties and prime brokers (collectively, 'Counterparties') and manipulative trading designed to artificially move the market, which, in tandem, increased Archegos's assets under management from around $4 billion to over $36 billion in just under six months." On the instrument: "From March 2020 until its collapse in March 2021, Archegos, at Hwang's direction, underwent a period of rapid and exponential growth, achieved largely through the entry into SBSs with about a dozen Counterparties, which subjected Archegos to significant exposure to rising and falling share prices of the issuers referenced in its SBSs." On the alleged manipulation: Archegos "engaged in a brazen scheme to manipulate the market for the securities of the issuers that represented Archegos's top 10 holdings", "effected this scheme by dominating the market for its Top 10 Holdings, as well as by 'setting the tone' (i.e., engaging in large pre-market trading), bidding up prices by entering incrementally higher limit orders throughout the trading day, and 'marking the close' (i.e., engaging in large trading in the last 30 minutes of the trading day) and by other non-economic trading, all with the goal of artificially inflating the share prices of its Top 10 Holdings." On the fuel: "The margin and capacity extended by Archegos's Counterparties served as the fuel for its manipulative trading", and the defendants are alleged to have "deliberately misled many of Archegos's Counterparties" with "false assurances concerning its portfolio composition, its concentrated exposure, and its liquidity profile", which "induced Archegos's Counterparties to continue to transact with it and extend leverage beyond what the Counterparties' risk tolerance would have otherwise permitted had they known the truth". A DETAIL THAT CUTS AGAINST THE BANKS-AS-VICTIMS READING, in the complaint's own words: "as of the beginning of the Relevant Period, certain of Archegos's Counterparties already had begun asking Archegos questions to evaluate its risk profile", and the deception succeeded "despite varying degrees and quality of risk management and proactive questioning of Archegos by its Counterparties". On the collapse: over "less than a week in late March 2021, the house of cards collapsed", and the default "resulted in billions of dollars in credit losses among its Counterparties and significant losses to the market participants who invested in the stocks at inflated prices." The criminal proceedings that followed were NOT sourced for this dossier and no verdict or sentence is asserted in it.

citations.title: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, "SEC Charges Archegos and its Founder with Massive Market Manipulation Scheme", Press Release 2022-70, 27 April 2022
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from sec.gov. citations.title: Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA), "Archegos: FINMA concludes proceedings against Credit Suisse", press release, 24 July 2023
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from FINMA's own site. INHERITED WITH A PLACEHOLDER quoteOrFact ("Source carried over from the Crash Conduits entry") and now actually opened and read. This is a REGULATORY FINDING, not an allegation, and it is about the bank rather than the fund: "In the course of its enforcement proceedings, the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority FINMA found that Credit Suisse had seriously and systematically violated financial market law in the context of its business relationship with the Archegos family office. FINMA is ordering corrective measures from its legal successor, UBS. In addition, FINMA has opened enforcement proceedings against a former Credit Suisse manager." On scale: "In March 2021, several investment banks incurred large losses due to the collapse of the Archegos hedge fund. Credit Suisse suffered the biggest loss of over USD 5 billion." On the instrument, in FINMA's own description: "the Archegos family office took synthetic (i.e. without owning the corresponding stock) stock positions (“long” or “short” depending on price expectations) with investment banks such as Credit Suisse. These are instruments that replicate the performance of an underlying asset, for example, a share (total return swaps)." FINMA records that it "took various immediate risk-reducing measures in April 2021" and that "At the same time as FINMA, the authorities in the USA and the UK are also announcing their findings in this matter." Note on the source: the page is served from a multilingual site whose title element came back in French on fetch; the body read and quoted here is the English text.

citations.title: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, consent order and $268.5 million fine with UBS Group AG for misconduct by Credit Suisse, press release, 24 July 2023
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from the Board's own site. INHERITED WITH A PLACEHOLDER quoteOrFact and now opened and read. This is an enforcement action concluded by consent, and it is the most important document for the counterparty half of this dossier: "The Federal Reserve Board on Monday announced a consent order and a $268.5 million fine with UBS Group AG, of Zurich, Switzerland, for misconduct by Credit Suisse, which UBS subsequently acquired in June 2023. The misconduct involved Credit Suisse's unsafe and unsound counterparty credit risk management practices with its former counterparty, Archegos Capital Management LP. In 2021, Credit Suisse suffered approximately $5.5 billion in losses because of the default of Archegos, an investment fund. During Credit Suisse's relationship with Archegos, Credit Suisse failed to adequately manage the risk posed by Archegos despite repeated warnings." The Board required Credit Suisse "to improve counterparty credit risk management practices and to address additional longstanding deficiencies in other risk management programs at Credit Suisse's U.S. operations", and records that the action was taken "in conjunction with actions by the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority and the Bank of England's Prudential Regulation Authority", with the Board's and the PRA's penalties totalling "approximately $387 million". crash-conduits.title: Thirty Dollars of Debt to One of Capital: the Rescue the Fed Convened and Did Not Fund
participants: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was taken before the loss, and it is the detail most often left out: "At the end of 1997, LTCM returned capital to its investors, without reducing the scale of its investments, thereby further increasing its already high leverage." Money went out of the fund while the positions stayed on. By the end of that year "LTCM was holding about $30 in debt for every $1 of capital", after reported returns of 20, 43, 41 and 17 percent across 1994 to 1997.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The structure was leverage applied to convergence: a strategy that "exploited temporary price differences between similar types of securities" and was described as market-neutral, which earns little per dollar and therefore must borrow heavily to earn much at all. The fund extended the same approach across government bonds, mortgage-backed securities and equities, and "entered into derivatives contracts extensively, including those for swaps, forwards, and options".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was on the supervisor's side, and the essay is explicit about when it lifted: "While the Fed had been aware of LTCM's situation through its usual market monitoring activities, the dangerous scale and scope of LTCM's positions became apparent only upon closer inspection" — an inspection that happened on 20 September 1998, two days after the fund itself telephoned the New York Fed, and after it had already lost 44 percent of its value in a single month.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: What was rescued was the orderly unwind, not the owners. Fourteen firms put up $3.625 billion "in exchange for 90 percent of the fund's ownership"; the partners were left running day-to-day operations "with no bonuses and limited salaries", reporting to an oversight committee of the consortium; and "LTCM's partners and other investors suffered substantial losses when their claim was reduced to 10 percent". The consortium had its $3.6 billion back by the end of 1999.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment was a room at the New York Fed and a deadline, and the essay names what it avoided as well as what it did: creditors funded the rescue, "thereby mitigating the moral hazard concerns that might have arisen had public funds been used". Its closing criticism is structural rather than exculpatory — the episode "suggests the need for an established mechanism to address the risks of fire sales arising from failing financial firms, rather than relying on the Fed to coordinate ad hoc private sector solutions at the last minute."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A hedge fund outside the prudential perimeter, financed by regulated dealers whose individual exposures were each tolerable and whose aggregate was not visible to any of them.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The convening precedent itself: a central bank assembling a private consortium in its own building, which the essay treats as an ad hoc solution standing in for a mechanism that did not exist.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Returns attracted leverage; leverage required ever-finer spreads; the capital return of 1997 raised leverage again without reducing the book; and when the spreads diverged, the counterparties who had supplied the leverage were the only parties with enough at stake to fund the unwind.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Federal Reserve bailed out a hedge fund run by Nobel laureates with public money — the first and clearest case of Wall Street being rescued at the taxpayer's expense.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: No public money was lent. The Federal Reserve History account states it twice: "While the Federal Reserve brought the market participants together and oversaw the refinancing, it did not put its own funds at risk. Rather, creditors of LTCM—who had the most to lose from its bankruptcy—arranged and financed the rescue", and the episode "represents an instance where the Federal Reserve was able to facilitate the rescue of a failing financial institution without lending its own funds." The avoidance of public funds was the point, "mitigating long-term moral hazard concerns". Nor did the owners walk away whole: the partners' claim was cut to 10 percent, they ran the wind-down on limited salaries and no bonuses under a creditors' oversight committee, and they had already lost 44 percent of the fund's value in August alone. What the record does support is a different and narrower criticism, which the essay makes itself: that a central bank had to convene an ad hoc private solution at the last minute because no established mechanism existed.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Reported returns of 20 percent in 1994, 43 in 1995, 41 in 1996 and 17 in 1997. Capital returned to investors at the end of 1997 without reducing the scale of the investments, raising leverage to about $30 of debt for every $1 of capital. A 44 percent loss of value in August 1998 after Russia devalued and defaulted. The fund's own call to the New York Fed on 18 September 1998, a Fed team on site on 20 September, and the scale of the positions becoming apparent to the supervisor only then. A Buffett-led offer of $250 million for the partners plus $3.75 billion of capital that was not accepted. And, on 23 September 1998, fourteen firms putting up $3.625 billion for 90 percent of the fund, with no Federal Reserve money at risk, the money returned by the end of 1999, and the partners reduced to a tenth.

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Near Failure of Long-Term Capital Management, September 1998", by Michael Fleming and Weiling Liu
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from federalreservehistory.org. THE ESSAY CONTRADICTS THE "FED BAILOUT" FRAMING DIRECTLY: "On September 23, 1998, a group of fourteen banks and brokerage firms invested $3.6 billion in Long-Term Capital Management L.P. (LTCM) to prevent the firm's imminent collapse ... While the Federal Reserve brought the market participants together and oversaw the refinancing, it did not put its own funds at risk. Rather, creditors of LTCM—who had the most to lose from its bankruptcy—arranged and financed the rescue. The effort thereby addressed the near-term concerns of a possible fire sale of LTCM assets, while mitigating long-term moral hazard concerns that might have arisen from the use of public funds." On the leverage: "At the end of 1997, LTCM returned capital to its investors, without reducing the scale of its investments, thereby further increasing its already high leverage", and "As of the end of 1997, LTCM was holding about $30 in debt for every $1 of capital". On the returns that preceded it: "LTCM generated above-normal returns of 20 percent in 1994, 43 percent in 1995, 41 percent in 1996, and 17 percent in 1997". On the collapse: after Russia devalued and defaulted in August 1998, "LTCM had largely been betting on the spreads in its portfolios to converge, but in almost every case, they diverged. The fund lost 44 percent of its value in August alone." On what the Fed actually did: LTCM contacted the New York Fed president on 18 September; a Fed team visited two days later; "While the Fed had been aware of LTCM's situation through its usual market monitoring activities, the dangerous scale and scope of LTCM's positions became apparent only upon closer inspection"; the Fed convened firms on 22 and 23 September. A Warren Buffett-led offer to buy out the partners for $250 million and inject $3.75 billion was not accepted "due to reported legal issues". The consortium agreed about 6:00 p.m. on 23 September: "fourteen firms put up $3.625 billion in capital in exchange for 90 percent of the fund's ownership (two firms included in the talks declined to participate)." LTCM's partners ran day-to-day operations "with no bonuses and limited salaries", reporting to an oversight committee; the consortium's $3.6 billion was returned by the end of 1999; and "LTCM's partners and other investors suffered substantial losses when their claim was reduced to 10 percent". The essay's own closing judgement: the episode "represents an instance where the Federal Reserve was able to facilitate the rescue of a failing financial institution without lending its own funds", while suggesting "the need for an established mechanism to address the risks of fire sales arising from failing financial firms, rather than relying on the Fed to coordinate ad hoc private sector solutions at the last minute." crash-conduits.title: Corrective Action Should Be Instigated Quickly: the Memo That Was Ignored, and the Phrase That Followed
participants: Continental Illinois National Bank and Trust Company
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The growth was bought wholesale. Continental competed aggressively for oil and gas loans "amid the United States' drive for energy independence and funded that expansion with large-scale borrowing from money markets", acquiring by 1981 "a large amount of oil and gas loans from Penn Square Bank", an Oklahoma bank the essay describes as having "a freewheeling culture". A Penn Square client is quoted: "I could hardly believe it — they loaned me $2.5 million hardly asking any questions and then sold the loan to Continental."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was in the funding mix and it was partly statutory: Illinois law forbade branch banking, so the bank "had little ability to scale up funding from stable retail deposits", and at the time of its rescue "insured deposits comprised only about 15 percent of Continental's total liabilities." A bank funded by large uninsured creditors is a bank that can be left in a morning.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The warning existed, in writing, inside the bank, and this node exists because of it. An employee in Continental's oil and gas division "warned in an internal memo that 'potential credit problems could be going unnoticed' in those loans, and recommended that 'corrective action should be instigated quickly.' Her warnings, largely ignored, proved prescient when Penn Square failed in 1982". The essay extends the failure outward: "Neither Continental's own internal control system nor federal regulators' supervisory efforts fully appreciated the extent of these problems."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was a guarantee no depositor had paid for. The run began around 7 May 1984 and took about 30 percent of the bank's funding in ten days, "generally electronic and spearheaded by depositors with large uninsured deposits and other bank creditors". It stopped on 17 May when the FDIC, Federal Reserve and OCC announced an assistance programme whose "most important element was the FDIC's announcement that it would guarantee of all of the bank's creditors", with a $2 billion FDIC loan and a Federal Reserve statement that it was "prepared to meet any extraordinary liquidity requirements".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The resolution was ownership rather than an inquiry: when the run resumed the FDIC took "80 percent ownership in Continental's holding company" and assumed its Federal Reserve loan. The losses were distributed unevenly and the essay records it: "its shareholders lost their investments in the bank and its management was fired", while uninsured creditors were made whole, and "The FDIC ultimately estimated its loss was about $1.1 billion, equal to about 3 percent of Continental's assets at the time of its intervention."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Deposit insurance designed for small depositors, applied to a bank whose liabilities were overwhelmingly uninsured and wholesale, under a state branching prohibition that made retail funding impossible.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The doctrine itself: "The phrase 'too big to fail' became commonly used for the first time after Continental's crisis", and with it the expectation that the creditors of a sufficiently large bank are covered whether or not the insurance says so.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Wholesale funding bought loan growth; loan growth required more wholesale funding; the uninsured creditors who supplied it could leave electronically in a morning, which is precisely why they had to be guaranteed when they tried to.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Continental Illinois was the first bank bailout, in which Washington simply handed public money to a reckless bank and nobody suffered.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The distribution of loss is on the record and it is not "nobody". Continental's "shareholders lost their investments in the bank and its management was fired", and the FDIC estimated its own loss at about $1.1 billion. What was rescued was the creditor class: the FDIC guaranteed all of the bank's creditors, including the large uninsured depositors whose electronic withdrawals had caused the run. That is the precise thing worth naming, and it is more specific than "bailout" — it is a guarantee extended to people who had not bought one, in a bank whose insured deposits were only about 15 percent of its liabilities. The counter-reading, that regulators acted on a whim, also fails: the essay records the decision following "vigorous internal debate about a range of possible options".
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Oil and gas loans purchased in volume from Penn Square Bank by 1981. An internal memo from Continental's own oil and gas division warning that "potential credit problems could be going unnoticed" and that "corrective action should be instigated quickly", largely ignored, before Penn Square failed in 1982. Neither the bank's internal controls nor federal supervision appreciating the extent of the problem. Insured deposits at about 15 percent of total liabilities. A run from about 7 May 1984 taking roughly 30 percent of funding in ten days, led by large uninsured depositors and other creditors. An assistance programme announced on 17 May guaranteeing all of the bank's creditors, with a $2 billion FDIC loan and a Federal Reserve commitment on liquidity. A second run, then 80 percent FDIC ownership of the holding company. Shareholders wiped out, management fired, and an FDIC loss of about $1.1 billion — and a phrase that entered common use for the first time.

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Continental Illinois: A Bank That Was Too Big to Fail, May 1984" (published 15 May 2023)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from federalreservehistory.org. On the origin of the phrase: the essay is subtitled "A Bank That Was Too Big to Fail" and records that "The phrase 'too big to fail' became commonly used for the first time after Continental's crisis", and that the episode "ignited a national debate that continues to this day over whether large financial institutions enjoy undue privileges because regulators consider them too big to fail." THE WARNING THAT WAS IGNORED, which is the heart of this node: as Continental's purchases of oil and gas loans from Penn Square Bank accumulated, "an employee in Continental's oil and gas division warned in an internal memo that 'potential credit problems could be going unnoticed' in those loans, and recommended that 'corrective action should be instigated quickly.' Her warnings, largely ignored, proved prescient when Penn Square failed in 1982". The essay adds: "Neither Continental's own internal control system nor federal regulators' supervisory efforts fully appreciated the extent of these problems." On the funding structure: Illinois law forbade branch banking, so the bank "had little ability to scale up funding from stable retail deposits", and "At the time of its rescue, insured deposits comprised only about 15 percent of Continental's total liabilities." On the run: "A large-scale run by depositors on Continental began around May 7, 1984 ... Over the next ten days, the bank lost about 30 percent of its funding. The run was generally electronic and spearheaded by depositors with large uninsured deposits and other bank creditors." On the rescue: it stopped on 17 May when the FDIC, Federal Reserve and OCC announced a temporary assistance program, of which "The most important element was the FDIC's announcement that it would guarantee of all of the bank's creditors" (the grammatical slip is the essay's); the FDIC also lent $2 billion, and the Federal Reserve announced it "is prepared to meet any extraordinary liquidity requirements". When the run resumed, the FDIC took "80 percent ownership in Continental's holding company". On who bore the loss: "its shareholders lost their investments in the bank and its management was fired", and "The FDIC ultimately estimated its loss was about $1.1 billion, equal to about 3 percent of Continental's assets at the time of its intervention."
