crash-conduits.title: With the Encouragement of the US Government: Petrodollars Lent Out, and a Warning from 1977

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The fee was the spread on recycling somebody else's surplus. Two oil shocks "created current account deficits in many Latin American countries" and "current account surpluses among oil-exporting countries", and, in the essay's own words, "With the encouragement of the US government, large US money-center banks were willing intermediaries between the two groups, providing the exporting countries with a safe, liquid place for their funds and then lending those funds to Latin America."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was concentration, and it is quantified. Total outstanding Latin American debt went from "$29 billion" at the end of 1970 to "$159 billion" by the end of 1978 and "$327 billion" by 1982. On the lenders' side, "by 1982, the nine largest US money-center banks held Latin American debt amounting to 176 percent of their capital; their total LDC debt was nearly 290 percent of capital." A loss on that book was not a loss of profit; it was a loss of the banks.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: There was no fog about the risk, which is what makes this node a foreknowledge node rather than a misfortune. "The potential risk of the growing involvement of US banks in Latin American and other less-developed country (LDC) debt didn't go unnoticed. In 1977, during a speech at the Columbia University Graduate School of Business, then-Fed Chairman Arthur Burns criticized commercial banks for assuming excessive risk in their Third World lending." The lending roughly doubled again after that.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall ran for a decade and the bill was presented to the borrowers. The essay calls the 1980s for Latin America "a period often referred to as the 'lost decade'" in which "many Latin American countries became unable to service their foreign debt", and records that the international response "ultimately helped alleviate the situation, albeit with some unintended consequences".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment was the workout itself, conducted through the IMF and the central banks over years rather than through any inquiry into how banks came to hold sovereign exposure at 176 percent of capital after their own regulator had warned about it in 1977. The essay records the response and its unintended consequences; it apportions no blame and no liability, and neither does this dossier.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Eurodollar market and a sovereign-lending convention that treated states as unable to go bankrupt, with deposits from oil exporters available to be lent on at a margin.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The decade-long sovereign workout apparatus — IMF programmes, rescheduling rounds and ultimately the Brady restructuring — which converted bank exposure into tradable sovereign paper.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Oil surpluses were deposited with the banks; the banks lent them to oil-importing states; the states' repayments depended on commodity prices and on rates the banks' own central bank set; and when rates rose, the exposure that had been the banks' profit became the reason they could not be allowed to take the loss.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Latin America borrowed recklessly in the 1970s and the lost decade was the natural price of its own profligacy — or, inverted, that the whole episode was a deliberate plot to capture the continent through debt.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The profligacy reading omits who arranged the lending and on whose encouragement. The essay records that the recycling of oil surpluses into Latin American debt was done by large US money-center banks acting "With the encouragement of the US government", and that by 1982 those banks held Latin American debt at 176 percent of their capital — a structure built by lenders, not only by borrowers. The plot reading fails on the 1977 warning: if the exposure had been designed as a trap, the Federal Reserve chairman criticising commercial banks publicly "for assuming excessive risk in their Third World lending" five years before the default would be an odd move. What the record shows is a known risk that was named by the regulator and run anyway because it was profitable.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Oil shocks producing matched deficits and surpluses; US money-center banks intermediating between them with the encouragement of the US government. Debt rising from $29 billion at the end of 1970 to $159 billion by the end of 1978 and $327 billion by 1982. A public warning by Fed Chairman Arthur Burns at Columbia in 1977 about commercial banks assuming excessive risk in Third World lending. Nine largest money-center banks holding Latin American debt at 176 percent of capital and total less-developed-country debt at nearly 290 percent of capital by 1982. And a decade in which many of the borrowing countries could not service the debt, with an international response that helped "albeit with some unintended consequences".

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Latin American Debt Crisis of the 1980s, 1982-1989", by Jocelyn Sims and Jessie Romero
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from federalreservehistory.org. On the recycling mechanism: "During the 1970s, two large oil price shocks created current account deficits in many Latin American countries. At the same time, these shocks created current account surpluses among oil-exporting countries. With the encouragement of the US government, large US money-center banks were willing intermediaries between the two groups, providing the exporting countries with a safe, liquid place for their funds and then lending those funds to Latin America." The phrase "With the encouragement of the US government" is the essay's. On the scale: "At the end of 1970, total outstanding debt from all sources totaled only $29 billion, but by the end of 1978, that number had skyrocketed to $159 billion. By 1982, the debt level reached $327 billion." THE WARNING ON THE RECORD, and its date: "The potential risk of the growing involvement of US banks in Latin American and other less-developed country (LDC) debt didn't go unnoticed. In 1977, during a speech at the Columbia University Graduate School of Business, then-Fed Chairman Arthur Burns criticized commercial banks for assuming excessive risk in their Third World lending." And what happened anyway: "Still, by 1982, the nine largest US money-center banks held Latin American debt amounting to 176 percent of their capital; their total LDC debt was nearly 290 percent of capital." The essay describes the decade as one "often referred to as the 'lost decade'" in which "many Latin American countries became unable to service their foreign debt", and says the international response "ultimately helped alleviate the situation, albeit with some unintended consequences." crash-conduits.title: Caught By Surprise: a Devaluation in Thailand and the Reversal of the Flows

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The inflow came first and the essay treats its reversal as the mechanism: "Across East Asia, capital inflows slowed or reversed direction, and growth slowed sharply." What had been invested on the way in was withdrawn on the way out, and the currencies carried the difference.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was the peg, defended until the reserves ran down. Thailand devalued on 2 July 1997 after "months of speculative pressures that had substantially depleted Thailand's official foreign exchange reserves". Hong Kong "faced several large but unsuccessful speculative attacks on its currency peg to the dollar".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The honest finding here is an absence, and the dossier says so rather than inventing foreknowledge: "The events that came to be known as the Asian Financial Crisis generally caught market participants and policymakers by surprise", though some vulnerabilities were recognised beforehand. This node sits in an atlas about things that were known in advance; this one, on the source read here, largely was not.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: What spread was contagion rather than a windfall. Thailand's difficulties "evolved into a twin balance-of-payments and banking crisis"; Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia let their currencies weaken, "with Indonesia gradually falling into a multifaceted financial and political crisis"; and "severe balance-of-payments pressures in South Korea brought the country to the brink of default". The first Hong Kong attack "triggered short-term stock market sell-offs across the globe".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The essay read here describes the crisis and its spread; it does not adjudicate the rescue terms, and this dossier does not either. What it records is the cost: "Banks came under significant pressures, investment rates plunged, and some Asian countries entered deep recessions, producing important spillovers to trading partners across the globe."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Dollar-pegged currencies in open capital accounts, where a fixed rate invites foreign borrowing and the reserves backing it can be tested by anyone.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-1998 reserve accumulation by East Asian states — self-insurance against ever needing the rescue again — and the lasting political argument about the terms on which it was offered.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The peg encouraged unhedged foreign-currency borrowing; the borrowing raised the cost of defending the peg; the defence depleted the reserves that made the peg credible; and the devaluation that followed multiplied the local-currency value of the debt.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Asian crisis was engineered — a deliberate raid by Western speculators and the IMF to force open the region's economies — or, from the other side, that it was simply crony capitalism getting what it deserved.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The source read here supports neither as a single explanation, and it says something that cuts against the engineered reading in particular: the crisis "generally caught market participants and policymakers by surprise". A raid that surprises its beneficiaries is a poor raid. The crony-capitalism reading is equally incomplete against an account in which the proximate mechanism is a balance-of-payments one — depleted reserves, a devaluation, then capital inflows that "slowed or reversed direction" across an entire region including economies with very different domestic arrangements. This dossier is deliberately thin where the evidence is thin: the essay cited is a secondary account of what happened, and the rescue terms, the IMF conditionality and the question of who profited are not sourced here and are not asserted.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Thailand's devaluation on 2 July 1997, following months of speculative pressure that had substantially depleted its official reserves. Its difficulties evolving into a twin balance-of-payments and banking crisis. Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia allowing substantial currency weakening, with Indonesia falling into a multifaceted financial and political crisis. Unsuccessful speculative attacks on Hong Kong's dollar peg, the first triggering short-term stock market sell-offs globally. South Korea brought to the brink of default. Capital inflows across East Asia slowing or reversing, banks under significant pressure, investment rates plunging, deep recessions in some countries and spillovers to trading partners. And the fact that it generally caught market participants and policymakers by surprise.

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Asian Financial Crisis, July 1997-December 1998", by Michael Carson and John Clark
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from federalreservehistory.org. On the trigger and spread: "On July 2, 1997, Thailand devalued its currency relative to the U.S. dollar. This development, which followed months of speculative pressures that had substantially depleted Thailand's official foreign exchange reserves, marked the beginning of a deep financial crisis across much of East Asia. In subsequent months, Thailand's currency, equity, and property markets weakened further as its difficulties evolved into a twin balance-of-payments and banking crisis." It records that "Malaysia, the Philippines, and Indonesia also allowed their currencies to weaken substantially in the face of market pressures, with Indonesia gradually falling into a multifaceted financial and political crisis"; that Hong Kong "faced several large but unsuccessful speculative attacks on its currency peg to the dollar, the first of which triggered short-term stock market sell-offs across the globe"; and that "severe balance-of-payments pressures in South Korea brought the country to the brink of default." On the consequences: "Across East Asia, capital inflows slowed or reversed direction, and growth slowed sharply. Banks came under significant pressures, investment rates plunged, and some Asian countries entered deep recessions, producing important spillovers to trading partners across the globe." crash-conduits.title: Eight Central Banks Holding a Price: the Pool That Collapsed in March 1968

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was spent was reserves, to hold a number. After a run sent the London price to $40 an ounce on 20 October 1960, the Pool was formed on 1 November 1961 by eight central banks, which "agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system" and keep the price at $35.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was the promise itself: since 1958 "countries settled their international balances in dollars, and U.S. dollars were convertible to gold at a fixed exchange rate of $35 an ounce", with the United States responsible for keeping that price fixed. A convertibility pledge is only as good as the metal behind it, and the Pool existed because the market had begun to test it.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The intervention was the fog: a price maintained by coordinated central bank selling looks, to anyone reading the quote, like a market price. The essay records the parallel machinery of swap lines with nine central banks providing "up to $900 million equivalent in foreign exchange", and notes that "What started as a small, short-term credit facility grew to be a large, intermediate-term facility" — a temporary fix that was "a sign of a fundamental problem in the monetary system".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The arrangement bought seven years. "The pool was successful for six years until another gold crisis ensued", and in that time the dollar's convertibility was treated as sound because its price did not move.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The ending was a two-tier fiction rather than an admission. Sterling devalued, a run on gold followed, France withdrew, and "The pool collapsed in March 1968." The seven remaining members then "agreed to formulate a two-tiered system", with central banks using gold only to settle international debts — one price for governments and another for everyone else. The gold window closed entirely in August 1971.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Bretton Woods: fixed currencies against the dollar and the dollar fixed to gold at $35, with the United States carrying the convertibility obligation for the system.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The two-tier gold market of March 1968, and then the closing of the gold window in August 1971 — the end of the convertibility the Pool had been built to defend.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Defending the price required selling reserves; selling reserves reduced the backing that made the price credible; the weaker the backing, the more the price had to be defended. The swap lines that were meant to bridge the gap grew into a standing facility, which the essay reads as the symptom rather than the cure.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the gold price was secretly rigged by a cartel of central banks, and that the public was never told.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The price was indeed held by coordinated central bank intervention — but not secretly, and the source for that is a Federal Reserve publication stating it plainly: the London Gold Pool "was formed on November 1, 1961", consisted of eight named central banks, and "agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system" and keep gold at $35 an ounce. An arrangement whose membership, date, mechanism and purpose are published by one of its members is a policy, not a conspiracy. What the record does support is the thing the decoy gestures at without naming: the price people could observe was an administered price, it was administered until it could not be, and when it failed the response was a two-tier system that kept one price for central banks and let the other float.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A run that sent the London gold price to $40 an ounce on 20 October 1960. The London Gold Pool formed on 1 November 1961 by eight central banks — Great Britain, West Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, France and the United States — pooling reserves to hold the price at $35. Parallel swap lines with nine central banks providing up to $900 million equivalent, which grew from a short-term facility into an intermediate-term one. Success for six years. Then sterling's devaluation, another run on gold, France's withdrawal, and the Pool's collapse in March 1968, followed by a two-tier system in which the seven remaining members used gold only to settle international debts. Convertibility ended altogether in August 1971.

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Nixon Ends Convertibility of U.S. Dollars to Gold and Announces Wage/Price Controls, August 1971", by Sandra Kollen Ghizoni
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from federalreservehistory.org. NOTE ON FIT: the essay's subject is August 1971, not March 1968. It is cited here because it contains the passage on the London Gold Pool, which is this node's subject, and nothing in this dossier is drawn from the essay beyond what it says about the Pool and the system around it. On the system: under Bretton Woods "countries agreed to keep their currencies fixed (but adjustable in exceptional situations) to the dollar, and the dollar was fixed to gold. Since 1958 ... countries settled their international balances in dollars, and U.S. dollars were convertible to gold at a fixed exchange rate of $35 an ounce." ON THE POOL ITSELF: "A run in the London gold market sent the price to $40 an ounce on October 20, 1960, exacerbating the threat to the system. In response, the London Gold Pool was formed on November 1, 1961. The pool consisted of a group of eight central banks (Great Britain, West Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, France, and the United States). In order to keep the price of gold at $35 an ounce, the group agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system. The pool was successful for six years until another gold crisis ensued. The British pound sterling devalued and another run on gold occurred, and France withdrew from the pool. The pool collapsed in March 1968. At that time the seven remaining members of the London Gold Pool ... agreed to formulate a two-tiered system." On the swap lines that ran alongside it: credit lines with nine central banks "provided up to $900 million equivalent in foreign exchange", and "What started as a small, short-term credit facility grew to be a large, intermediate-term facility until the U.S. gold window closed in August 1971. The growth and need for the swap lines signaled that they were not just a temporary fix, but a sign of a fundamental problem in the monetary system." SOURCE CHARACTER: Federal Reserve History is an educational project of the Federal Reserve System. This is a signed secondary essay with its own bibliography, not a primary record, and it is tiered and attributed accordingly: the dossier says what the essay states, not what a contemporaneous document shows. crash-conduits.title: Standing for Delivery: a Dominant Copper Position, and $150 Million Neither Admitted Nor Denied

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The motive the order records is loss, not greed: "In the wake of accumulating large losses from speculative trading, the principal copper trader for Sumitomo engaged in a scheme, in conjunction with an entity operating in the United States, with the intent of manipulating the price of copper." The manipulation began as a way of not realising what had already been lost.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was physical control of a market through its delivery mechanism. During 1995 and 1996 Sumitomo "established and maintained large and dominant futures positions in copper metal on the LME", and "In the fall of 1995, Sumitomo stood for delivery on a significant percentage of its maturing futures contracts. It thereby acquired a dominant and controlling cash and futures market position".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was the price itself. A dominant holder standing for delivery produces a quoted price that looks like scarcity, and the order finds the effect "directly and predictably caused copper prices, including prices on the United States cash and futures markets, to reach artificially high levels" — prices paid by everyone who used copper, none of whom could see the position producing them.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is stated as the object of the exercise: the actions were taken "expressly for the purpose of creating artificially high absolute prices and an artificially high premium of nearby prices over futures prices", which Sumitomo "intentionally exploited ... in order to profit on the liquidation of its large portfolio of futures contracts and holdings of LME warrants."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The settlement is the containment and its shape is worth reading closely. $150 million in total, of which $125 million was an immediate civil penalty and $25 million was escrowed for up to four years for restitution to injured persons — reverting to the Treasury as penalty if unclaimed. The findings were "neither admitted nor denied". And the chairperson's statement credits the company for "constructive actions it has taken and losses it has suffered in the wake of the public disclosure of the misconduct", which is a regulator explaining why the number is what it is.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A metals exchange whose price is set by physical delivery against warrants, and a cross-border market in which the dominant position sat on one exchange while the affected prices were in several jurisdictions.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The cooperation precedent the Commission emphasises — "unprecedented cooperation with regulatory authorities in the United Kingdom, in particular the Financial Services Authority, and with the Japanese Government" — and the assertion of US jurisdiction over manipulation conducted on a London exchange.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Speculative losses created the need to support the price; supporting the price required a larger position; the larger position made the price more artificial and the eventual unwind more damaging, which is the position the trader was trying not to have.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That one rogue trader secretly cornered the world copper market for a decade while his employer knew nothing, and that regulators never got to the bottom of it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Commission’s order is against the corporation, not an individual: it found "that Sumitomo Corporation of Japan (Sumitomo) manipulated the copper market in 1995 and 1996", acting "through its agent or agents". That is a finding of corporate liability, which is the opposite of the lone-rogue framing. It is also narrower in time than the legend — 1995 and 1996, not a decade. But the dossier must not overstate it in the other direction either: the order settled the matter by consent and "Sumitomo neither admitted nor denied the findings", so this is a settled regulatory finding rather than an adjudicated verdict, and no individual is found liable in it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A CFTC order of 11 May 1998, settled by consent, finding that Sumitomo manipulated the copper market in 1995 and 1996 in violation of Sections 6(c), 6(d) and 9(a)(2) of the Commodity Exchange Act. Large and dominant LME futures positions; standing for delivery on a significant percentage of maturing contracts in autumn 1995; a resulting dominant and controlling cash and futures position that directly and predictably drove US cash and futures prices to artificially high levels; and the express purpose of creating an artificially high price and nearby premium to profit on liquidating the futures portfolio and LME warrants. $150 million total: $125 million immediate civil penalty, $25 million escrowed up to four years for restitution. Findings neither admitted nor denied.

citations.title: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, "CFTC Files and Settles Action Against Sumitomo Corporation for Manipulating the Copper Market in 1995-96", Release 4144-98, 11 May 1998
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from cftc.gov. The Commission issued an order "in connection with settling the matter by consent, finding that Sumitomo Corporation of Japan (Sumitomo) manipulated the copper market in 1995 and 1996", in which "Sumitomo neither admitted nor denied the findings". THE MECHANISM AS THE ORDER DESCRIBES IT: "In the wake of accumulating large losses from speculative trading, the principal copper trader for Sumitomo engaged in a scheme, in conjunction with an entity operating in the United States, with the intent of manipulating the price of copper. In particular, during 1995 and 1996, Sumitomo, acting through its agent or agents, established and maintained large and dominant futures positions in copper metal on the LME. In the fall of 1995, Sumitomo stood for delivery on a significant percentage of its maturing futures contracts. It thereby acquired a dominant and controlling cash and futures market position, which directly and predictably caused copper prices, including prices on the United States cash and futures markets, to reach artificially high levels." The purpose is stated: "expressly for the purpose of creating artificially high absolute prices and an artificially high premium of nearby prices over futures prices", which Sumitomo "intentionally exploited ... in order to profit on the liquidation of its large portfolio of futures contracts and holdings of LME warrants", in violation of Sections 6(c), 6(d) and 9(a)(2) of the Commodity Exchange Act. THE PENALTY: "a total of $150 million", of which "$125 million will be paid as a civil monetary penalty immediately" and "The remaining $25 million will be placed into escrow for a period of up to four years" available "to provide restitution to persons injured by Sumitomo's unlawful conduct", reverting to the Treasury as penalty if unclaimed. CFTC Chairperson Brooksley Born called it "an historic moment in the Commission's work to protect the people of the United States, the United States cash and futures markets and their participants against market manipulation", noting also "the credit Sumitomo deserves for constructive actions it has taken and losses it has suffered in the wake of the public disclosure of the misconduct", and describing "unprecedented cooperation with regulatory authorities in the United Kingdom, in particular the Financial Services Authority, and with the Japanese Government". A settled consent order whose findings were neither admitted nor denied. crash-conduits.title: One Hundred Percent Restitution: $1.212 Billion Back, and an Admission of Liability
participants: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was taken was customer money held under a statutory protection. The CFTC’s complaint charged MF Global and other defendants "with unlawful use of customer funds", and charged the firm, "a registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM), with violating provisions of the Commodity Exchange Act and CFTC Regulations intended to protect FCM customer funds and requiring diligent supervision by registrants."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was of segregation itself — the rule that a futures commission merchant holds customer property apart from its own. The charge is not of a bad trade but of using funds that were not the firm’s to use, and of failing in the supervision the registration carries with it.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The shortfall became visible only at failure, which is what segregation rules exist to prevent: the restitution ordered was "to ensure customers recover their losses sustained when MF Global failed in 2011", and the trustee had to seek permission "to pay restitution in full to customers to remedy any shortfall with funds of the MF Global general estate."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: There was no windfall; there was a hole, and it was filled. The consent order required "$1.212 billion in restitution to customers", and the acting enforcement director framed the objective as "100 percent restitution ... to satisfy customer losses".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The disposition is unusually un-whitewashed for this atlas and the dossier should say so. The order was entered by a federal judge, it imposed a $100 million civil penalty subordinated to customer and priority-creditor recovery, and — unlike most settlements in this file — "In the consent Order, MF Global admits to the allegations pertaining to its liability based on the acts and omissions of its employees". As at the date of the release, "The CFTC's litigation continues against the remaining defendants: MF Global Holdings Ltd., Jon S. Corzine, and Edith O'Brien" — pending matters whose outcomes are not sourced here and are not asserted.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The futures commission merchant regime: customer funds segregated by rule, with the firm permitted to invest them within limits and the protection resting on the firm’s own compliance.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-MF Global tightening of customer-funds protection and residual-interest rules, and a consent order in which an FCM admitted liability rather than neither admitting nor denying.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Customer property was the cheapest liquidity available to a firm under funding stress; using it relieved the stress that made it attractive; and the protection that should have prevented it depended on the same firm reporting its own compliance.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That MF Global’s customers were simply robbed and never made whole, and that nobody admitted anything or paid a penny.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Both halves are contradicted by the order. Customers were made whole: the consent order required $1.212 billion in restitution and the trustee obtained permission to pay customers in full from the general estate, with the enforcement division describing the aim as 100 percent restitution. And an admission was made: "In the consent Order, MF Global admits to the allegations pertaining to its liability based on the acts and omissions of its employees" — which is rarer than the usual neither-admit-nor-deny formula and should be reported as such. What the document does not establish is anything about the individuals: the litigation against MF Global Holdings, Jon S. Corzine and Edith O'Brien was continuing as at this release, and nothing about its outcome is sourced here.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A CFTC complaint of 27 June 2013 charging MF Global with unlawful use of customer funds and with violating Commodity Exchange Act provisions and CFTC regulations protecting FCM customer funds and requiring diligent supervision. A federal court consent order entered on 8 November 2013 by Judge Victor Marrero in the Southern District of New York requiring $1.212 billion in restitution to customers, and imposing a $100 million civil monetary penalty payable only after customers and priority creditors are paid. The firm’s admission of liability for the acts and omissions of its employees. The trustee’s bankruptcy-court permission to pay customers in full from the general estate. And continuing litigation, as at 18 November 2013, against MF Global Holdings Ltd., Jon S. Corzine and Edith O'Brien.

citations.title: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, "Federal Court in New York Orders MF Global Inc. to Pay over $1 Billion in Restitution to Customers", Release 6776-13, 18 November 2013
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from cftc.gov. The CFTC "obtained a federal court consent Order against Defendant MF Global Inc. The release records that "The CFTC's litigation continues against the remaining defendants: MF Global Holdings Ltd., Jon S. crash-conduits.title: Identified by Management: the Risk-System Deficiencies the Board and the Fed Were Not Told About
participants: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The position was built inside a unit meant to manage the bank’s own balance sheet: the Board’s earlier order "followed the disclosure of significant losses in a large synthetic credit portfolio that was managed by the CIO". The trading loss is the part everybody remembers; it is not what the penalty is for.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was the risk apparatus around that portfolio, and the Board characterises it as unsafe: its January 2013 cease and desist order required prompt corrective action on deficiencies "which represented unsafe or unsound practices at JPMC".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: This is the sentence the node exists for, and the key words are "identified by management": the September 2013 consent order "cites the failure by JPMC to appropriately inform its board of directors and the Federal Reserve of deficiencies in risk-management systems identified by management." The deficiencies were known inside the firm before the board or the supervisor were told. The fog was internal and directed upward.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: What the silence bought was time for the position and for the people running it — and the cost of it was later assessed across four regulators: the Board’s action "was taken in coordination with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the Financial Conduct Authority of the United Kingdom", and "The penalties issued by the agencies total approximately $920 million."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment is a consent order: a $200 million penalty assessed against the holding company "for deficiencies in the bank holding company's oversight, management, and controls governing its Chief Investment Office", with no individual named in this document and no admission recorded in it. closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A chief investment office managing a bank’s own excess deposits in instruments whose risk was measured by models the same institution built and reported on.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A coordinated four-regulator penalty across two countries for a single episode, and an enforcement theory aimed at the reporting failure rather than the loss.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Management identified deficiencies in the systems measuring the portfolio; not reporting them kept the portfolio inside its stated limits; the portfolio continued to grow inside limits that the unreported deficiencies had made meaningless.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the London Whale was one trader in a foreign office losing billions on a bet nobody at the top knew about.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Federal Reserve’s penalty is not for the bet and not against a trader. It is a $200 million civil money penalty against the holding company "for deficiencies in the bank holding company's oversight, management, and controls governing its Chief Investment Office", and the conduct it cites is a failure "to appropriately inform its board of directors and the Federal Reserve of deficiencies in risk-management systems identified by management." The phrase "identified by management" is the Board's: somebody knew. The loss was the occasion of the enforcement, not its subject. What this document does not do is name or sanction any individual, or record any admission.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A Federal Reserve consent Order of Assessment of a Civil Money Penalty announced on 19 September 2013, assessing $200 million against JPMorgan Chase & Co. for deficiencies in oversight, management and controls governing the Chief Investment Office, and citing the failure to appropriately inform its own board and the Federal Reserve of risk-management system deficiencies that management had identified. extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was the published rating, and the charges describe the gap precisely. extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was underwriting business won on the strength of coverage, and the settlement prices it: ten firms paying "$875 million in penalties and disgorgement", plus "$432.5 million to fund independent research" and "$80 million from seven of the firms" for investor education — "The total of all payments is roughly $1.4 billion."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment has two features worth naming because they cut against the usual pattern. The firms "will not seek reimbursement or indemnification for any penalties that they pay" and "will not seek a tax deduction or tax credit ... for any penalty amounts" — closing the two routes by which a penalty is normally passed on. closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: An integrated investment bank in which research is a cost centre justified by the banking revenue it helps win, and published ratings are the firm’s product rather than the analyst’s opinion.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The structural separation imposed by the settlement — "separating the research and investment banking departments at the firms", changing how research is reviewed and supervised, and "making independent research available to investors", funded by $432.5 million from the firms themselves.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Favourable coverage won mandates; mandates paid for the research department; the research department produced the coverage. The investor reading the rating was the only party to the loop who was not inside it.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the dot-com crash was mass delusion — everybody believed, everybody was wrong, and nobody did anything improper — or, inverted, that it was a single orchestrated pump in which every analyst was bought.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The delusion reading fails on the regulators’ central charge, which is not error but divergence: research "inconsistent with privately expressed negative views", reports "contrary to privately expressed negative views", "recommendations contrary to the actual views regarding the companies". The orchestration reading fails on the shape of the actions: they allege inappropriate influence of banking over research and supervisory deficiencies at the firms, not a coordinated scheme among them, and the specific fraud findings attach to named individuals at two firms. Note too that the allegations against the firms were neither admitted nor denied, and both individuals settled; none of this was tried.

deep-state.title: The Rigged Compass: Panel Banks Bent the World's Reference Rate to Profit Their Own Swap Books

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Daily basis-point shifts in LIBOR fixings, requested by derivatives traders at panel banks, moved payouts on interest-rate-swap and other positions priced off the benchmark — a continuous skim across hundreds of trillions in notional instruments.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: LIBOR was set not from actual transactions but from submissions by the very banks that traded against it, administered by the British Bankers' Association — a self-polled benchmark with no independent verification, constructed for capture.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Rigging ran through chat rooms, broker intermediaries and oral requests off any transaction record; the absence of an observable market rate meant the manipulation left no direct pricing trail for counterparties to detect.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Panel banks held privileged knowledge of their own submissions and positions, harvesting gains on swap books and — during 2008 — lower perceived funding costs by lowballing submissions to appear healthier.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Regulators collected fines (Barclays ~£290m, UBS $1.5bn, RBS ~$612m), a single trader (Tom Hayes) was convicted, and the consolidated private antitrust suit was dismissed at the pleading stage with the Second Circuit affirming in May 2016 — no bank-level criminal conviction on the rate rigging, and the benchmark was quietly re-homed to ICE in 2014.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Thatcher-era Big Bang architecture left benchmark construction to the British Bankers' Association and a submission panel of the same banks that traded on the rate — self-regulation inherited from the 1986 settlement of LIBOR administration.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Financial Services (Banking Reform) Act 2013 criminalised benchmark manipulation and transferred LIBOR to ICE Benchmark Administration — formalising the benchmark while leaving the dealer-panel structure and derivative pricing power intact.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Fines and settlement payments flowed to treasuries and regulators, not to the counterparties, municipalities, and borrowers whose student loans, mortgages and municipal swaps were priced off the rigged rate; the derivative gains stayed on bank books.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The dismissal of antitrust injury claims pushed benchmark-rigging claims into commodity and fraud theories, narrowing private enforcement and hardening the pleading-stage shield later deployed across FX-rigging and other benchmark scandals.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: Regulators (the Fed / Bank of England) ordered the low submissions in 2008, so the whole scandal was official policy and no one was defrauded.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The pre-2008 profit-driven rigging is documented independently in DOJ settlement statements and the court record; regulator awareness of crisis-period lowballing is a separate, narrower fact that cannot explain seven years of trader-directed fixings.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Extraction ran through the derivative books — panel banks moved the world's reference rate to win their own swaps, with UBS, RBS and Barclays settlements and the Tom Hayes conviction on the record.

deep-state.title: The Bank Nobody Could Kill: Basel's Reparations Machine Outlives Its Mandate and Captures Its Founders

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The Hague Agreements of January 1930 chartered the BIS to collect and administer Germany's Young Plan reparation payments — a perpetual toll on a sovereign's output, extracted via intergovernmental debt schedules inherited from the Dawes Plan.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The victors' central banks seated the institution in Basel, outside any single nation's jurisdiction, with constituent charters granting legal immunity to its assets and archives — an extraction instrument built constitutionally beyond audit, seizure, or subpoena.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Charter-level archive immunity meant the BIS's ledgers were closed to national parliaments and courts; during WWII it operated gold and foreign-exchange channels with all belligerents while its American president Thomas H. McKittrick kept lines open to both Allied and Axis central banks, all under diplomatic darkness.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: After the Hoover Moratorium (1931) and Lausanne (1932) killed the reparations flow it existed to manage, the BIS did not dissolve — it repurposed into the monopoly clearinghouse and club of central bankers, a wartime intermediary whose neutrality charter was itself the market.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The March 1939 Czech gold affair — transfer of Czechoslovak National Bank gold to the Reichsbank after the German occupation of Prague — scandalised Westminster, yet no charter was revoked; Bretton Woods (July 1944) resolved the BIS should be liquidated 'at the earliest possible moment,' and the 1948 post-war settlement quietly let it stand.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: It inherited the Dawes Plan machinery and the victors' central-bank cartel of the 1920s, hardening the Young Plan's reparations administration into a treaty-chartered institution with sovereign immunity.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: It created the permanent unelected central bankers' club in Basel — the model for post-war machinery including the Basel Committee on bank capital standards, drafted outside any democratic legislature.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Reparations revenue died in 1932, but the immunity and neutrality frameworks kept the BIS earning on gold and exchange operations for all belligerents throughout WWII, recycling crisis into institutional endowment and insider standing.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: Its survival past Bretton Woods's liquidation resolution established that crisis machinery outlives its mandate — the operating template for the offshore black-ledger and capital-standards architecture that governs sovereign and bank debt ever since.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The BIS was Hitler's bank — a Nazi plot from the start.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: It was designed by the victors' central bankers under the Young Plan committee in January 1930, before Hitler took power; its wartime service to all belligerents flowed from the immunity and neutrality written into its 1930 charters, not from any Nazi origin.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The institution's documented purpose was debt collection on Germany; its acceptance of Czechoslovak National Bank gold for the Reichsbank in March 1939, its survival past the death of reparations in 1932, and its defiance of Bretton Woods's 1944 liquidation resolution show how crisis machinery outlives its mandate and captures its founders.

deep-state.title: South Sea Directors Convert the National Debt Into Bubbled Equity, Bribe Parliament, and Crash a Nation

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The South Sea Company charged holders of government annuities steep conversion premiums to swap solid debt for its own shares, skimming the spread between par and the inflated market price on every exchange.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The June 1720 Bubble Act outlawed rival joint-stock promotion, legislating a speculation monopoly for a company that simultaneously bribed ministers and MPs with ledger-entered stock, as the 1721 Commons inquiry documented.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Insider knowledge of the conversion terms and bribes circulated through the subscription ledger while the public was fed visions of Spanish South American trade windfalls the company could not legally deliver at scale.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Directors, ministers, and well-placed subscribers sold into a tenfold 1720 price rise ahead of the September crash, capturing windfalls from stock issued against debt the state still had to service.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Walpole's resolution — known as the Screen — restored the tainted elite rather than prosecuting it, and his management of the cover propelled him into lasting control of the government by 1721-1722.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The 1694 Bank-of-England settlement of public debt onto a chartered monopoly was weaponized: the South Sea Company replicated the debt-conversion model with equity instead of banknotes.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Bubble Act and the 1721 inquiry established the template for a captured regulator-lawmaker complex — Parliament criminalizing rivals while laundering its own members' corruption through a managed inquiry.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Recovered or preserved fortunes, Walpole's included, flowed back into Whig financing and ministerial patronage, converting scandal into the working capital of a generation-long oligarchy.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The Screen demonstrated that systemic fraud could be resolved by elite self-pardon, a precedent that shaped every subsequent receivership, whitewash inquiry, and managed collapse from the 1720s forward.

deep-state.title: Famine as Fiscal Policy: How the East India Company Taxed Bengal's Dead to Repay Parliament

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Post-Plassey, the Company converted the Bengal diwani into a fixed land-tax annuity, seizing the revenue stream of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa before any famine pressure existed.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Company tax collectors maintained the fixed revenue demand through 1769-1770 while grain prices soared, structurally prioritizing shareholder remittance over subsistence in the tax-yielding provinces.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Famine mortality — estimated at roughly a third of the affected population in contemporaneous Company and Indian sources — was reported slowly to London, where the Company's insolvency, not the dead, framed parliamentary debate.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Parliament answered with the 1773 Regulating and Tea Acts: a 1.4 million pound loan to the Company, its monopoly left intact, serviced by the very Bengal revenue the famine had gutted the population to collect.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Company inherited the joint-stock monopoly charter east of the Cape and, via Plassey, the Mughal revenue-farming apparatus of Bengal, fusing corporate trade privilege with sovereign tax power.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The 1773-1784 acts created the permanent template of state-bailed monopoly: parliamentary 'regulation' that socialized the Company's debts while privatizing its monopoly rents.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Bengal land tax serviced the parliamentary loan and Company dividends, recirculating colonial extraction upward to British creditors and shareholders at the direct cost of the taxed famine population.

decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Contemporaneous Company and Indian sources record fixed tax demand sustained through the famine, mortality near a third of the affected provinces, and the 1773 loan and 1784 subordination — a documented chain from tax collection to parliamentary bailout to continued monopoly.

extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What is verifiable is worse than one lucky trade: Rothschild's agents and correspondents delivered news of Napoleon's return and defeat faster than His Majesty's own government, exposing that a private bank had effectively captured the state's intelligence function it was financing.

extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: After Waterloo the Rothschild brothers (London and Paris) dominated government loan issuance across Europe; their first major operation was financing the French indemnity payment to the Allied powers, converting the speed advantage into a standing franchise over public debt.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The courier legend became a durable viral story about insider advantage at the heart of modern finance, while the documented record — a family bank that built a private intelligence network faster than the governments of Europe — was accepted without regulation of the underlying asymmetry.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Rothschild inherited the financier networks of the Napoleonic wars — William of Hesse's offshore placements, smuggled bullion channels, and the exchange arbitrage of a blockaded Europe — and militarized them into a standing private intelligence service.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: Waterloo established the private international banking network as sovereign-grade infrastructure: thereafter no European government could mount a major loan operation without access to a Rothschild-level syndicate.

deep-state.title: Coffin Ships: How British Shipowners Monetized Drowned Crews Until One MP Drew the Line

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Shipowners pocketed freight revenue from vessels loaded past any safe draught, knowing that over-insured hulls would pay out on loss — the freight skim was underwritten by the coffins the crews sailed in.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The law of the sea put no load-line duty on owners: freeboard was a matter of contract and custom, and the marine insurance market priced the practice in rather than refusing it, structurally normalizing the coffin-ship economy.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Casualty statistics were scattered across registries and Lloyd's listings, and wreck inquests were local and brief; the systematic pattern — overloaded, over-insured, lost with all hands — was invisible until Plimsoll assembled it in Parliament.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was the freight-and-payout duality: owners whose ships sank often collected more than owners whose ships arrived, making mass death a rational business model sustained by the insurance market's pricing.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The shipowners' bloc in Parliament fought every load-line bill to a compromise, and the Merchant Shipping (Load Line) Act 1876 passed only softened — owner-empowered enforcement, diluted penalties, and Plimsoll briefly suspended from the Commons for refusing to accept the watering-down.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Plimsoll's campaign inherited the Victorian liberal-reform machinery of Royal Commissions and Commons select committees, and ran it against an owners' interest seated in both Houses.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The 1876 Act created the load-line obligation itself — the state marking on every hull of the maximum safe draught — a permanent, visible, inspection-based safety framework where none had existed.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The diluted enforcement left owners collecting on pre-load-line losses while the new marking re-valued survivors' freight rates upward; the industry absorbed the reform as a cost, not a forfeiture, with no liability reopened for the drowned.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The load line became universal standard practice in merchant shipping, and the pattern — a safety marking fought to a compromised first law — stands behind every later maritime safety regime, including the SOLAS convention after the Titanic.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The cozy Victorian image of Plimsoll the saintly MP versus a few wicked greedy owners — a morality tale with one hero and some villains.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The decoy personalizes a structural machine: the profits flowed from the insurance market's pricing of loss, from Parliamentary representation of the owning class, and from the absence of any marking duty at all — not from a handful of rogue characters.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The ledger is the coffin-ship economics: overload, heavy overinsurance, payout on sinking, and a legislative fight recorded in Hansard against owners who profited when crews drowned; the 1876 Merchant Shipping (Load Line) Act and its load line are the surviving framework, and Plimsoll's Commons suspension for disorderly protest is on the record.

extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Courts of equity appointed receivers on application of creditors or friendly interests, installing the very financial houses that had underwritten the roads as receivers and masters of the reorganization committees — a structure contemporaries flatly labeled 'friendly receivership'.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Receivership proceedings, foreclosure mechanics, and committee deposit agreements were opaque to scattered junior security holders, who could not see that the same interests sat on both sides of the table.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Reorganization committees marshalled junior holders into depositing securities under threat of exclusion, then closed via foreclosure sales that conveyed the properties to new companies organized by the same interests — wiping old claims and re-concentrating the assets.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The wave was defended as necessary continuity of operation and drew only belated legislative criticism, with reform not arriving until railroad reorganization law was rebuilt decades later in Section 77 (1933).

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The panic-era machinery inherited federal equity receivership doctrine and the Gilded Age pattern of banker-controlled corporate reorganization perfected in earlier railroad collapses.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The 1893-95 wave institutionalized the banker-dominated reorganization committee — deposit agreements, foreclosure sale, and recapitalization by the incumbents — as the standard template for American railroad receivership.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Operating income was routed to fixed charges during receivership, while the same underwriters recaptured the properties cheaply at foreclosure and reissued securities at the top of the new capital structures.

deep-state.title: All Passengers Saved: The Night a Private Wire Outran Every Official Channel and Printed a Lie
participants: press associations of the North Atlantic ports

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Wireless telegraphy was a private commercial service — Marconi Company operators aboard ships, paid by message and by contract, whose bulletins were the product sold to a hungry press within hours of the disaster.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: No government or company channel existed to verify or suppress wireless traffic; the Marconi operators' relayed dispatches moved directly from the ether to front pages, and the press associations ran them without source discipline.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The first bulletins — Titanic safe, in tow, all passengers saved, Halifax the destination of the towed liner — ran the morning of April 16 in Halifax and across the North Atlantic press; the garbled relay chain and the operators' commercial incentives structured the fog.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The wireless companies' monopoly on fast news was the windfall: speed sold papers and messages, and the error was corrected only when slower official channels caught up — when the Carpathia docked in New York on April 18 and the first accurate lists replaced the fiction.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The fog closed as a story of technology's teething pains rather than a structural account of a private information infrastructure printing unverified disaster news; the falsified casualty reports were left to folklore, not to any accounting.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The fog inherited the Marconi Company's monopoly on ship-to-shore traffic and the press associations' competitive wire economy, both built on speed as the salable product.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The April 1912 fog established the standard crisis-information pattern of the twentieth century: private infrastructure first, official confirmation last, with the gap between filled by whoever owns the fastest channel.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The error cost the press nothing that mattered to the wire companies: the same channels that printed the false safety of the morning sold the corrected horror of the evening, and speed — not accuracy — remained the priced good.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The pattern of private-speed, official-silence information gaps became the standard fog of every later market crash and disaster in this atlas, priced and sold by whoever owned the wire.

decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The hero story erases the opposite ledger: the same commercial wire that transmitted the distress calls also transmitted the false dispatches that Halifax printed as truth, and its owners sold speed with no verification duty at all.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The documented record: April 15-16 bulletins reporting the Titanic safe and in tow, Halifax papers running the false report the morning of April 16, and the correction arriving only with the Carpathia's April 18 landing — preserved in the Library of Congress's contemporary press record.

deep-state.title: Operation Ajax: How a Spy Alliance Foreclosed a Democracy to Recover an Oil Concession

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The Anglo-Iranian Oil Company's Abadan refinery — Britain's single largest overseas asset — had skimmed Iran's oil wealth for decades under a concession whose royalty terms Iran had long contested as inequitable.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Iran's March 1951 nationalization of the refinery triggered a British embargo and the closure of the facility, and when negotiations failed and Mossadegh moved toward the Soviet bloc, the intelligence services of two states organized his removal — regime change as a remedy for the nationalization of an extraction concession.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The operation ran under the pretext of indigenous disorder — hired crowds, staged religious and communist street fighting, and a royal decree dismissing the prime minister — so that the coup would read to the world as Iran's own political crisis.

deep-state.title: Senator Aldrich and Wall Street Bankers Draft a National Reserve Association in Secret at Jekyll Island

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The Panic of 1907 left the banking system without a lender of last resort, and the bankers who had privately organized the rescue stood to profit from institutionalizing that role. A legislated national reserve mechanism, with banker-dominated district boards as proposed in the Aldrich Plan, would give the large New York banks standing access to emergency liquidity and a central clearing of credit.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The Aldrich–Vreeland Act of May 1908 created the National Monetary Commission, chaired by Senator Nelson W. Aldrich, putting the writing of banking reform in the hands of the very interests to be regulated. The commission's tour of Europe and its 1910–1912 reports produced the Aldrich Plan for a National Reserve Association with 15 district associations under banker-dominated boards, embedding private control in the institutional architecture.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: In November 1910 Aldrich met a small group of banking figures at the Jekyll Island Club, Georgia, to draft the reserve plan — established by later accounts of participants, and only later itself framed by conspiracy writing as a secret cabal. The drafting was removed from public view, and the mechanism of who would control the new liquidity spigot was buried inside technical commission reports issued between 1910 and 1912.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was structural rather than a one-time sum: the drafters of the plan stood to hold the governance boards of the proposed National Reserve Association, the institutional heart of national credit allocation. Banker-dominated district associations would have given the drafters a durable grip on liquidity creation.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The Aldrich Plan was rejected in Congress and attacked in the 1912 campaign as a 'money trust' instrument, with Woodrow Wilson running against it. Yet the Federal Reserve Act of December 1913 adopted the reserve-association architecture as a compromise, placing a presidentially appointed public Board over it — normalizing the Jekyll Island design while the original secret drafting was absorbed into founding mythology, later distorted further by conspiracy framing that obscured the documented mechanism.

closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The commission's 1910–1912 findings and the Jekyll Island draft circulated as an official reform blueprint, converting private banking priorities into legislative text despite the plan's rejection in Congress.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The Federal Reserve Act of December 1913, which adopted the reserve-association architecture under a public Board, establishes the central-bank liquidity machinery that subsequent dossiers in this lineage trace through the twentieth century.

Aldrich under the Aldrich–Vreeland Act of May 1908, openly touring Europe and issuing reports from 1910 to 1912, whose plan was in fact rejected in Congress and attacked by Woodrow Wilson in 1912. The capture attempt was contested and partially defeated — a fact the conspiracy story flattens into inevitability.

deep-state.title: Strong, Norman, and the Call-Money Machine: How a Transatlantic Gold Pact Fueled Wall Street's Margin Bubble
participants: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Before the fog, the profit sat in the New York call-loan market, where lenders charged call rates on collateralized broker loans financing stock margin purchases. Non-bank lenders — "others" in the Federal Reserve data — supplied most of the growth as broker loans roughly doubled between 1927 and 1929, standing to collect interest on an expanding leveraged book.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The structural arrangement was transatlantic and personal: Benjamin Strong at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, from the bank's founding in November 1914 until his death in October 1928, maintained a working partnership with Bank of England Governor Montagu Norman (1920–1944), including shared views on gold-sterilisation and market management. The July 1927 Long Island conference — Strong, Norman, Rist, Schacht — produced an agreement to ease.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The mechanism stayed invisible because the easing decision was made privately among central-bank chiefs, not through any public legislative or regulatory channel, and its transmission ran through the call-rate structure of the NYSE rather than through visible policy announcements. That the 1927 ease fed the late-1920s speculation was identified only later, and even then contested.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall accrued to holders of the call-loan book and to leveraged equity positions financed on margin: broker loans roughly doubled 1927–1929, with non-bank lenders capturing most of that growth in interest income while stock collateral kept rising. The rate structure sat atop a market the Fed managed rather than constrained.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Strong's death in October 1928 removed the transatlantic coordination, and the story was subsequently framed around whether the NY Fed alone could manage the call-rate structure — a technical question that launders the prior arrangement. The 1927 ease's role in feeding speculation remains contested in the historiography rather than plainly accounted for.

closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Eased conditions rolled into the New York call-loan market: broker loans roughly doubled 1927–1929, with non-bank lenders recycling interest income into a still-larger margin book.

extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The arrangement was laundered through the bland institutional form of the Joint Commission and normalized as ordinary Treasury market operations. The strong 'secret treaty binding oil to the dollar' version is unsupported.

deep-state.title: Cheney's Old Firm Wins Cost-Plus War Logistics: Halliburton's LOGCAP III Rakes Fees From Iraq Occupancy

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Before any fog settled, Brown & Root — the Halliburton subsidiary later operating as KBR — stood to profit directly from a pre-awarded contingency logistics contract. LOGCAP III, won in December 2001 to cover Kuwait, Afghanistan and Iraq, guaranteed revenue on a cost-plus award-fee basis: every dollar of cost incurred generated fee on top. The revenue asset was war itself, locked in before the wars fully began.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The structural arrangement was LOGCAP itself, launched by the US Army in 1985 to pre-award contingency logistics so military operations would not require new wartime procurement. By 2001 the incumbent from LOGCAP I (1992, Balkans support) was the same firm, giving it an entrenched position no competitor could dislodge once troops deployed. Dick Cheney had been Halliburton CEO from 1995 to 2000, and his deferred compensation from the company continued into his vice presidency — publicly documented, and publicly attacked as a conflict of interest, the framing this node keeps exact.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Cost-plus award-fee structure meant the public could not see what a 'fair' price for fuel or a meal was; every cost was reimbursed, so scrutiny had to come after the fact through GAO and DoD-IG reports and congressional hearings. KBR fuel-import pricing (2003–04) and dining-facility cost claims (2004–05) only surfaced through those investigations, not through contract oversight at the point of spending.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall accrued to KBR/Halliburton as sole incumbent across Kuwait, Afghanistan and Iraq simultaneously, with fees scaled to costs rather than outcomes. Congressional investigators later scrutinised the fee structure itself. The positions — and the liabilities, including the electrocution deaths of US soldiers in KBR-built showers documented by DoD-IG in 2009 — stayed with the contractor while the fees flowed the other way.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The arrangement was normalized as procurement policy: LOGCAP was a 1985 program, the award was lawful, and the conflict-of-interest attack on Cheney was public and openly litigated rather than hidden. GAO and DoD-IG findings on fuel pricing, dining facilities, and shower electrocutions were published, but the cost-plus structure that generated them was never dismantled — KBR separated as KBR Inc in 2007 and carried the model forward.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: LOGCAP, the US Army's 1985 contingency logistics program, and Brown & Root's incumbent position from LOGCAP I (1992, Balkans).
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: LOGCAP III (December 2001) as a rolling cost-plus award-fee occupation-logistics contract spanning Kuwait, Afghanistan and Iraq.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Fees proportional to costs meant higher wartime spending directly enlarged contractor revenue, incentivizing cost expansion rather than restraint, and insulating the incumbent across successive task orders.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The entrenched cost-plus occupation-logistics position establishes the template of fee-on-spend war contracting that later reconstruction and contingency dossiers inherit.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The pop-culture version is 'Cheney got rich off the Iraq War' — a personal-corruption story about deferred compensation and one man's greed.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: That frame erases the documented mechanism: the deferred compensation was publicly documented and publicly attacked, but the extraction ran through LOGCAP III's cost-plus award-fee structure — a pre-awarded 1985 program that guaranteed fees on every cost incurred, regardless of who held office.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The US Army launched LOGCAP in 1985 to pre-award contingency logistics contracts. Brown & Root — later a Halliburton subsidiary operating as KBR, separated as KBR Inc in 2007 — won LOGCAP I in 1992 for Balkans support and LOGCAP III in December 2001, covering Kuwait, Afghanistan and Iraq, on a cost-plus award-fee basis. Dick Cheney, Halliburton CEO from 1995 to 2000, retained deferred compensation into his vice presidency — publicly documented and publicly attacked as a conflict of interest. GAO and DoD-IG reports and congressional hearings documented KBR fuel-import pricing (2003–04), dining-facility cost claims (2004–05), and the electrocution deaths of US soldiers in KBR-built showers (DoD-IG 2009).

deep-state.title: Twenty-One Million Dollars for Burnt Contraband: The Opium Traders’ Loss Becomes China’s Sovereign Debt

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The Bengal opium monopoly the East India Company built after the Diwani is sold at Calcutta auction and carried to Canton by private firms — Jardine, Matheson & Co. and Dent & Co. the largest — who take the margin on a trade Chinese law prohibits and British law does not reach.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: When Commissioner Lin Zexu confiscates the 20,283 chests at Canton in March 1839, Superintendent Charles Elliot takes them into Crown hands first and promises the holders that the British government will make the loss good. A private stock of contraband becomes, in a single administrative act, a claim on the Treasury.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The claim is argued in London as a question of national honour and the liberty of British subjects, not as compensation for a drug cargo. Sir James Graham’s censure motion of 7 April 1840 keeps the Commons three nights on the imprudence of ministers; the expedition sails either way.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The Treaty of Nanking charges the whole bill to the Chinese state: six million dollars for the destroyed opium, three million for Hong-merchant debts, twelve million for the expedition itself, twenty-one million in all on a schedule to 1845, plus Hong Kong in perpetuity and five ports opened to British trade.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: No British party pays. The indemnity is settled on China as sovereign debt, the traders are made whole for a cargo their own government had surrendered, and the treaty-port system becomes the template for the next century of forced-trade settlements.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The East India Company’s Bengal revenue and opium monoculture, and the Crown’s habit of standing behind chartered traders’ losses.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The gunboat indemnity: a state-to-state treaty that converts a private trading loss into sovereign debt with a payment schedule, secured by ceded territory and treaty ports.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The firms whose stock was surrendered are paid out of the indemnity; the indemnity is collected from Chinese customs revenue; the ports opened to collect it carry the next decade of the same trade.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: A clash of civilisations over free trade and diplomatic protocol — an arrogant empire refusing to open its ports, met by a Britain defending the rights of its merchants abroad.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The treaty itself names the consideration. Article IV pays six million dollars ‘as the value of the Opium which was delivered up at Canton in the month of March, 1839’ — the destroyed contraband is written into the settlement as a priced item, before the war costs in Article VI.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Elliot took the traders’ opium into government hands against a promise of compensation; the Commons debated and narrowly declined to censure the ministry on 7 April 1840; and the Treaty of Nanking recovered the whole sum — twenty-one million dollars under Articles IV to VII — from the Chinese state, with Hong Kong and five treaty ports attached.

citations.title: Treaty of Nanking (29 August 1842), Articles IV–VII, in W. F. Mayers (ed.), Treaties Between the Empire of China and Foreign Powers (Shanghai, 1877), p. 1
citations.quoteOrFact: Art. IV: "The Emperor of China agrees to pay the sum of Six Millions of Dollars, as the value of the Opium which was delivered up at Canton in the month of March, 1839, as a ransom for the lives of Her Britannic Majesty’s Superintendent and Subjects". Art. V adds three millions for insolvent Hong-merchants’ debts, Art. VI twelve millions for the expedition’s expenses, and Art. VII fixes the total at "Twenty-one Millions of Dollars" payable by the end of 1845.
