And Madoff’s own account of the moment: he "stated that he had thought he was caught after his testimony about the DTC account, noting that when they asked for the DTC account number, 'I thought it was the end game, over. Monday morning they'll call DTC and this will be over . . . and it never happened'", and that when Enforcement did not follow up he "was astonished". This is an inspector-general report on the conduct of a regulator. It makes no finding about any investor’s losses and determines no liability.

deep-state.title: Knowingly Allowed: Six Findings Against a Board That Witnessed and Chose to Ignore

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was taken at the top and the Subcommittee counts it as its own finding: the Board "approved excessive compensation for company executives, failed to monitor the cumulative cash drain caused by Enron’s 2000 annual bonus and performance unit plans, and failed to monitor or halt abuse by Board Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Kenneth Lay of a company-financed, multi-million dollar, personal credit line."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What was compromised was the balance sheet, with the Board’s knowledge. Finding (4): the Board "knowingly allowed Enron to conduct billions of dollars in off-the-books activity to make its financial condition appear better than it was and failed to ensure adequate public disclosure of material off-the-books liabilities that contributed to Enron’s collapse." Finding (2) is one sentence long and does the same work: the Board "knowingly allowed Enron to engage in high risk accounting practices."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was aimed outward while the Board could see in. The Subcommittee’s first finding records that "The Board witnessed numerous indications of questionable practices by Enron management over several years, but chose to ignore them to the detriment of Enron shareholders, employees and business associates." The public disclosure that would have shown the liabilities was, on finding (4), not made.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall ran through a vehicle the Board itself authorised. Finding (3): "Despite clear conflicts of interest, the Enron Board of Directors approved an unprecedented arrangement allowing Enron’s Chief Financial Officer to establish and operate the LJM private equity funds which transacted business with Enron and profited at Enron’s expense. The Board exercised inadequate oversight of LJM transaction and compensation controls and failed to protect Enron shareholders from unfair dealing."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The check that should have been independent was not. Finding (6): "The independence of the Enron Board of Directors was compromised by financial ties between the company and certain Board members." The Subcommittee reached its findings on "over one million pages of subpoenaed documents, interviews of 13 Enron Board members, and the Subcommittee hearing on May 7, 2002" — and it is a congressional report, which determines no liability and adjudicates nothing against any individual director.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A board model in which the audit and compensation committees rely on management’s own presentation of the numbers, and in which directors may hold financial relationships with the company they oversee.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-Enron governance regime — audit committee independence requirements, certification of financial statements, and restrictions on auditor conflicts — built directly on findings of this kind.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The off-books structures improved the reported condition; the improved condition supported the compensation the Board approved; the Board that approved it was, on the Subcommittee’s finding, compromised by financial ties to the company whose numbers it was signing off.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Enron was a handful of rogue executives running a scheme nobody upstairs understood — a conjuring trick too clever for its own directors to see.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Senate Subcommittee found the opposite, twice, in the same word. The Board "knowingly allowed Enron to engage in high risk accounting practices", and "knowingly allowed Enron to conduct billions of dollars in off-the-books activity to make its financial condition appear better than it was". It also found that the Board "witnessed numerous indications of questionable practices by Enron management over several years, but chose to ignore them", and that it approved — "Despite clear conflicts of interest" — the arrangement under which the chief financial officer ran private funds that "transacted business with Enron and profited at Enron’s expense". What should not be drawn from this document is any individual’s liability: it is a congressional subcommittee report, not an adjudication, and it determines none.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Six findings of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, reached on over one million pages of subpoenaed documents and interviews with 13 directors: fiduciary failure; high risk accounting knowingly allowed; inappropriate conflicts of interest in the LJM arrangement approved despite clear conflicts; extensive undisclosed off-the-books activity knowingly allowed, with inadequate public disclosure of material off-the-books liabilities; excessive compensation, including a failure to monitor or halt abuse of a company-financed multi-million dollar personal credit line by the chairman and chief executive; and a board whose independence was compromised by financial ties between the company and certain of its members.

citations.title: U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Committee on Governmental Affairs, The Role of the Board of Directors in Enron’s Collapse, S. Prt. 107-70, 8 July 2002
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. The report states its own evidentiary basis: "Based upon the evidence before it, including over one million pages of subpoenaed documents, interviews of 13 Enron Board members, and the Subcommittee hearing on May 7, 2002", it makes six numbered findings, reproduced here in its own words. "(1) Fiduciary Failure. The Enron Board of Directors failed to safeguard Enron shareholders and contributed to the collapse of the seventh largest public company in the United States, by allowing Enron to engage in high risk accounting, inappropriate conflict of interest transactions, extensive undisclosed off-the-books activities, and excessive executive compensation. The Board witnessed numerous indications of questionable practices by Enron management over several years, but chose to ignore them to the detriment of Enron shareholders, employees and business associates." "(2) High Risk Accounting. The Enron Board of Directors knowingly allowed Enron to engage in high risk accounting practices." "(3) Inappropriate Conflicts of Interest. Despite clear conflicts of interest, the Enron Board of Directors approved an unprecedented arrangement allowing Enron’s Chief Financial Officer to establish and operate the LJM private equity funds which transacted business with Enron and profited at Enron’s expense. The Board exercised inadequate oversight of LJM transaction and compensation controls and failed to protect Enron shareholders from unfair dealing." "(4) Extensive Undisclosed Off-The-Books Activity. The Enron Board of Directors knowingly allowed Enron to conduct billions of dollars in off-the-books activity to make its financial condition appear better than it was and failed to ensure adequate public disclosure of material off-the-books liabilities that contributed to Enron’s collapse." "(5) Excessive Compensation. The Enron Board of Directors approved excessive compensation for company executives, failed to monitor the cumulative cash drain caused by Enron’s 2000 annual bonus and performance unit plans, and failed to monitor or halt abuse by Board Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Kenneth Lay of a company-financed, multi-million dollar, personal credit line." "(6) Lack of Independence. The independence of the Enron Board of Directors was compromised by financial ties between the company and certain Board members." The phrase "knowingly allowed" is the report's own, used in findings (2) and (4). This is a congressional subcommittee report about the conduct of a board. It determines no liability, and it is not a criminal or civil adjudication of any individual director.

deep-state.title: A Virtually Unlimited Line of Credit, Funded by the Customers: What the SEC Alleged About FTX and Alameda

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The equity raise is the figure the Commission puts first: more than $1.8 billion from investors "who bought an equity stake in FTX believing that FTX had appropriate controls and risk management measures". The customer float is the larger pool, and the complaint alleges it was moving out from the beginning: "from the start, Bankman-Fried improperly diverted customer assets to his privately-held crypto hedge fund".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise alleged is an exemption written into the platform itself. Investors were told "that FTX had top-notch, sophisticated automated risk measures in place to protect customer assets, that those assets were safe and secure, and that Alameda was just another platform customer with no special privileges." The complaint alleges the opposite was true: Alameda was exempted from the risk mitigation measures and given "significant special treatment on the FTX platform, including a virtually unlimited 'line of credit' funded by the platform's customers."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was a public persona maintained while the diversion ran. "Throughout this period, Bankman-Fried portrayed himself as a responsible leader of the crypto community. He touted the importance of regulation and accountability. He told the public, including investors, that FTX was both innovative and responsible." The complaint alleges the customer funds went to "undisclosed venture investments, lavish real estate purchases, and large political donations" — the undisclosed venture book and the political giving both being, in effect, reputational spend financed from the float.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was time. When crypto prices fell in May 2022 and Alameda's lenders called their loans, the complaint alleges Bankman-Fried "directed FTX to divert billions more in customer assets to Alameda to ensure that Alameda maintained its lending relationships, and that money could continue to flow in from lenders and other investors." Through that summer he is alleged to have directed hundreds of millions more, used for further venture investments and for "loans" to himself and other executives.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: There is no commission and no liability shield in this one; it ended in a filing. FTX, Alameda "and their tangled web of affiliated entities filed for bankruptcy on November 11, 2022", and the Commission sued a month later, charging violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5. A complaint is an accusation: this dossier records it as one.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: An offshore crypto exchange holding customer assets in commingled form, with an affiliated proprietary trading firm on the other side of the platform and no regulator examining either.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-FTX enforcement posture and custody debate; and, as precedent, the Commission's use of the ordinary anti-fraud provisions — Section 17(a), Section 10(b), Rule 10b-5 — against the operator of a crypto platform.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Customer deposits funded the affiliate's positions; the affiliate's apparent strength supported the platform's reputation; the reputation attracted the next round of deposits and the next equity raise, which were needed because the earlier deposits were no longer there.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That FTX was a sound exchange brought down by a bank run — bad luck, a liquidity crunch, a crypto winter — or alternatively that the whole thing was obvious to anyone paying attention and the investors were simply greedy.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The run account is not what the Commission alleges. Its complaint puts the diversion of customer assets "from the start", years before November 2022, and describes the May 2022 price fall as the moment an existing hole became unservable rather than its cause. The blame-the-investors account fails on the complaint's own description of what they were told: that FTX had "top-notch, sophisticated automated risk measures", that customer assets were "safe and secure", and that Alameda was "just another platform customer with no special privileges" — statements the Commission alleges were false, concealing an exemption from the risk engine and a virtually unlimited line of credit funded by customers. What this dossier does not do is treat any of that as established: it is a civil complaint, and the criminal case that followed was not sourced here, so no verdict is asserted.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A complaint filed by the Securities and Exchange Commission in the Southern District of New York on 13 December 2022, alleging a scheme running from at least May 2019 to November 2022; more than $1.8 billion raised from equity investors; customer assets diverted to Alameda Research from the start and used for undisclosed venture investments, real estate and political donations; Alameda exempted from the platform's risk measures and given a virtually unlimited line of credit funded by customers; billions more diverted after May 2022 to keep Alameda's lenders in place; and charges under Section 17(a) of the Securities Act and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 of the Exchange Act. The bankruptcy filing of 11 November 2022 is recorded in the same document. Everything else about this matter — including anything decided in a courtroom afterwards — is outside what was read for this dossier.

citations.title: Securities and Exchange Commission v. Samuel Bankman-Fried, Complaint, No. 1:22-cv-10501 (S.D.N.Y., filed 13 December 2022)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from sec.gov and read as extracted text. (sec.gov refuses a generic browser user-agent and serves the file to a request declaring an identity and contact address, so automated link checks report sec.gov URLs as blocked.) EVERYTHING BELOW IS AN ALLEGATION IN A CIVIL COMPLAINT, NOT A FINDING. The Summary alleges: "From at least May 2019 through November 2022, Bankman-Fried engaged in a scheme to defraud equity investors in FTX Trading Ltd. ('FTX'), the crypto asset trading platform of which he was CEO and co-founder, at the same time that he was also defrauding the platform's customers. Bankman-Fried raised more than $1.8 billion from investors, including U.S. investors, who bought an equity stake in FTX believing that FTX had appropriate controls and risk management measures. Unbeknownst to those investors (and to FTX's trading customers), Bankman-Fried was orchestrating a massive, years-long fraud, diverting billions of dollars of the trading platform's customer funds for his own personal benefit and to help grow his crypto empire." On the public posture: "Throughout this period, Bankman-Fried portrayed himself as a responsible leader of the crypto community. He touted the importance of regulation and accountability." On the mechanism alleged: "from the start, Bankman-Fried improperly diverted customer assets to his privately-held crypto hedge fund, Alameda Research LLC ('Alameda'), and then used those customer funds to make undisclosed venture investments, lavish real estate purchases, and large political donations." On what investors were told: "He told investors and prospective investors that FTX had top-notch, sophisticated automated risk measures in place to protect customer assets, that those assets were safe and secure, and that Alameda was just another platform customer with no special privileges. These statements were false and misleading. In truth, Bankman-Fried had exempted Alameda from the risk mitigation measures and had provided Alameda with significant special treatment on the FTX platform, including a virtually unlimited 'line of credit' funded by the platform's customers." On the collapse: when crypto prices fell in May 2022 and Alameda's lenders demanded repayment, "Bankman-Fried directed FTX to divert billions more in customer assets to Alameda"; through the summer of 2022 he "directed hundreds of millions more in FTX customer funds to Alameda, which he then used for additional venture investments and for 'loans' to himself and other FTX executives"; and the scheme ended when "FTX, Alameda, and their tangled web of affiliated entities filed for bankruptcy on November 11, 2022." The complaint charges violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5. The criminal proceedings in the Southern District of New York were NOT sourced for this dossier — justice.gov serves a not-found page for the press releases and nothing from it was read — so no verdict or sentence is asserted anywhere in it.

deep-state.title: $4 Billion to $36 Billion in Six Months: Swaps, "Marking the Close", and Counterparties Who Had Started Asking
participants: Prime brokers and security-based swap counterparties
Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The growth figure is the Commission's headline and it is the whole shape of the case: the scheme alleged "increased Archegos's assets under management from around $4 billion to over $36 billion in just under six months", achieved "largely through the entry into SBSs with about a dozen Counterparties".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What the instrument did was hold the exposure off anyone's view but the counterparty's. Security-based swaps gave Archegos "significant exposure to rising and falling share prices of the issuers referenced in its SBSs" without the firm appearing as the holder, and with about a dozen counterparties each seeing only their own slice of a book none of them saw whole.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is alleged to have been deliberate and specific. Archegos "knowingly provided these Counterparties with false assurances concerning its portfolio composition, its concentrated exposure, and its liquidity profile", which "fraudulently convinced its Counterparties that Archegos's overall positioning was less concentrated and more liquid than it actually was". The point of the deception was capacity: it "induced Archegos's Counterparties to continue to transact with it and extend leverage beyond what the Counterparties' risk tolerance would have otherwise permitted had they known the truth".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was a price the firm set for itself. The Commission alleges Archegos "chose not to rely on ordinary market forces" and instead manipulated the market in its top ten holdings "by dominating the market" for them, by "setting the tone" with large pre-market trading, "by bidding up prices by entering incrementally higher limit orders throughout the trading day", and by "marking the close" with large trading in the final thirty minutes — "all with the goal of artificially inflating the share prices of its Top 10 Holdings". The inflated marks then supported the margin that funded the next round.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment came two years later, and it fell on the bank rather than the fund. On 24 July 2023 the Federal Reserve announced a consent order and a $268.5 million fine with UBS for misconduct by Credit Suisse, finding "unsafe and unsound counterparty credit risk management practices" and stating that "During Credit Suisse’s relationship with Archegos, Credit Suisse failed to adequately manage the risk posed by Archegos despite repeated warnings." FINMA, acting the same day, "found that Credit Suisse had seriously and systematically violated financial market law in the context of its business relationship with the Archegos family office", ordered corrective measures from UBS as legal successor, and opened proceedings against a former Credit Suisse manager. The Federal Reserve and Prudential Regulation Authority penalties totalled approximately $387 million — against a Credit Suisse loss the Board puts at approximately $5.5 billion.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Security-based swaps as a route to equity exposure that does not appear in the holder's own disclosure, and prime brokerage relationships in which each counterparty prices the risk of a client whose total book it cannot see.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-Archegos tightening of security-based swap position reporting and of prime-broker counterparty risk practice, and a set of concluded enforcement actions — a Federal Reserve consent order, a FINMA finding, a Prudential Regulation Authority penalty — directed at the counterparties’ risk management rather than at the fund.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Margin extended by the counterparties funded the trading that inflated the prices; the inflated prices raised the value of the collateral; the richer collateral justified more margin. The loop ran until a price it did not set moved against it.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Archegos was a freak event — one secretive family office that fooled a dozen of the most sophisticated banks in the world, who were its victims.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The complaint does allege deception of the counterparties, and that half stands. But the banks-as-victims reading does not survive the regulators. The Federal Reserve’s July 2023 consent order found Credit Suisse’s counterparty credit risk management "unsafe and unsound" and stated that it "failed to adequately manage the risk posed by Archegos despite repeated warnings" — "despite repeated warnings" being the Board’s phrase, not an inference drawn here. FINMA found that in the same relationship Credit Suisse had "seriously and systematically violated financial market law". The SEC’s own complaint says the deception worked "despite varying degrees and quality of risk management and proactive questioning of Archegos by its Counterparties", and that "certain of Archegos’s Counterparties already had begun asking Archegos questions to evaluate its risk profile" before the relevant period began. Nor was the fund merely secretive: it is alleged to have been setting the prices of its own collateral by pre-market trading, incremental limit orders and marking the close. What remains allegation is what the SEC alleges against the individuals; the findings against the bank are concluded regulatory actions. The dossier keeps the two apart.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: An SEC complaint filed in the Southern District of New York on 27 April 2022 alleging that between March 2020 and March 2021 Archegos grew from around $4 billion to over $36 billion in assets under management — the Commission’s press release putting it as "approximately $1.5 billion with $10 billion in exposure in March 2020 to a value of more than $36 billion with $160 billion in exposure at its peak" — largely through security-based swaps with about a dozen counterparties; that it manipulated the market in its top ten holdings by dominating trading, setting the tone pre-market, entering incrementally higher limit orders and marking the close; and that it gave counterparties false assurances about exposure, concentration and liquidity to obtain trading capacity. Those are allegations. What is concluded, by consent and by finding: the Federal Reserve’s $268.5 million fine on UBS for Credit Suisse’s "unsafe and unsound counterparty credit risk management practices", its statement that Credit Suisse "failed to adequately manage the risk posed by Archegos despite repeated warnings", and approximately $5.5 billion of Credit Suisse losses from the default; FINMA’s finding that Credit Suisse "seriously and systematically violated financial market law" in the relationship, with corrective measures ordered against UBS and proceedings opened against a former manager; and combined Federal Reserve and Prudential Regulation Authority penalties of approximately $387 million.

citations.title: Securities and Exchange Commission v. Sung Kook (Bill) Hwang, Patrick Halligan, William Tomita and Scott Becker, Complaint, No. 1:22-cv-03402 (S.D.N.Y., filed 27 April 2022)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from sec.gov and read as extracted text. EVERYTHING BELOW IS AN ALLEGATION IN A CIVIL COMPLAINT, NOT A FINDING. The Summary alleges "a fraudulent scheme by Defendants that included interlocking deceptive acts and misconduct, through false and misleading statements to security-based swap ('SBS') counterparties and prime brokers (collectively, 'Counterparties') and manipulative trading designed to artificially move the market, which, in tandem, increased Archegos's assets under management from around $4 billion to over $36 billion in just under six months." On the instrument: "From March 2020 until its collapse in March 2021, Archegos, at Hwang's direction, underwent a period of rapid and exponential growth, achieved largely through the entry into SBSs with about a dozen Counterparties, which subjected Archegos to significant exposure to rising and falling share prices of the issuers referenced in its SBSs." On the alleged manipulation: Archegos "engaged in a brazen scheme to manipulate the market for the securities of the issuers that represented Archegos's top 10 holdings", "effected this scheme by dominating the market for its Top 10 Holdings, as well as by 'setting the tone' (i.e., engaging in large pre-market trading), bidding up prices by entering incrementally higher limit orders throughout the trading day, and 'marking the close' (i.e., engaging in large trading in the last 30 minutes of the trading day) and by other non-economic trading, all with the goal of artificially inflating the share prices of its Top 10 Holdings." On the fuel: "The margin and capacity extended by Archegos's Counterparties served as the fuel for its manipulative trading", and the defendants are alleged to have "deliberately misled many of Archegos's Counterparties" with "false assurances concerning its portfolio composition, its concentrated exposure, and its liquidity profile", which "induced Archegos's Counterparties to continue to transact with it and extend leverage beyond what the Counterparties' risk tolerance would have otherwise permitted had they known the truth". A DETAIL THAT CUTS AGAINST THE BANKS-AS-VICTIMS READING, in the complaint's own words: "as of the beginning of the Relevant Period, certain of Archegos's Counterparties already had begun asking Archegos questions to evaluate its risk profile", and the deception succeeded "despite varying degrees and quality of risk management and proactive questioning of Archegos by its Counterparties". On the collapse: over "less than a week in late March 2021, the house of cards collapsed", and the default "resulted in billions of dollars in credit losses among its Counterparties and significant losses to the market participants who invested in the stocks at inflated prices." The criminal proceedings that followed were NOT sourced for this dossier and no verdict or sentence is asserted in it.

deep-state.title: Thirty Dollars of Debt to One of Capital: the Rescue the Fed Convened and Did Not Fund
participants: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was taken before the loss, and it is the detail most often left out: "At the end of 1997, LTCM returned capital to its investors, without reducing the scale of its investments, thereby further increasing its already high leverage." Money went out of the fund while the positions stayed on. By the end of that year "LTCM was holding about $30 in debt for every $1 of capital", after reported returns of 20, 43, 41 and 17 percent across 1994 to 1997.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The structure was leverage applied to convergence: a strategy that "exploited temporary price differences between similar types of securities" and was described as market-neutral, which earns little per dollar and therefore must borrow heavily to earn much at all. The fund extended the same approach across government bonds, mortgage-backed securities and equities, and "entered into derivatives contracts extensively, including those for swaps, forwards, and options".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was on the supervisor's side, and the essay is explicit about when it lifted: "While the Fed had been aware of LTCM's situation through its usual market monitoring activities, the dangerous scale and scope of LTCM's positions became apparent only upon closer inspection" — an inspection that happened on 20 September 1998, two days after the fund itself telephoned the New York Fed, and after it had already lost 44 percent of its value in a single month.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: What was rescued was the orderly unwind, not the owners. Fourteen firms put up $3.625 billion "in exchange for 90 percent of the fund's ownership"; the partners were left running day-to-day operations "with no bonuses and limited salaries", reporting to an oversight committee of the consortium; and "LTCM's partners and other investors suffered substantial losses when their claim was reduced to 10 percent". The consortium had its $3.6 billion back by the end of 1999.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment was a room at the New York Fed and a deadline, and the essay names what it avoided as well as what it did: creditors funded the rescue, "thereby mitigating the moral hazard concerns that might have arisen had public funds been used". Its closing criticism is structural rather than exculpatory — the episode "suggests the need for an established mechanism to address the risks of fire sales arising from failing financial firms, rather than relying on the Fed to coordinate ad hoc private sector solutions at the last minute."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A hedge fund outside the prudential perimeter, financed by regulated dealers whose individual exposures were each tolerable and whose aggregate was not visible to any of them.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The convening precedent itself: a central bank assembling a private consortium in its own building, which the essay treats as an ad hoc solution standing in for a mechanism that did not exist.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Returns attracted leverage; leverage required ever-finer spreads; the capital return of 1997 raised leverage again without reducing the book; and when the spreads diverged, the counterparties who had supplied the leverage were the only parties with enough at stake to fund the unwind.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Federal Reserve bailed out a hedge fund run by Nobel laureates with public money — the first and clearest case of Wall Street being rescued at the taxpayer's expense.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: No public money was lent. The Federal Reserve History account states it twice: "While the Federal Reserve brought the market participants together and oversaw the refinancing, it did not put its own funds at risk. Rather, creditors of LTCM—who had the most to lose from its bankruptcy—arranged and financed the rescue", and the episode "represents an instance where the Federal Reserve was able to facilitate the rescue of a failing financial institution without lending its own funds." The avoidance of public funds was the point, "mitigating long-term moral hazard concerns". Nor did the owners walk away whole: the partners' claim was cut to 10 percent, they ran the wind-down on limited salaries and no bonuses under a creditors' oversight committee, and they had already lost 44 percent of the fund's value in August alone. What the record does support is a different and narrower criticism, which the essay makes itself: that a central bank had to convene an ad hoc private solution at the last minute because no established mechanism existed.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Reported returns of 20 percent in 1994, 43 in 1995, 41 in 1996 and 17 in 1997. Capital returned to investors at the end of 1997 without reducing the scale of the investments, raising leverage to about $30 of debt for every $1 of capital. A 44 percent loss of value in August 1998 after Russia devalued and defaulted. The fund's own call to the New York Fed on 18 September 1998, a Fed team on site on 20 September, and the scale of the positions becoming apparent to the supervisor only then. A Buffett-led offer of $250 million for the partners plus $3.75 billion of capital that was not accepted. And, on 23 September 1998, fourteen firms putting up $3.625 billion for 90 percent of the fund, with no Federal Reserve money at risk, the money returned by the end of 1999, and the partners reduced to a tenth.

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Near Failure of Long-Term Capital Management, September 1998", by Michael Fleming and Weiling Liu
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from federalreservehistory.org. THE ESSAY CONTRADICTS THE "FED BAILOUT" FRAMING DIRECTLY: "On September 23, 1998, a group of fourteen banks and brokerage firms invested $3.6 billion in Long-Term Capital Management L.P. (LTCM) to prevent the firm's imminent collapse ... While the Federal Reserve brought the market participants together and oversaw the refinancing, it did not put its own funds at risk. Rather, creditors of LTCM—who had the most to lose from its bankruptcy—arranged and financed the rescue. The effort thereby addressed the near-term concerns of a possible fire sale of LTCM assets, while mitigating long-term moral hazard concerns that might have arisen from the use of public funds." On the leverage: "At the end of 1997, LTCM returned capital to its investors, without reducing the scale of its investments, thereby further increasing its already high leverage", and "As of the end of 1997, LTCM was holding about $30 in debt for every $1 of capital". On the returns that preceded it: "LTCM generated above-normal returns of 20 percent in 1994, 43 percent in 1995, 41 percent in 1996, and 17 percent in 1997". On the collapse: after Russia devalued and defaulted in August 1998, "LTCM had largely been betting on the spreads in its portfolios to converge, but in almost every case, they diverged. The fund lost 44 percent of its value in August alone." On what the Fed actually did: LTCM contacted the New York Fed president on 18 September; a Fed team visited two days later; "While the Fed had been aware of LTCM's situation through its usual market monitoring activities, the dangerous scale and scope of LTCM's positions became apparent only upon closer inspection"; the Fed convened firms on 22 and 23 September. A Warren Buffett-led offer to buy out the partners for $250 million and inject $3.75 billion was not accepted "due to reported legal issues". The consortium agreed about 6:00 p.m. on 23 September: "fourteen firms put up $3.625 billion in capital in exchange for 90 percent of the fund's ownership (two firms included in the talks declined to participate)." LTCM's partners ran day-to-day operations "with no bonuses and limited salaries", reporting to an oversight committee; the consortium's $3.6 billion was returned by the end of 1999; and "LTCM's partners and other investors suffered substantial losses when their claim was reduced to 10 percent". The essay's own closing judgement: the episode "represents an instance where the Federal Reserve was able to facilitate the rescue of a failing financial institution without lending its own funds", while suggesting "the need for an established mechanism to address the risks of fire sales arising from failing financial firms, rather than relying on the Fed to coordinate ad hoc private sector solutions at the last minute." SOURCE CHARACTER: Federal Reserve History is an educational project of the Federal Reserve System. This is a signed secondary essay with its own bibliography, not a primary record, and it is tiered and attributed accordingly: the dossier says what the essay states, not what a contemporaneous document shows. deep-state.title: Corrective Action Should Be Instigated Quickly: the Memo That Was Ignored, and the Phrase That Followed
participants: Continental Illinois National Bank and Trust Company
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The growth was bought wholesale. Continental competed aggressively for oil and gas loans "amid the United States' drive for energy independence and funded that expansion with large-scale borrowing from money markets", acquiring by 1981 "a large amount of oil and gas loans from Penn Square Bank", an Oklahoma bank the essay describes as having "a freewheeling culture". A Penn Square client is quoted: "I could hardly believe it — they loaned me $2.5 million hardly asking any questions and then sold the loan to Continental."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was in the funding mix and it was partly statutory: Illinois law forbade branch banking, so the bank "had little ability to scale up funding from stable retail deposits", and at the time of its rescue "insured deposits comprised only about 15 percent of Continental's total liabilities." A bank funded by large uninsured creditors is a bank that can be left in a morning.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The warning existed, in writing, inside the bank, and this node exists because of it. An employee in Continental's oil and gas division "warned in an internal memo that 'potential credit problems could be going unnoticed' in those loans, and recommended that 'corrective action should be instigated quickly.' Her warnings, largely ignored, proved prescient when Penn Square failed in 1982". The essay extends the failure outward: "Neither Continental's own internal control system nor federal regulators' supervisory efforts fully appreciated the extent of these problems."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was a guarantee no depositor had paid for. The run began around 7 May 1984 and took about 30 percent of the bank's funding in ten days, "generally electronic and spearheaded by depositors with large uninsured deposits and other bank creditors". It stopped on 17 May when the FDIC, Federal Reserve and OCC announced an assistance programme whose "most important element was the FDIC's announcement that it would guarantee of all of the bank's creditors", with a $2 billion FDIC loan and a Federal Reserve statement that it was "prepared to meet any extraordinary liquidity requirements".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The resolution was ownership rather than an inquiry: when the run resumed the FDIC took "80 percent ownership in Continental's holding company" and assumed its Federal Reserve loan. The losses were distributed unevenly and the essay records it: "its shareholders lost their investments in the bank and its management was fired", while uninsured creditors were made whole, and "The FDIC ultimately estimated its loss was about $1.1 billion, equal to about 3 percent of Continental's assets at the time of its intervention."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Deposit insurance designed for small depositors, applied to a bank whose liabilities were overwhelmingly uninsured and wholesale, under a state branching prohibition that made retail funding impossible.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The doctrine itself: "The phrase 'too big to fail' became commonly used for the first time after Continental's crisis", and with it the expectation that the creditors of a sufficiently large bank are covered whether or not the insurance says so.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Wholesale funding bought loan growth; loan growth required more wholesale funding; the uninsured creditors who supplied it could leave electronically in a morning, which is precisely why they had to be guaranteed when they tried to.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Continental Illinois was the first bank bailout, in which Washington simply handed public money to a reckless bank and nobody suffered.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The distribution of loss is on the record and it is not "nobody". Continental's "shareholders lost their investments in the bank and its management was fired", and the FDIC estimated its own loss at about $1.1 billion. What was rescued was the creditor class: the FDIC guaranteed all of the bank's creditors, including the large uninsured depositors whose electronic withdrawals had caused the run. That is the precise thing worth naming, and it is more specific than "bailout" — it is a guarantee extended to people who had not bought one, in a bank whose insured deposits were only about 15 percent of its liabilities. The counter-reading, that regulators acted on a whim, also fails: the essay records the decision following "vigorous internal debate about a range of possible options".
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Oil and gas loans purchased in volume from Penn Square Bank by 1981. An internal memo from Continental's own oil and gas division warning that "potential credit problems could be going unnoticed" and that "corrective action should be instigated quickly", largely ignored, before Penn Square failed in 1982. Neither the bank's internal controls nor federal supervision appreciating the extent of the problem. Insured deposits at about 15 percent of total liabilities. A run from about 7 May 1984 taking roughly 30 percent of funding in ten days, led by large uninsured depositors and other creditors. An assistance programme announced on 17 May guaranteeing all of the bank's creditors, with a $2 billion FDIC loan and a Federal Reserve commitment on liquidity. A second run, then 80 percent FDIC ownership of the holding company. Shareholders wiped out, management fired, and an FDIC loss of about $1.1 billion — and a phrase that entered common use for the first time.

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Continental Illinois: A Bank That Was Too Big to Fail, May 1984" (published 15 May 2023)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from federalreservehistory.org. On the origin of the phrase: the essay is subtitled "A Bank That Was Too Big to Fail" and records that "The phrase 'too big to fail' became commonly used for the first time after Continental's crisis", and that the episode "ignited a national debate that continues to this day over whether large financial institutions enjoy undue privileges because regulators consider them too big to fail." THE WARNING THAT WAS IGNORED, which is the heart of this node: as Continental's purchases of oil and gas loans from Penn Square Bank accumulated, "an employee in Continental's oil and gas division warned in an internal memo that 'potential credit problems could be going unnoticed' in those loans, and recommended that 'corrective action should be instigated quickly.' Her warnings, largely ignored, proved prescient when Penn Square failed in 1982". The essay adds: "Neither Continental's own internal control system nor federal regulators' supervisory efforts fully appreciated the extent of these problems." On the funding structure: Illinois law forbade branch banking, so the bank "had little ability to scale up funding from stable retail deposits", and "At the time of its rescue, insured deposits comprised only about 15 percent of Continental's total liabilities." On the run: "A large-scale run by depositors on Continental began around May 7, 1984 ... Over the next ten days, the bank lost about 30 percent of its funding. The run was generally electronic and spearheaded by depositors with large uninsured deposits and other bank creditors." On the rescue: it stopped on 17 May when the FDIC, Federal Reserve and OCC announced a temporary assistance program, of which "The most important element was the FDIC's announcement that it would guarantee of all of the bank's creditors" (the grammatical slip is the essay's); the FDIC also lent $2 billion, and the Federal Reserve announced it "is prepared to meet any extraordinary liquidity requirements". When the run resumed, the FDIC took "80 percent ownership in Continental's holding company". On who bore the loss: "its shareholders lost their investments in the bank and its management was fired", and "The FDIC ultimately estimated its loss was about $1.1 billion, equal to about 3 percent of Continental's assets at the time of its intervention." SOURCE CHARACTER: Federal Reserve History is an educational project of the Federal Reserve System. deep-state.title: With the Encouragement of the US Government: Petrodollars Lent Out, and a Warning from 1977

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The fee was the spread on recycling somebody else's surplus. Two oil shocks "created current account deficits in many Latin American countries" and "current account surpluses among oil-exporting countries", and, in the essay's own words, "With the encouragement of the US government, large US money-center banks were willing intermediaries between the two groups, providing the exporting countries with a safe, liquid place for their funds and then lending those funds to Latin America."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was concentration, and it is quantified. Total outstanding Latin American debt went from "$29 billion" at the end of 1970 to "$159 billion" by the end of 1978 and "$327 billion" by 1982. On the lenders' side, "by 1982, the nine largest US money-center banks held Latin American debt amounting to 176 percent of their capital; their total LDC debt was nearly 290 percent of capital." A loss on that book was not a loss of profit; it was a loss of the banks.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: There was no fog about the risk, which is what makes this node a foreknowledge node rather than a misfortune. "The potential risk of the growing involvement of US banks in Latin American and other less-developed country (LDC) debt didn't go unnoticed. In 1977, during a speech at the Columbia University Graduate School of Business, then-Fed Chairman Arthur Burns criticized commercial banks for assuming excessive risk in their Third World lending." The lending roughly doubled again after that.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall ran for a decade and the bill was presented to the borrowers. The essay calls the 1980s for Latin America "a period often referred to as the 'lost decade'" in which "many Latin American countries became unable to service their foreign debt", and records that the international response "ultimately helped alleviate the situation, albeit with some unintended consequences".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment was the workout itself, conducted through the IMF and the central banks over years rather than through any inquiry into how banks came to hold sovereign exposure at 176 percent of capital after their own regulator had warned about it in 1977. The essay records the response and its unintended consequences; it apportions no blame and no liability, and neither does this dossier.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Eurodollar market and a sovereign-lending convention that treated states as unable to go bankrupt, with deposits from oil exporters available to be lent on at a margin.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The decade-long sovereign workout apparatus — IMF programmes, rescheduling rounds and ultimately the Brady restructuring — which converted bank exposure into tradable sovereign paper.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Oil surpluses were deposited with the banks; the banks lent them to oil-importing states; the states' repayments depended on commodity prices and on rates the banks' own central bank set; and when rates rose, the exposure that had been the banks' profit became the reason they could not be allowed to take the loss.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Latin America borrowed recklessly in the 1970s and the lost decade was the natural price of its own profligacy — or, inverted, that the whole episode was a deliberate plot to capture the continent through debt.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The profligacy reading omits who arranged the lending and on whose encouragement. The essay records that the recycling of oil surpluses into Latin American debt was done by large US money-center banks acting "With the encouragement of the US government", and that by 1982 those banks held Latin American debt at 176 percent of their capital — a structure built by lenders, not only by borrowers. The plot reading fails on the 1977 warning: if the exposure had been designed as a trap, the Federal Reserve chairman criticising commercial banks publicly "for assuming excessive risk in their Third World lending" five years before the default would be an odd move. What the record shows is a known risk that was named by the regulator and run anyway because it was profitable.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Oil shocks producing matched deficits and surpluses; US money-center banks intermediating between them with the encouragement of the US government. Debt rising from $29 billion at the end of 1970 to $159 billion by the end of 1978 and $327 billion by 1982. A public warning by Fed Chairman Arthur Burns at Columbia in 1977 about commercial banks assuming excessive risk in Third World lending. Nine largest money-center banks holding Latin American debt at 176 percent of capital and total less-developed-country debt at nearly 290 percent of capital by 1982. And a decade in which many of the borrowing countries could not service the debt, with an international response that helped "albeit with some unintended consequences".

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Latin American Debt Crisis of the 1980s, 1982-1989", by Jocelyn Sims and Jessie Romero
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from federalreservehistory.org. On the recycling mechanism: "During the 1970s, two large oil price shocks created current account deficits in many Latin American countries. At the same time, these shocks created current account surpluses among oil-exporting countries. With the encouragement of the US government, large US money-center banks were willing intermediaries between the two groups, providing the exporting countries with a safe, liquid place for their funds and then lending those funds to Latin America." The phrase "With the encouragement of the US government" is the essay's. On the scale: "At the end of 1970, total outstanding debt from all sources totaled only $29 billion, but by the end of 1978, that number had skyrocketed to $159 billion. By 1982, the debt level reached $327 billion." THE WARNING ON THE RECORD, and its date: "The potential risk of the growing involvement of US banks in Latin American and other less-developed country (LDC) debt didn't go unnoticed. In 1977, during a speech at the Columbia University Graduate School of Business, then-Fed Chairman Arthur Burns criticized commercial banks for assuming excessive risk in their Third World lending." And what happened anyway: "Still, by 1982, the nine largest US money-center banks held Latin American debt amounting to 176 percent of their capital; their total LDC debt was nearly 290 percent of capital." The essay describes the decade as one "often referred to as the 'lost decade'" in which "many Latin American countries became unable to service their foreign debt", and says the international response "ultimately helped alleviate the situation, albeit with some unintended consequences." SOURCE CHARACTER: Federal Reserve History is an educational project of the Federal Reserve System. This is a signed secondary essay with its own bibliography, not a primary record, and it is tiered and attributed accordingly: the dossier says what the essay states, not what a contemporaneous document shows. deep-state.title: Eight Central Banks Holding a Price: the Pool That Collapsed in March 1968

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was spent was reserves, to hold a number. After a run sent the London price to $40 an ounce on 20 October 1960, the Pool was formed on 1 November 1961 by eight central banks, which "agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system" and keep the price at $35.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was the promise itself: since 1958 "countries settled their international balances in dollars, and U.S. dollars were convertible to gold at a fixed exchange rate of $35 an ounce", with the United States responsible for keeping that price fixed. A convertibility pledge is only as good as the metal behind it, and the Pool existed because the market had begun to test it.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The intervention was the fog: a price maintained by coordinated central bank selling looks, to anyone reading the quote, like a market price. The essay records the parallel machinery of swap lines with nine central banks providing "up to $900 million equivalent in foreign exchange", and notes that "What started as a small, short-term credit facility grew to be a large, intermediate-term facility" — a temporary fix that was "a sign of a fundamental problem in the monetary system".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The arrangement bought seven years. "The pool was successful for six years until another gold crisis ensued", and in that time the dollar's convertibility was treated as sound because its price did not move.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The ending was a two-tier fiction rather than an admission. Sterling devalued, a run on gold followed, France withdrew, and "The pool collapsed in March 1968." The seven remaining members then "agreed to formulate a two-tiered system", with central banks using gold only to settle international debts — one price for governments and another for everyone else. The gold window closed entirely in August 1971.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Bretton Woods: fixed currencies against the dollar and the dollar fixed to gold at $35, with the United States carrying the convertibility obligation for the system.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The two-tier gold market of March 1968, and then the closing of the gold window in August 1971 — the end of the convertibility the Pool had been built to defend.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Defending the price required selling reserves; selling reserves reduced the backing that made the price credible; the weaker the backing, the more the price had to be defended. The swap lines that were meant to bridge the gap grew into a standing facility, which the essay reads as the symptom rather than the cure.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the gold price was secretly rigged by a cartel of central banks, and that the public was never told.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The price was indeed held by coordinated central bank intervention — but not secretly, and the source for that is a Federal Reserve publication stating it plainly: the London Gold Pool "was formed on November 1, 1961", consisted of eight named central banks, and "agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system" and keep gold at $35 an ounce. An arrangement whose membership, date, mechanism and purpose are published by one of its members is a policy, not a conspiracy. What the record does support is the thing the decoy gestures at without naming: the price people could observe was an administered price, it was administered until it could not be, and when it failed the response was a two-tier system that kept one price for central banks and let the other float.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A run that sent the London gold price to $40 an ounce on 20 October 1960. The London Gold Pool formed on 1 November 1961 by eight central banks — Great Britain, West Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, France and the United States — pooling reserves to hold the price at $35. Parallel swap lines with nine central banks providing up to $900 million equivalent, which grew from a short-term facility into an intermediate-term one. Success for six years. Then sterling's devaluation, another run on gold, France's withdrawal, and the Pool's collapse in March 1968, followed by a two-tier system in which the seven remaining members used gold only to settle international debts. Convertibility ended altogether in August 1971.

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Nixon Ends Convertibility of U.S. Dollars to Gold and Announces Wage/Price Controls, August 1971", by Sandra Kollen Ghizoni
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from federalreservehistory.org. NOTE ON FIT: the essay's subject is August 1971, not March 1968. It is cited here because it contains the passage on the London Gold Pool, which is this node's subject, and nothing in this dossier is drawn from the essay beyond what it says about the Pool and the system around it. On the system: under Bretton Woods "countries agreed to keep their currencies fixed (but adjustable in exceptional situations) to the dollar, and the dollar was fixed to gold. Since 1958 ... countries settled their international balances in dollars, and U.S. dollars were convertible to gold at a fixed exchange rate of $35 an ounce." ON THE POOL ITSELF: "A run in the London gold market sent the price to $40 an ounce on October 20, 1960, exacerbating the threat to the system. In response, the London Gold Pool was formed on November 1, 1961. The pool consisted of a group of eight central banks (Great Britain, West Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, France, and the United States). In order to keep the price of gold at $35 an ounce, the group agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system. The pool was successful for six years until another gold crisis ensued. The British pound sterling devalued and another run on gold occurred, and France withdrew from the pool. The pool collapsed in March 1968. At that time the seven remaining members of the London Gold Pool ... agreed to formulate a two-tiered system." On the swap lines that ran alongside it: credit lines with nine central banks "provided up to $900 million equivalent in foreign exchange", and "What started as a small, short-term credit facility grew to be a large, intermediate-term facility until the U.S. gold window closed in August 1971. The growth and need for the swap lines signaled that they were not just a temporary fix, but a sign of a fundamental problem in the monetary system." SOURCE CHARACTER: Federal Reserve History is an educational project of the Federal Reserve System. This is a signed secondary essay with its own bibliography, not a primary record, and it is tiered and attributed accordingly: the dossier says what the essay states, not what a contemporaneous document shows. deep-state.title: Standing for Delivery: a Dominant Copper Position, and $150 Million Neither Admitted Nor Denied

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The motive the order records is loss, not greed: "In the wake of accumulating large losses from speculative trading, the principal copper trader for Sumitomo engaged in a scheme, in conjunction with an entity operating in the United States, with the intent of manipulating the price of copper." The manipulation began as a way of not realising what had already been lost.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was physical control of a market through its delivery mechanism. During 1995 and 1996 Sumitomo "established and maintained large and dominant futures positions in copper metal on the LME", and "In the fall of 1995, Sumitomo stood for delivery on a significant percentage of its maturing futures contracts. It thereby acquired a dominant and controlling cash and futures market position".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was the price itself. A dominant holder standing for delivery produces a quoted price that looks like scarcity, and the order finds the effect "directly and predictably caused copper prices, including prices on the United States cash and futures markets, to reach artificially high levels" — prices paid by everyone who used copper, none of whom could see the position producing them.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is stated as the object of the exercise: the actions were taken "expressly for the purpose of creating artificially high absolute prices and an artificially high premium of nearby prices over futures prices", which Sumitomo "intentionally exploited ... in order to profit on the liquidation of its large portfolio of futures contracts and holdings of LME warrants."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The settlement is the containment and its shape is worth reading closely. $150 million in total, of which $125 million was an immediate civil penalty and $25 million was escrowed for up to four years for restitution to injured persons — reverting to the Treasury as penalty if unclaimed. The findings were "neither admitted nor denied". And the chairperson's statement credits the company for "constructive actions it has taken and losses it has suffered in the wake of the public disclosure of the misconduct", which is a regulator explaining why the number is what it is.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A metals exchange whose price is set by physical delivery against warrants, and a cross-border market in which the dominant position sat on one exchange while the affected prices were in several jurisdictions.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The cooperation precedent the Commission emphasises — "unprecedented cooperation with regulatory authorities in the United Kingdom, in particular the Financial Services Authority, and with the Japanese Government" — and the assertion of US jurisdiction over manipulation conducted on a London exchange.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Speculative losses created the need to support the price; supporting the price required a larger position; the larger position made the price more artificial and the eventual unwind more damaging, which is the position the trader was trying not to have.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That one rogue trader secretly cornered the world copper market for a decade while his employer knew nothing, and that regulators never got to the bottom of it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Commission’s order is against the corporation, not an individual: it found "that Sumitomo Corporation of Japan (Sumitomo) manipulated the copper market in 1995 and 1996", acting "through its agent or agents". That is a finding of corporate liability, which is the opposite of the lone-rogue framing. It is also narrower in time than the legend — 1995 and 1996, not a decade. But the dossier must not overstate it in the other direction either: the order settled the matter by consent and "Sumitomo neither admitted nor denied the findings", so this is a settled regulatory finding rather than an adjudicated verdict, and no individual is found liable in it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A CFTC order of 11 May 1998, settled by consent, finding that Sumitomo manipulated the copper market in 1995 and 1996 in violation of Sections 6(c), 6(d) and 9(a)(2) of the Commodity Exchange Act. Large and dominant LME futures positions; standing for delivery on a significant percentage of maturing contracts in autumn 1995; a resulting dominant and controlling cash and futures position that directly and predictably drove US cash and futures prices to artificially high levels; and the express purpose of creating an artificially high price and nearby premium to profit on liquidating the futures portfolio and LME warrants. $150 million total: $125 million immediate civil penalty, $25 million escrowed up to four years for restitution. Findings neither admitted nor denied.

citations.title: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, "CFTC Files and Settles Action Against Sumitomo Corporation for Manipulating the Copper Market in 1995-96", Release 4144-98, 11 May 1998
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from cftc.gov. The Commission issued an order "in connection with settling the matter by consent, finding that Sumitomo Corporation of Japan (Sumitomo) manipulated the copper market in 1995 and 1996", in which "Sumitomo neither admitted nor denied the findings". THE MECHANISM AS THE ORDER DESCRIBES IT: "In the wake of accumulating large losses from speculative trading, the principal copper trader for Sumitomo engaged in a scheme, in conjunction with an entity operating in the United States, with the intent of manipulating the price of copper. In particular, during 1995 and 1996, Sumitomo, acting through its agent or agents, established and maintained large and dominant futures positions in copper metal on the LME. In the fall of 1995, Sumitomo stood for delivery on a significant percentage of its maturing futures contracts. It thereby acquired a dominant and controlling cash and futures market position, which directly and predictably caused copper prices, including prices on the United States cash and futures markets, to reach artificially high levels." The purpose is stated: "expressly for the purpose of creating artificially high absolute prices and an artificially high premium of nearby prices over futures prices", which Sumitomo "intentionally exploited ... in order to profit on the liquidation of its large portfolio of futures contracts and holdings of LME warrants", in violation of Sections 6(c), 6(d) and 9(a)(2) of the Commodity Exchange Act. THE PENALTY: "a total of $150 million", of which "$125 million will be paid as a civil monetary penalty immediately" and "The remaining $25 million will be placed into escrow for a period of up to four years" available "to provide restitution to persons injured by Sumitomo's unlawful conduct", reverting to the Treasury as penalty if unclaimed. CFTC Chairperson Brooksley Born called it "an historic moment in the Commission's work to protect the people of the United States, the United States cash and futures markets and their participants against market manipulation", noting also "the credit Sumitomo deserves for constructive actions it has taken and losses it has suffered in the wake of the public disclosure of the misconduct", and describing "unprecedented cooperation with regulatory authorities in the United Kingdom, in particular the Financial Services Authority, and with the Japanese Government". A settled consent order whose findings were neither admitted nor denied. deep-state.title: One Hundred Percent Restitution: $1.212 Billion Back, and an Admission of Liability
participants: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was taken was customer money held under a statutory protection. The CFTC’s complaint charged MF Global and other defendants "with unlawful use of customer funds", and charged the firm, "a registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM), with violating provisions of the Commodity Exchange Act and CFTC Regulations intended to protect FCM customer funds and requiring diligent supervision by registrants."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was of segregation itself — the rule that a futures commission merchant holds customer property apart from its own. The charge is not of a bad trade but of using funds that were not the firm’s to use, and of failing in the supervision the registration carries with it.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The shortfall became visible only at failure, which is what segregation rules exist to prevent: the restitution ordered was "to ensure customers recover their losses sustained when MF Global failed in 2011", and the trustee had to seek permission "to pay restitution in full to customers to remedy any shortfall with funds of the MF Global general estate."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: There was no windfall; there was a hole, and it was filled. The consent order required "$1.212 billion in restitution to customers", and the acting enforcement director framed the objective as "100 percent restitution ... to satisfy customer losses".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The disposition is unusually un-whitewashed for this atlas and the dossier should say so. The order was entered by a federal judge, it imposed a $100 million civil penalty subordinated to customer and priority-creditor recovery, and — unlike most settlements in this file — "In the consent Order, MF Global admits to the allegations pertaining to its liability based on the acts and omissions of its employees". As at the date of the release, "The CFTC's litigation continues against the remaining defendants: MF Global Holdings Ltd., Jon S. Corzine, and Edith O'Brien" — pending matters whose outcomes are not sourced here and are not asserted.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The futures commission merchant regime: customer funds segregated by rule, with the firm permitted to invest them within limits and the protection resting on the firm’s own compliance.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-MF Global tightening of customer-funds protection and residual-interest rules, and a consent order in which an FCM admitted liability rather than neither admitting nor denying.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Customer property was the cheapest liquidity available to a firm under funding stress; using it relieved the stress that made it attractive; and the protection that should have prevented it depended on the same firm reporting its own compliance.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That MF Global’s customers were simply robbed and never made whole, and that nobody admitted anything or paid a penny.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Both halves are contradicted by the order. Customers were made whole: the consent order required $1.212 billion in restitution and the trustee obtained permission to pay customers in full from the general estate, with the enforcement division describing the aim as 100 percent restitution. And an admission was made: "In the consent Order, MF Global admits to the allegations pertaining to its liability based on the acts and omissions of its employees" — which is rarer than the usual neither-admit-nor-deny formula and should be reported as such. What the document does not establish is anything about the individuals: the litigation against MF Global Holdings, Jon S. Corzine and Edith O'Brien was continuing as at this release, and nothing about its outcome is sourced here.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A CFTC complaint of 27 June 2013 charging MF Global with unlawful use of customer funds and with violating Commodity Exchange Act provisions and CFTC regulations protecting FCM customer funds and requiring diligent supervision. A federal court consent order entered on 8 November 2013 by Judge Victor Marrero in the Southern District of New York requiring $1.212 billion in restitution to customers, and imposing a $100 million civil monetary penalty payable only after customers and priority creditors are paid. The firm’s admission of liability for the acts and omissions of its employees. The trustee’s bankruptcy-court permission to pay customers in full from the general estate. And continuing litigation, as at 18 November 2013, against MF Global Holdings Ltd., Jon S. Corzine and Edith O'Brien.

citations.title: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, "Federal Court in New York Orders MF Global Inc. to Pay over $1 Billion in Restitution to Customers", Release 6776-13, 18 November 2013
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from cftc.gov. The CFTC "obtained a federal court consent Order against Defendant MF Global Inc. (MF Global) requiring it to pay $1.212 billion in restitution to customers of MF Global to ensure customers recover their losses sustained when MF Global failed in 2011." The order was "entered on November 8, 2013 by U.S. District Court Judge Victor Marrero of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York", and "also imposes a $100 million civil monetary penalty on MF Global, to be paid after MF Global has fully paid customers and certain other creditors entitled to priority under bankruptcy law." On the shortfall being made good: "The Trustee for MF Global obtained permission from the bankruptcy court to pay restitution in full to customers to remedy any shortfall with funds of the MF Global general estate." THE ADMISSION, which distinguishes this from a neither-admit-nor-deny settlement: "In the consent Order, MF Global admits to the allegations pertaining to its liability based on the acts and omissions of its employees as set forth in the consent Order and the Complaint." The underlying complaint, filed 27 June 2013, charged MF Global and other defendants "with unlawful use of customer funds", and charged the firm, "a registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM), with violating provisions of the Commodity Exchange Act and CFTC Regulations intended to protect FCM customer funds and requiring diligent supervision by registrants." The release records that "The CFTC's litigation continues against the remaining defendants: MF Global Holdings Ltd., Jon S. carbon-class.title: Famine as Fiscal Policy: How the East India Company Taxed Bengal's Dead to Repay Parliament

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Post-Plassey, the Company converted the Bengal diwani into a fixed land-tax annuity, seizing the revenue stream of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa before any famine pressure existed.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Company tax collectors maintained the fixed revenue demand through 1769-1770 while grain prices soared, structurally prioritizing shareholder remittance over subsistence in the tax-yielding provinces.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Famine mortality — estimated at roughly a third of the affected population in contemporaneous Company and Indian sources — was reported slowly to London, where the Company's insolvency, not the dead, framed parliamentary debate.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Parliament answered with the 1773 Regulating and Tea Acts: a 1.4 million pound loan to the Company, its monopoly left intact, serviced by the very Bengal revenue the famine had gutted the population to collect.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The 1784 India Act subordinated the Company to a Board of Control, recasting insolvency and famine as an accountability problem solved by parliamentary oversight — no forfeiture, no shareholder liability, extraction machinery preserved.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Company inherited the joint-stock monopoly charter east of the Cape and, via Plassey, the Mughal revenue-farming apparatus of Bengal, fusing corporate trade privilege with sovereign tax power.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The 1773-1784 acts created the permanent template of state-bailed monopoly: parliamentary 'regulation' that socialized the Company's debts while privatizing its monopoly rents.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Bengal land tax serviced the parliamentary loan and Company dividends, recirculating colonial extraction upward to British creditors and shareholders at the direct cost of the taxed famine population.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: This bailout-monopoly template — cheap monopoly goods dumped to service debt, exemplified by the Tea Act — set the mechanism for the 1773 Boston Tea Party and the state-chartered extraction conduits that followed.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The 'wicked monopoly company' framing reduces the episode to a morality tale of Company greed, resolved once Parliament asserted control.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: It obscures the ledger: Parliament did not break the monopoly or penalize the shareholders — it lent the Company 1.4 million pounds repaid from Bengal revenue, deepening the extraction loop it purported to reform.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Contemporaneous Company and Indian sources record fixed tax demand sustained through the famine, mortality near a third of the affected provinces, and the 1773 loan and 1784 subordination — a documented chain from tax collection to parliamentary bailout to continued monopoly.
