The 2006 seismic guidelines required a back-check; the official deadline was June 2009; "TEPCO made the decision internally and unilaterally to reschedule the deadline to January 2016", and the commission "verified the fact that TEPCO had added no reinforcements to Units 1 through 3 at the time of the March 11 earthquake". The IAEA’s Director General records the same gap in cooler language: the plant’s vulnerability to external hazards "had not been reassessed in a systematic and comprehensive manner during its lifetime", there were no regulatory requirements in Japan that it be, and the tsunami guidance was "generic and brief". The design basis flood level stood at 3.1 m; a 2009 in-house estimate of 6.1 m produced one change, the raising of residual-heat-removal pump motors, and "No other safety measures had been implemented to enhance flood protection, such as measures to avoid the flooding of emergency diesel generators."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: After the accident the fog fell on the people living around the plant. Many residents "were unaware that the accident had occured, or of its drastic escalation and the radiation leakage, even after the government and some municipalities were informed". The evacuation zone went from 3 km to 10 km to 20 km in a single day, moving people each time; 146,520 were evacuated under government orders; "Some evacuees were unaware that they had been relocated to sites with high levels of radiation"; 60 patients died in March from complications of the evacuation; and areas inside the 30 km zone shown to be badly contaminated once SPEEDI data was released on 23 March were not evacuated for another month. The commission’s own words: "the government effectively abandoned their responsibility for public safety."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was the twenty years of operation that the unbuilt defences bought, and the arrangement that made them unnecessary. NISA sat inside METI, the ministry promoting nuclear power. The commission found the regulators would "explicitly ask about the operators’ intentions whenever a new regulation was to be implemented" — in one instance telling operators they need not consider a station blackout, then asking them to write the report justifying why not.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The attempt at containment was an account of cause, and it is named as such by the body set up to test it. "We conclude that TEPCO was too quick to cite the tsunami as the cause of the nuclear accident and deny that the earthquake caused any damage ... The Commission believes that this is an attempt to avoid responsibility by putting all the blame on the unexpected (the tsunami), as they wrote in their midterm report, and not on the more foreseeable earthquake." The Diet commission was the first investigative body in Japan’s constitutional history empowered by the legislature and independent of the bureaucracy; the whitewash it describes is the one it was created to break.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A promotional ministry holding the safety regulator inside it, an industry association negotiating standards on the operators’ behalf, and a consensus hazard methodology — the Japan Society of Civil Engineers model published in 2002 — that assumed no tsunami-generating earthquake along the Japan Trench offshore of the site.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Nuclear Regulation Authority, created outside METI after the accident, and a Diet commission precedent for an investigation with subpoena-backed independence from the bureaucracy it examines.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The operator opposed the rules through the industry association; the regulator asked the operator what it was prepared to accept; the resulting standard was met without reinforcement; and the saving stayed with the company until the cost fell on 146,520 evacuated people and on the state.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That TEPCO’s own engineers calculated a 15.7-metre wave in 2008, that the company buried the finding, and that the meltdowns were therefore a concealed and knowing choice.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Neither document read for this dossier contains that figure. The Diet commission’s executive summary does not state it; the IAEA Director General’s report does not state it, and gives instead a 2009 in-house estimate of 6.1 m against a 3.1 m design basis, on which one change was made. The two reports also differ from each other in a way the single-number story hides: the Diet commission finds collusion and safety measures "intentionally postponed", while the IAEA finds an absence of regulatory requirement and a hazard methodology that assumed the wrong source model. Neither of those is the same claim as a buried calculation, and asserting the figure would mean citing it to pages that do not carry it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The Diet commission’s finding, in its own words: the accident "was a profoundly manmade disaster — that could and should have been foreseen and prevented", the result "of collusion between the government, the regulators and TEPCO", and "The direct causes of the accident were all foreseeable prior to March 11, 2011." Specifically: "Since 2006, the regulators and TEPCO were aware of the risk that a total outage of electricity at the Fukushima Daiichi plant might occur if a tsunami were to reach the level of the site", and "NISA knew that TEPCO had not prepared any measures to lessen or eliminate the risk, but failed to provide specific instructions to remedy the situation"; they "either intentionally postponed putting safety measures in place, or made decisions based on their organization’s self interest, and not in the interest of public safety." The seismic back-check deadline was moved by the operator alone from 2009 to 2016 and no reinforcement had been added to Units 1 to 3. The IAEA records the reassessments that did happen under the 2002 JSCE methodology, the 2009 estimate of 6.1 m, the single resulting design change, and that no other flood protection was added. And on the aftermath: 146,520 people evacuated under orders that changed three times in a day, some into areas of higher contamination, 60 deaths in March from evacuation complications, and a month’s delay in moving people out of contaminated areas inside the 30 km zone after 23 March.

citations.title: The National Diet of Japan, The official report of The Fukushima Nuclear Accident Independent Investigation Commission (NAIIC) — Executive summary, Global edition (2012)
citations.quoteOrFact: The Commission's own site (naiic.go.jp) no longer exists; the PDF was downloaded from the National Diet Library's web archive capture of 25 October 2012 and read as extracted text. The chairman's message states that the accident "cannot be regarded as a natural disaster. It was a profoundly manmade disaster — that could and should have been foreseen and prevented." The Commission's conclusion: "The TEPCO Fukushima Nuclear Power Plant accident was the result of collusion between the government, the regulators and TEPCO, and the lack of governance by said parties. They effectively betrayed the nation's right to be safe from nuclear accidents. Therefore, we conclude that the accident was clearly 'manmade.'" On foreknowledge of the hazard specifically: "The direct causes of the accident were all foreseeable prior to March 11, 2011"; "Since 2006, the regulators and TEPCO were aware of the risk that a total outage of electricity at the Fukushima Daiichi plant might occur if a tsunami were to reach the level of the site. They were also aware of the risk of reactor core damage from the loss of seawater pumps in the case of a tsunami larger than assumed in the Japan Society of Civil Engineers estimation. NISA knew that TEPCO had not prepared any measures to lessen or eliminate the risk, but failed to provide specific instructions to remedy the situation." And: "There were many opportunities for taking preventive measures prior to March 11. The accident occurred because TEPCO did not take these measures, and NISA and the Nuclear Safety Commission (NSC) went along. They either intentionally postponed putting safety measures in place, or made decisions based on their organization's self interest, and not in the interest of public safety." On the motive it ascribes: "From TEPCO's perspective, new regulations would have interfered with plant operations and weakened their stance in potential lawsuits." On the seismic backcheck it records that although the official deadline was June 2009, "TEPCO made the decision internally and unilaterally to reschedule the deadline to January 2016", and that the Commission "verified the fact that TEPCO had added no reinforcements to Units 1 through 3 at the time of the March 11 earthquake." On attribution of cause it goes against TEPCO: "We conclude that TEPCO was too quick to cite the tsunami as the cause of the nuclear accident and deny that the earthquake caused any damage ... The Commission believes that this is an attempt to avoid responsibility by putting all the blame on the unexpected (the tsunami), as they wrote in their midterm report, and not on the more foreseeable earthquake." On what residents were told: "The Commission's investigation revealed that many residents were unaware that the accident had occured, or of its drastic escalation and the radiation leakage, even after the government and some municipalities were informed"; evacuation zones were widened from 3 km to 10 km to 20 km in a single day, 146,520 residents were evacuated under government orders, "Some evacuees were unaware that they had been relocated to sites with high levels of radiation", 60 patients died in March from complications related to the evacuation, and areas inside the 30 km zone known to be highly contaminated once SPEEDI data was released on 23 March were only evacuated "one month later". The Commission states: "the government effectively abandoned their responsibility for public safety." NOTE ON A FIGURE NOT IN THIS DOCUMENT: this executive summary contains no reference to a 15.7 metre in-house TEPCO tsunami estimate, and no such figure is asserted anywhere in this dossier. The Global edition is a translation of selected elements; the Japanese-language version is the official one and prevails on any discrepancy.

citations.title: International Atomic Energy Agency, The Fukushima Daiichi Accident — Report by the Director General (IAEA, Vienna, 2015)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the IAEA's own publications server and read as extracted text. The Director General's report is more measured than the Diet commission's and is cited here for that reason. It finds that "The vulnerability of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant to external hazards had not been reassessed in a systematic and comprehensive manner during its lifetime. At the time of the accident, there were no regulatory requirements in Japan for such reassessments, and relevant domestic and international operating experience was not adequately considered in the existing regulations and guidelines. The regulatory guidelines in Japan on methods for dealing with the effects of events associated with earthquakes, such as tsunamis, were generic and brief, and did not provide specific criteria or detailed guidance." It records that "Before the accident, the operator had conducted some reassessments of extreme tsunami flood levels, using a consensus based methodology developed in Japan in 2002, which had resulted in values higher than the original design basis estimates", that methodology being the Japan Society of Civil Engineers model published in 2002, "in which no earthquake generating a tsunami is assumed to occur along the Japan Trench offshore of the Fukushima Daiichi site". It states that "TEPCO did not consider large magnitude earthquakes that had occurred elsewhere and did not postulate them as a local tsunami source at the Japan Trench", and that "At the time of the accident, TEPCO had not completed the re-assessment of the vulnerability of the plant to earthquakes and tsunamis." On the reassessment that was acted on: "In 2009, TEPCO estimated a value of 6.1 m for the maximum tsunami height, using the latest bathymetric and tidal data. As a result of this new estimate, some design changes were made at the Fukushima Daiichi NPP, notably raising the motors of the pumps used for the removal of residual heat. During the accident, this measure alone proved to be insufficient. No other safety measures had been implemented to enhance flood protection, such as measures to avoid the flooding of emergency diesel generators." The design basis flood level in force was 3.1 m. This report does not use the language of collusion or of intentional postponement, and it does not state a 15.7 metre in-house estimate.

carbon-class.title: The Milking Program: $11 Billion Out, $4.325 Billion Offered Back, and the Release the Supreme Court Refused
participants: U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York
U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
Supreme Court of the United States

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim is dated and quantified in the Supreme Court's own opinion, and its timing is the whole point. Before the 2007 federal plea, distributions to the family "represented less than 15% of its annual revenue". After it, "the Sacklers began taking as much as 70% of the company's revenue each year". Between 2008 and 2016 those distributions "totaled approximately $11 billion, draining Purdue's total assets by 75% and leaving it in 'a significantly weakened financial' state", with much of it diverted "to overseas trusts and family-owned companies". One family member's own word for it, as recorded below and quoted by the Court, was a "milking" program.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What was compromised first was the drug's description. In 2007 a Purdue affiliate "pleaded guilty to a federal felony for misbranding OxyContin as a less-addictive" and less abusable drug. The plea is the hinge of the sequence: it established, as a matter of record, that the company had misrepresented the product — and it is the moment after which the withdrawals accelerated from under 15% to as much as 70% of revenue.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog in this dossier is structural rather than informational, and it is made of corporate form. The money left an operating company that would later file for bankruptcy and went to individuals and entities that would not. By 2019, when Purdue entered Chapter 11, the assets that claimants might have reached were largely somewhere else, and the people who held them were not before the court as debtors.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall sought was not money but immunity. The family "proposed to return to Purdue's bankruptcy estate $4.325 billion of the $11 billion they had withdrawn from the company in recent years" — roughly thirty-nine cents on their own dollar, paid over years — in exchange for a release extinguishing claims against them. As the Court put it: "the Sacklers have not filed for bankruptcy or placed all their assets on the table for distribution to creditors, yet they seek what essentially amounts to a discharge."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: And here the mechanism this atlas tracks since 1912 fails, which is why the node is worth carrying. A bankruptcy court approved the release; a divided Second Circuit panel revived it; the Supreme Court held on 27 June 2024 that "the bankruptcy code does not authorize a release and injunction that, as part of a plan of reorganization under Chapter 11, effectively seeks to discharge claims against a nondebtor without the consent of affected claimants." The containment step was attempted through an ordinary, well-worn instrument, and a court said the instrument does not reach that far.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Chapter 11 reorganisation and the practice, built up in the asbestos and mass-tort cases that preceded this one, of resolving a company's liabilities and its owners' liabilities together through a third-party release.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A Supreme Court rule that the code does not authorise nonconsensual nondebtor releases — closing, for now, the route by which solvent owners of an insolvent company could buy a discharge without entering bankruptcy themselves.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The 2007 plea established the misrepresentation and set the price of it; the withdrawals that followed moved the assets beyond the reach of the claims the plea foreshadowed; and the bankruptcy was then offered as the forum in which those claims would be settled, by people who were not in it. Each step used the remedy created by the step before.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Sacklers were let off: that they bought their way out of the opioid epidemic for a fraction of what they took, and that the courts waved it through.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The courts did not wave it through. The United States Trustee objected, the Supreme Court took the case, and on 27 June 2024 it held the release unauthorised by the code. But the opposite reading fails too, and it is the one that a triumphant retelling slips into: the decision is not a judgment against anyone. The Court said expressly that it was "Confining ourselves to the question presented", that it "hold[s] only" that the code does not authorise such a release, and that because the case involved "only a stayed reorganization plan" it was not deciding whether already-consummated plans could be unwound. No finding of liability was made against any member of the family, no damages were awarded, and the ruling left the claims to be litigated rather than resolving them.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A 2007 federal felony guilty plea by a Purdue affiliate for misbranding OxyContin. Distributions to the family that ran under 15% of annual revenue before that plea and as much as 70% after it. Approximately $11 billion withdrawn between 2008 and 2016, draining 75% of the company's total assets, much of it moved to overseas trusts and family-owned companies. A Chapter 11 filing in 2019. An offer of $4.325 billion, paid over years, in exchange for a release of claims against people who had not filed for bankruptcy. And a Supreme Court holding that the bankruptcy code does not authorise that release — a holding about the limits of an instrument, expressly confined to the question presented.

citations.title: Harrington, United States Trustee for Region 2 v. Purdue Pharma L.P. et al., No. 23-124 (U.S. Supreme Court, decided 27 June 2024)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the Court's own opinions server and read as extracted text. THE HOLDING, from the syllabus and repeated verbatim in the opinion: "the bankruptcy code does not authorize a release and injunction that, as part of a plan of reorganization under Chapter 11, effectively seeks to discharge claims against a nondebtor without the consent of affected claimants." The Court states the reason plainly: "the Sacklers have not filed for bankruptcy or placed all their assets on the table for distribution to creditors, yet they seek what essentially amounts to a discharge. No provision of the code authorizes that kind of relief." ON WHAT CAME BEFORE: "In 2007 one of its affiliates pleaded guilty to a federal felony for misbranding OxyContin as a less-addictive" and less abusable drug. The opinion records what the family did next, in the words of the record below: the Sacklers began what one family member described as a "milking" program; "In the years before the 2007 plea agreement, Purdue's distributions to the Sacklers represented less than 15% of its annual revenue. After the plea agreement, the Sacklers began taking as much as 70% of the company's revenue each year. Between 2008 and 2016, the family's distributions totaled approximately $11 billion, draining Purdue's total assets by 75% and leaving it in 'a significantly weakened financial' state. The Sacklers diverted much of that money to overseas trusts and family-owned companies." Purdue filed for Chapter 11 in 2019; the Sacklers "proposed to return to Purdue's bankruptcy estate $4.325 billion of the $11 billion they had withdrawn from the company in recent years", in payments spread over years, in exchange for the release. THE COURT'S OWN LIMIT ON ITS HOLDING, which matters and is usually dropped: "because this case involves only a stayed reorganization plan, we do not address whether our reading of the bankruptcy code would justify unwinding reorganization plans that have already become effective and been substantially consummated. Confining ourselves to the question presented, we hold only that the bankruptcy code does not authorize a release and injunction..." The decision is about what Chapter 11 permits. It makes no finding that any member of the family is liable for anything, and it awards nothing to anyone.

carbon-class.title: Four Seconds Assumed, Ten Seconds Measured: MCAS, the Authorized Representatives, and the Alert That Did Not Work
participants: U.S. House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was taken was schedule and cost. The committee's first theme is "tremendous financial pressure on Boeing and the 737 MAX program to compete with Airbus' new A320neo aircraft", which "resulted in extensive efforts to cut costs, maintain the 737 MAX program schedule, and avoid slowing the 737 MAX production line" — and it identifies "several instances where the desire to meet these goals and expectations jeopardized the safety of the flying public". Keeping the aircraft inside an existing type rating is what kept the schedule and the training cost down.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was architectural and documented. MCAS was permitted "to activate on input from a single angle of attack (AOA) sensor". Boeing "failed to classify MCAS as a safety-critical system, which would have attracted greater FAA scrutiny during the certification process". And its operation "violated Boeing's own internal design guidelines", which required that the system "not have any objectionable interaction with the piloting of the airplane" and "not interfere with dive recovery". The mitigation relied on was the crew — "pilots, who were largely unaware that the system existed".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The committee calls this theme "Culture of Concealment" and gives it three documented instances: "concealing the very existence of MCAS from 737 MAX pilots"; "failing to disclose that the AOA Disagree alert was inoperable on the vast majority of the 737 MAX fleet, despite having been certified as a standard aircraft feature", while continuing "to deliver MAX aircraft to its customers knowing that" it was inoperable; and concealing "internal test data it had that revealed it took a Boeing test pilot more than 10 seconds to diagnose and respond to uncommanded MCAS activation in a flight simulator, a condition the pilot found to be 'catastrophic'". The certification case assumed four seconds. The committee: "it is inconceivable and inexcusable that Boeing withheld this information from them."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was the certification itself, obtained through a structure in which the regulated firm supplied the regulator's eyes. Boeing Authorized Representatives are "Boeing employees who are granted special permission to represent the interests of the FAA and to act on the agency's behalf in validating aircraft systems and designs' compliance with FAA requirements". The committee found "inherent conflicts of interest" in that structure, and an instance in which an AR "raised concerns internally in 2016 but did not relay these issues to the FAA" — concerns about "repetitive MCAS activation and the impact of faulty AOA data on MCAS" that "were the core contributing factors that led to the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines crashes more than two years later".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment in this dossier is not a commission but an oversight relationship that had already absorbed the dissent. "Multiple career FAA officials have documented examples where FAA management overruled a determination of the FAA's own technical experts at the behest of Boeing." The committee's own verdict on the agency: "the FAA's certification review of Boeing's 737 MAX was grossly insufficient and ... the FAA failed in its duty to identify key safety problems."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Delegated certification — the long-standing arrangement under which an aircraft manufacturer's own employees are authorised to find its designs compliant on the regulator's behalf, and the grandfathering of a 1960s type certificate through successive derivative aircraft.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-MAX certification reforms and, in the committee's own framing, the case for a disclosure requirement: it notes that Boeing "was not required to share" the ten-second test result "with the FAA or Boeing customers", which is an argument about what the rules did not then demand.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The schedule pressure produced the design shortcut; the design shortcut was classified so as not to trigger the scrutiny that would have caught it; the people who would have done the scrutinising were the manufacturer's own employees; and the agency that might have overruled them had a record of overruling its own experts the other way.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the two crashes were foreign pilot error — that better-trained crews would have flown through it — or, in the other direction, that Boeing simply knew the aircraft would crash and sold it anyway.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The pilot-error account fails on Boeing's own measurements. The certification case assumed pilots would respond to the condition within four seconds; Boeing's internal simulator data showed its own test pilot taking more than ten, and that pilot called the condition "catastrophic". The crews were, in the committee's words, "largely unaware that the system existed", because its existence had been concealed from them, and the alert designed to warn of disagreeing AOA sensors was inoperable on most of the fleet while being certified as standard. The knowing-murder account fails in the other direction: what the committee documents is a chain of omissions, misclassifications and withheld data across years and many hands, not a decision to sell an aircraft expected to crash. Its five themes are about pressure, assumption, concealment, conflicted delegation and influence — and it is a committee report, which determines no liability and convicts no one.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: MCAS permitted to trigger on a single AOA sensor, not classified as safety-critical, and operating against Boeing's own internal design guidelines. Its existence concealed from the pilots expected to mitigate it. The AOA Disagree alert certified as a standard feature, found inoperable on the vast majority of the fleet, not disclosed, and aircraft delivered anyway. Internal test data showing more than ten seconds to diagnose and respond, against a four-second assumption, withheld. A Boeing Authorized Representative raising, in 2016, internally and not to the FAA, the two concerns the committee identifies as "the core contributing factors" in both crashes. FAA management overruling its own technical experts at Boeing's behest. And the committee's finding that the agency's certification review was "grossly insufficient".

citations.title: U.S. House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, Final Committee Report: The Design, Development & Certification of the Boeing 737 MAX (September 2020)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the committee's own site and read as extracted text. The report sets out "five central themes that affected the design, development, and certification of the 737 MAX and FAA's oversight of Boeing": (1) Production Pressures — "tremendous financial pressure on Boeing and the 737 MAX program to compete with Airbus' new A320neo aircraft", which "resulted in extensive efforts to cut costs, maintain the 737 MAX program schedule, and avoid slowing the 737 MAX production line", with "several instances where the desire to meet these goals and expectations jeopardized the safety of the flying public"; (2) Faulty Design and Performance Assumptions — Boeing "permitted MCAS — software designed to automatically push the airplane's nose down in certain conditions — to activate on input from a single angle of attack (AOA) sensor", "expected that pilots, who were largely unaware that the system existed, would be able to mitigate any potential malfunction", and "failed to classify MCAS as a safety-critical system, which would have attracted greater FAA scrutiny during the certification process"; the report notes MCAS's operation "violated Boeing's own internal design guidelines", which said the system should "not have any objectionable interaction with the piloting of the airplane" and "not interfere with dive recovery"; (3) Culture of Concealment — "In several critical instances, Boeing withheld crucial information from the FAA, its customers, and 737 MAX pilots. This included concealing the very existence of MCAS from 737 MAX pilots and failing to disclose that the AOA Disagree alert was inoperable on the vast majority of the 737 MAX fleet, despite having been certified as a standard aircraft feature", and Boeing "continued to deliver MAX aircraft to its customers knowing that the AOA Disagree alert was inoperable on most of these aircraft"; it also "concealed internal test data it had that revealed it took a Boeing test pilot more than 10 seconds to diagnose and respond to uncommanded MCAS activation in a flight simulator, a condition the pilot found to be 'catastrophic'", against federal guidelines that "assume pilots will respond to this condition within four seconds", and the committee adds: "While it was not required to share this information with the FAA or Boeing customers, it is inconceivable and inexcusable that Boeing withheld this information from them."; (4) Conflicted Representation — "the FAA's current oversight structure with respect to Boeing creates inherent conflicts of interest", with Boeing Authorized Representatives "granted special permission to represent the interests of the FAA and to act on the agency's behalf", and an instance in which "a Boeing AR raised concerns internally in 2016 but did not relay these issues to the FAA", concerns "about repetitive MCAS activation and the impact of faulty AOA data on MCAS" that "were the core contributing factors that led to the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines crashes more than two years later"; (5) Boeing's Influence Over the FAA's Oversight Structure — "Multiple career FAA officials have documented examples where FAA management overruled a determination of the FAA's own technical experts at the behest of Boeing." The report separately finds "that the FAA's certification review of Boeing's 737 MAX was grossly insufficient and that the FAA failed in its duty to identify key safety problems." This is a congressional committee report, not a court judgment; it determines no liability and convicts no one.

carbon-class.title: Robust and Reliable: a Prosecutor Who Owned the Evidence, and 39 Trials That Could Not Be Fair
participants: Subpostmasters prosecuted by Post Office Limited
Mr Justice Fraser (High Court, Bates v Post Office)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was the shortfall itself, recovered from the people who appeared to have caused it. The court records that the Post Office prosecuted "against a background of asserting that SPMs were liable to make good all losses and could lose their employment if they did not do so" — and that it did so "despite the fact that POL itself had selected the SPMs as suitable persons to hold their position of trust". The money came back whether or not the shortfall was real.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was evidentiary and it was known. "Throughout the relevant period there were significant problems with Horizon, which gave rise to a material risk that an apparent shortfall in the branch accounts did not in fact reflect missing cash or stock, but was caused by one of the bugs, errors or defects in Horizon." In every one of the cases the court calls "Horizon cases", "there was no independent evidence of an actual shortfall, and it was essential to the prosecution case that the Horizon data was reliable."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The court's finding on knowledge is unusually flat for an appellate judgment, and it repeats the verb four times: "POL knew that there were problems with Horizon. POL knew that SPMs around the country had complained of inexplicable discrepancies in the accounts. POL knew that different bugs, defects and errors had been detected well beyond anything which might be regarded as a period of initial teething problems. In short, POL knew that there were serious issues about the reliability of Horizon." And against that: "On the contrary, it consistently asserted that Horizon was robust and reliable." The court offers a motive: the failure to be open "can in our view only be explained by a strong reluctance to say or do anything which might lead to other SPMs knowing about those issues."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: What the arrangement preserved was the assertion itself. "Those concerned with prosecutions of SPMs clearly wished to be able to maintain the assertion that Horizon data was accurate, and effectively steamrolled over any SPM who sought to challenge its accuracy." Each successful prosecution confirmed the reliability of the system on which the next prosecution would depend, and every individual contesting it faced an organisation that was at once the complainant, the investigator, the prosecutor and the owner of the only evidence.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment ran twelve to thirteen years and ended in the Court of Appeal. Of 42 cases referred by the Criminal Cases Review Commission, the Post Office conceded in all but three "that there were material failures of investigation and disclosure, which meant that 39 of the appellants could not have, and did not have, a fair trial". The court went further than category 1: it held that the same acts and omissions "may both render a fair trial impossible ... and make it an affront to the conscience of the court to prosecute at all", because "POL deliberately chose not to comply with its obligations in circumstances in which its prosecution of an SPM depended on the reliability of Horizon data".

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The private prosecution — a power retained in England and Wales by any person or body, exercised here by an organisation that was also the alleged victim, the investigator and the proprietor of the system generating the evidence.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: An appellate precedent that disclosure failures by a private prosecutor dependent on its own data can constitute abuse of process in both categories, and a body of quashed convictions that forced the question of statutory redress.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Shortfalls shown by the system were recovered from the subpostmaster; prosecutions founded on the system's reliability deterred challenges to it; the absence of successful challenges was then available as evidence of its reliability. The loop ran on the evidence it produced.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That hundreds of subpostmasters stole from the Post Office, and the convictions were only overturned later on a technicality about disclosure.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Court of Appeal did not quash on a technicality; it found the trials could not have been fair and that prosecuting at all was an affront to the conscience of the court. In the cases at issue "there was no independent evidence of an actual shortfall" — the Horizon data was the case. And the court found the prosecutor knew its data was unreliable while asserting the opposite for more than a decade. The opposite overstatement should also be resisted: this judgment concerns the safety of convictions in 42 referred cases, of which the Post Office conceded 39; it makes no finding of criminal liability against any individual at the Post Office or at Fujitsu, and it does not purport to settle what happened in every prosecution the organisation ever brought.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Prosecutions in which the reliability of Horizon data was essential and no independent evidence of a shortfall existed. A judicial finding, in terms, that the Post Office knew of problems with Horizon, knew of complaints of inexplicable discrepancies, and knew the bugs went well beyond teething problems — while consistently asserting that Horizon was robust and reliable. Failures of investigation and disclosure spanning 12 to 13 years. Subpostmasters told they were liable to make good all losses and could lose their employment otherwise. Thirty-nine of forty-two referred appellants conceded by the Post Office to have been denied a fair trial, and a finding of second-category abuse resting on a deliberate choice not to comply with disclosure obligations.

citations.title: Josephine Hamilton & Others v Post Office Limited [2021] EWCA Crim 577 (Court of Appeal, Criminal Division, 23 April 2021) — Holroyde LJ, Picken J and Farbey J
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from the National Archives' Find Case Law service (BAILII now serves a proof-of-work bot challenge to scripted requests, so the judgment was taken from the official service instead). A reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission of 42 linked cases. ON KNOWLEDGE, at paragraph 121: "We accept and adopt Fraser J's findings that throughout the relevant period there were significant problems with Horizon, which gave rise to a material risk that an apparent shortfall in the branch accounts did not in fact reflect missing cash or stock, but was caused by one of the bugs, errors or defects in Horizon. POL knew that there were problems with Horizon. POL knew that SPMs around the country had complained of inexplicable discrepancies in the accounts. POL knew that different bugs, defects and errors had been detected well beyond anything which might be regarded as a period of initial teething problems. In short, POL knew that there were serious issues about the reliability of Horizon. If POL needed further information, it could have obtained it from Fujitsu. It was POL's clear duty to investigate all reasonable lines of enquiry, to consider disclosure and to make disclosure to the appellants of anything which might reasonably be considered to undermine its case. Yet it does not appear that POL adequately considered or made relevant disclosure of problems with or concerns about Horizon in any of the cases at any point during that period. On the contrary, it consistently asserted that Horizon was robust and reliable." The court continues: "The consistent failure of POL to be open and honest about the issues affecting Horizon can in our view only be explained by a strong reluctance to say or do anything which might lead to other SPMs knowing about those issues. Those concerned with prosecutions of SPMs clearly wished to be able to maintain the assertion that Horizon data was accurate, and effectively steamrolled over any SPM who sought to challenge its accuracy." ON THE PERIOD AND THE CONCESSIONS: the failures of investigation and disclosure run "across a period of 12-13 years", and "in all but three of the 42 cases, POL concedes that there were material failures of investigation and disclosure, which meant that 39 of the appellants could not have, and did not have, a fair trial." ON THE SECOND CATEGORY OF ABUSE, at paragraphs 127 and 129: "the same acts and/or omissions may both render a fair trial impossible (thus, category 1) and make it an affront to the conscience of the court to prosecute at all (and thus, category 2)", and "we reiterate that POL deliberately chose not to comply with its obligations in circumstances in which its prosecution of an SPM depended on the reliability of Horizon data. It did so against a background of asserting that SPMs were liable to make good all losses and could lose their employment if they did not do so. It did so despite the fact that POL itself had selected the SPMs as suitable persons to hold their position of trust." The judgment concerns the safety of convictions. It makes no finding of criminal liability against any individual at the Post Office or at Fujitsu.

carbon-class.title: It Should Have Been Avoided: Forty Years of Defensive Lines, and the Documents That Were Destroyed
participants: Infected Blood Inquiry (Sir Brian Langstaff, chair)
UK Government and successive Health Departments
People with bleeding disorders treated with factor concentrates

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The saving was in supply and in cost: pooled factor concentrates, convenient and commercially available, carrying the risk of every donor in the pool. The Inquiry's judgment on the whole of it is that the disaster "could largely, though not entirely, have been avoided. And I have to report that it should have been."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The Inquiry finds "systemic, collective and individual failures to deal ethically, appropriately, and quickly, with the risk of infections being transmitted in blood, with the infections when the risk materialised, and with the consequences for thousands of families" — three distinct failures, at three distinct moments, each of which had its own chance to stop the harm.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog fell on the patients first and then on the record. The Inquiry lists, among the harms that compounded the infections: "Delaying informing people of their infections by weeks, months and sometimes years"; testing samples "which in most cases patients did not know were to be retained for the purpose" and "without their knowledge or consent"; and, at the institutional level, "A lack of openness, transparency and candour, shown by the NHS and government, such that the truth has been hidden for decades." Then the evidence itself: "Failures of record-keeping, such that many people's medical records have been destroyed or lost or are materially incomplete", and "Deliberate destruction of some documents and the loss of others."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: There is no commercial windfall at the end of this one, and the dossier does not manufacture one. What the decades of denial preserved was a position: that nothing had gone wrong. The Inquiry records the form it took — "Repeated and ongoing failures to acknowledge that they should not have been infected", "Repeated use of inaccurate, misleading and defensive lines to take which cruelly told people that they had received the best treatment available", and refusal of compensation "on the ground there had been no fault".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment here lasted long enough to outlive most of the people it was practised on, and the inquiry that ended it was granted only in 2017. Of around 1,250 people with bleeding disorders infected with HIV — an estimated 380 of them children — "Three quarters of these 1,250 adults and children have died." The Inquiry reports findings of fact and makes recommendations; like every statutory inquiry it determines no civil or criminal liability.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A health service purchasing a pooled blood product on commercial supply, and a culture of institutional defensiveness in which admitting avoidable harm was understood as conceding fault.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Inquiry's findings themselves, and the statutory compensation route that followed the admission they forced — redress arriving only after the denial had been examined in public and named.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Each refusal to acknowledge avoidable infection removed the ground for redress; the absence of redress was then cited as evidence that there had been no fault; and the records that would have settled it were incomplete, lost, or deliberately destroyed.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the infected blood disaster was a tragedy of its era — nobody could have known what was in the blood supply before the viruses were identified — and that the long delay in redress was bureaucratic slowness rather than anything deliberate.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Inquiry rejects the first in a single sentence: the calamity "could largely, though not entirely, have been avoided. And I have to report that it should have been." It rejects the second by naming conduct rather than inertia: "A lack of openness, transparency and candour, shown by the NHS and government, such that the truth has been hidden for decades", alongside "Deliberate destruction of some documents and the loss of others" and the "Repeated use of inaccurate, misleading and defensive lines to take which cruelly told people that they had received the best treatment available". What the Inquiry does not do is convict: it is a statutory inquiry, it determines no civil or criminal liability, and nothing here should be read as a finding against a named individual.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Around 4,000 to 6,000 people with bleeding disorders in the UK at any one time; around 1,250 infected with HIV, an estimated 380 of them children; almost all of those also infected with Hepatitis C; three quarters of the 1,250 now dead; and between 2,400 and 5,000 further people with bleeding disorders, not infected with HIV, who received products carrying one or more hepatitis viruses. A chair's finding that it could and should have been avoided, and of systemic, collective and individual failures at the point of risk, at the point of infection, and in the handling of the consequences. Infections disclosed to patients weeks, months or years late. Samples tested without knowledge or consent. Records destroyed, lost or materially incomplete, and some documents deliberately destroyed. Four decades of defensive lines telling infected people they had received the best treatment available, and compensation refused on the ground that there had been no fault.

citations.title: Infected Blood Inquiry, The Report (Sir Brian Langstaff, chair), Volume 1 (May 2024)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the Inquiry's own site and read as extracted text. The chair's central conclusion: "I have to report a catalogue of failures which caused this to happen. Each on its own is serious. Taken together they are a calamity. Lord Winston famously called these events 'the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS'. I have to report that it could largely, though not entirely, have been avoided. And I have to report that it should have been. I have also to report systemic, collective and individual failures to deal ethically, appropriately, and quickly, with the risk of infections being transmitted in blood, with the infections when the risk materialised, and with the consequences for thousands of families." On scale: "There were around 4,000 to 6,000 people with bleeding disorders in the UK at any one time. Around 1,250 were infected with HIV. The best estimate is that this included 380 children. Almost all infected with HIV were also infected with Hepatitis C and some with Hepatitis B and Hepatitis D as well. Three quarters of these 1,250 adults and children have died. A larger number still (between 2,400 and 5,000 people with bleeding disorders) who were not infected by HIV received blood products infected with one or more hepatitis viruses". On what followed the infections, listed by the report as harms that compounded them: "Delaying informing people of their infections by weeks, months and sometimes years"; "Failures of record-keeping, such that many people's medical records have been destroyed or lost or are materially incomplete"; "Repeated and ongoing failures to acknowledge that they should not have been infected"; "Repeated use of inaccurate, misleading and defensive lines to take which cruelly told people that they had received the best treatment available"; "A lack of openness, transparency and candour, shown by the NHS and government, such that the truth has been hidden for decades"; and "Deliberate destruction of some documents and the loss of others." The report also records testing of samples "which in most cases patients did not know were to be retained for the purpose" and "without their knowledge or consent". A statutory public inquiry: it reports findings of fact and makes recommendations, and determines no civil or criminal liability.

carbon-class.title: Removal Costs Plus $75 Million: the Cap Written in 1990 and the Blowout the Commission Called Preventable
participants: Minerals Management Service / Department of the Interior
National Commission on the BP Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill and Offshore Drilling
Congress of the United States (Oil Pollution Act 1990)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The saving was in time and procedure at the end of a well that was late and over budget, and the Commission locates it precisely: "BP's management process did not adequately identify or address risks created by late changes to well design and procedures", and BP "did not have adequate controls in place to ensure that key decisions in the months leading up to the blowout were safe or sound from an engineering perspective." Initial well design went through peer review; the changes made in the weeks and days before did not go through the same process.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The Commission declines to treat the failure as one firm's: the immediate causes "can be traced to a series of identifiable mistakes made by BP, Halliburton, and Transocean that reveal such systematic failures in risk management that they place in doubt the safety culture of the entire industry." And on the other side of the relationship, it finds "failures of government to provide effective regulatory oversight of offshore drilling."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog here is the one the Commission spends its root-cause chapter dispelling: the account of the blowout as an accident of the frontier, a statistical inevitability of deep water. "The blowout was not the product of a series of aberrational decisions made by rogue industry or government officials that could not have been anticipated or expected to occur again. Rather, the root causes are systemic and, absent significant reform in both industry practices and government policies, might well recur." And: "A blowout in deepwater was not a statistical inevitability."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is the cap, and it was written twenty years earlier. Under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, the total liability of a responsible party for an offshore facility is limited to "the total of all removal costs plus $75,000,000" — a figure fixed in 1990 and never indexed, against a well whose eventual costs ran to many billions. The limit does not apply where the incident was proximately caused by gross negligence, wilful misconduct or a regulatory violation, and whether it would have held at Macondo was never adjudicated. It did not need to be: a cap this far below the exposure shapes what is risked before anything goes wrong.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The Commission is the Mersey step in its benign form, and it says what such bodies usually do not. Its first conclusion is that "The explosive loss of the Macondo well could have been prevented", and its root-cause chapter refuses the exculpatory reading in advance: "Whatever irreducible uncertainty may persist regarding the precise contribution to the blowout of each of several potentially immediate causes, no such uncertainty exists about the blowout's root causes." It was nonetheless advisory. It determined no liability, brought no proceedings, and its recommendations bound no one.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The statutory liability limit, the instrument this atlas first meets in the 1851 Limitation of Liability Act and the 1914 Titanic judgment, rewritten for oil in 1990 as a removal-costs-plus-$75,000,000 ceiling on an offshore facility.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-Macondo reorganisation of offshore regulation — the splitting of the agency that had both collected royalties from drilling and policed its safety — and a standing recommendation set that the Commission itself noted would bind nobody.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The cap sets the maximum downside of a deepwater well; the upside is uncapped; the regulator that might have adjusted the balance was funded from the activity it policed. The Commission's finding that the root causes "might well recur" is a statement about that arithmetic, not about any particular crew.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Macondo was the price of the frontier — an unforeseeable accident in water too deep and pressures too high for anyone to have managed — or, the mirror image, that one company's uniquely reckless culture explains all of it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Commission rejected both in the same paragraph. Against the frontier account: "The explosive loss of the Macondo well could have been prevented", and "A blowout in deepwater was not a statistical inevitability." Against the single-bad-actor account: the mistakes were "made by BP, Halliburton, and Transocean" and reveal "systematic failures in risk management that they place in doubt the safety culture of the entire industry", with root causes that "are systemic" and extend to "failures of government to provide effective regulatory oversight". What the Commission did not do is assign liability — it was advisory, and said so.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A statutory liability ceiling for an offshore facility of removal costs plus $75,000,000, enacted in 1990 and unindexed, subject to exceptions for gross negligence, wilful misconduct and regulatory violation that were never adjudicated here. A presidential commission finding that the loss "could have been prevented"; that its immediate causes trace to identifiable mistakes by three named companies; that those mistakes reveal systematic risk-management failures placing the whole industry's safety culture in doubt; that most of them trace back to "a single overarching failure — a failure of management"; that BP's process did not address the risks created by late changes to well design and procedures; and that the root causes are systemic and, without reform in both industry practice and government policy, "might well recur".

citations.title: National Commission on the BP Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill and Offshore Drilling, Deep Water: The Gulf Oil Disaster and the Future of Offshore Drilling — Report to the President (January 2011)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. The Commission's own conclusions, stated as a list: "The explosive loss of the Macondo well could have been prevented." "The immediate causes of the Macondo well blowout can be traced to a series of identifiable mistakes made by BP, Halliburton, and Transocean that reveal such systematic failures in risk management that they place in doubt the safety culture of the entire industry." "Deepwater energy exploration and production, particularly at the frontiers of experience, involve risks for which neither industry nor government has been adequately prepared". On root causes: "Whatever irreducible uncertainty may persist regarding the precise contribution to the blowout of each of several potentially immediate causes, no such uncertainty exists about the blowout's root causes. The blowout was not the product of a series of aberrational decisions made by rogue industry or government officials that could not have been anticipated or expected to occur again. Rather, the root causes are systemic and, absent significant reform in both industry practices and government policies, might well recur. The missteps were rooted in systemic failures by industry management (extending beyond BP to contractors that serve many in the industry), and also by failures of government to provide effective regulatory oversight of offshore drilling." And: "most of the mistakes and oversights at Macondo can be traced back to a single overarching failure--a failure of management ... A blowout in deepwater was not a statistical inevitability." The Commission also records that "BP's management process did not adequately identify or address risks created by late changes to well design and procedures" and that BP "did not have adequate controls in place to ensure that key decisions in the months leading up to the blowout were safe or sound from an engineering perspective." The Commission was advisory; it determined no liability and brought no proceedings.

citations.title: Oil Pollution Act of 1990, section 1004, codified at 33 U.S.C. § 2704 — Limits on liability (U.S. Code, 2011 edition)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. The general rule caps a responsible party's total liability for removal costs and damages per incident, and subsection (a)(3) sets the figure that governed an offshore facility in 2010: "(3) for an offshore facility except a deepwater port, the total of all removal costs plus $75,000,000; and (4) for any onshore facility and a deepwater port, $350,000,000." Subsection (b) provides that a mobile offshore drilling unit used as an offshore facility is "deemed to be a tank vessel" first, and is "deemed to be an offshore facility" for liability in excess of the tank-vessel amount. A TEXT CAUTION WORTH RECORDING: the Statutes at Large scan of the same provision (STATUTE-104-Pg484) is an image whose OCR renders paragraph (3) as "for a n onshore facility", dropping the "ff" — which inverts the meaning, since onshore facilities are paragraph (4). The United States Code text above is the one read and cited here; the Statutes at Large scan was opened, found corrupt at this point, and is not cited. The cap does not apply where the incident was proximately caused by gross negligence, wilful misconduct, or violation of an applicable regulation (33 U.S.C. § 2704(c)); whether it would have applied to Macondo was never adjudicated, and nothing here asserts that it limited what was ultimately paid.

carbon-class.title: Systematic Dishonesty: Manipulated Tests, a Complicit Testing House, and a Department That Was Well Aware

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The saving was the price difference between combustible and fire-resistant product, taken by selling the cheaper one into a market told it was safe. The Inquiry finds Celotex "embarked on a dishonest scheme to mislead its customers and the wider market" in order "to break into the market for insulation suitable for use on high-rise buildings, created and then dominated by Kingspan K15"; and that Kingspan "knowingly created a false market in insulation for use on buildings over 18 metres in height".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was in the test, and it was physical. In May 2014 Celotex tested a system "that contained two sets of fire-resistant magnesium oxide boards placed in critical positions to ensure that it passed", then obtained a report "that omitted any reference to the magnesium oxide boards, thereby rendering it materially incomplete and misleading". The Inquiry finds the Building Research Establishment "was complicit in that strategy", and separately that senior BRE staff "gave advice to customers such as Kingspan and Celotex on the best way to satisfy the criteria for a system to be considered safe, thereby compromising its integrity and independence".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was manufactured and sustained for more than a decade. From early 2005 Arconic held test data showing Reynobond 55 PE in cassette form "reacted to fire in a very dangerous way and could not be classified in accordance with European standards", yet "persisted in telling the market that the panels had been classed B-s2, d0 without drawing any distinction between the cassette and riveted forms", and "deliberately concealed from the market the true extent of the danger" until after the fire. The Inquiry's summary of the whole class of conduct: "systematic dishonesty on the part of those who made and sold the rainscreen cladding panels and insulation products ... deliberate and sustained strategies to manipulate the testing processes, misrepresent test data and mislead the market".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was market access that honest testing would have denied, protected by the certificates that were supposed to police it. The certification bodies, the British Board of Agrément and Local Authority Building Control, "failed to ensure that the statements in their product certificates were accurate and based on test evidence", and UKAS, "the body charged with oversight of the certification bodies, failed to apply proper standards of monitoring and supervision". By summer 2011 Arconic "was determined to exploit what it saw as weak regulatory regimes in certain countries (including the UK)" to keep selling the cassette form for residential buildings.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment ran for twenty-six years and it was inaction rather than an inquiry. "In the years between the fire at Knowsley Heights in 1991 and the fire at Grenfell Tower in 2017 there were many opportunities for the government to identify the risks ... Indeed, by 2016 the department was well aware of those risks, but failed to act on what it knew." It had been warned in terms: the Inquiry records the department's failure "to heed the warning of the Environment and Transport Select Committee in December 1999 that it should not take a serious fire in which people were killed before steps were taken to minimise the risks posed by some external cladding systems."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A building-safety regime resting on manufacturer-commissioned testing, third-party certification of the resulting claims, and statutory guidance that the department had been advised for years was inadequate.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Inquiry's findings and recommendations, and the post-Grenfell reconstruction of building regulation around a single regulator — arriving, as the Inquiry notes of the 1999 warning, only after the fire in which people were killed.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The manipulated test produced the certificate; the certificate satisfied the specifier; the specification created the market; and the testing house that could have broken the loop was advising the manufacturers on how to pass. The department that might have changed the rule had been told what would happen if it did not.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Grenfell was a council's cost-cutting on one refurbishment — a cheap cladding choice by a landlord — or, alternatively, that it was an unforeseeable combination that no regulation could have anticipated.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Inquiry locates the cause well upstream of the refurbishment and well before 2017. Its conclusion is that the fire "was the culmination of decades of failure by central government and other bodies in positions of responsibility in the construction industry", that "by 2016 the department was well aware of those risks, but failed to act on what it knew", and that a select committee had warned in December 1999 against waiting for a fatal fire. And the products were not innocently misunderstood: the Inquiry finds "systematic dishonesty" by the manufacturers, a test manipulated with concealed magnesium oxide boards, a test report rendered "materially incomplete and misleading", and a testing house "complicit in that strategy". What the Inquiry does not do is determine liability: it is a statutory inquiry making findings of fact and recommendations, and criminal investigations remained separate from it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A finding of systematic dishonesty by the makers of the cladding panels and insulation, consisting of deliberate and sustained strategies to manipulate testing, misrepresent test data and mislead the market. A May 2014 BS 8414 test of Celotex RS5000 containing two sets of fire-resistant magnesium oxide boards placed to ensure a pass, and a resulting report omitting any mention of them. BRE found complicit in that strategy, and found to have advised Kingspan and Celotex how to satisfy the safety criteria while certifying them. Arconic holding test data from early 2005 on the cassette form's fire behaviour, telling the market the panels were B-s2, d0 without distinguishing the forms, and deliberately concealing the danger until after the fire. Kingspan knowingly creating a false market for use above 18 metres. Certification bodies failing to ensure their certificates were accurate and evidence-based, and UKAS failing to supervise them. And a department that, by 2016, was well aware of the risks and failed to act on what it knew.

citations.title: Grenfell Tower Inquiry: Phase 2 Report (Sir Martin Moore-Bick, chairman; Ali Akbor OBE and Thouria Istephan, panel), Volume 1, HC 19-I, presented to Parliament under section 26 of the Inquiries Act 2005, ordered printed 4 September 2024
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the UK government's own asset store and read as extracted text. NOTE ON ACCESS: the Inquiry's own site, grenfelltowerinquiry.org.uk, now redirects to the National Archives web archive, which serves a human-verification challenge; that challenge was not circumvented, and the report was taken from the government publishing host instead. THE OVERALL CONCLUSION, at paragraph 2.4: "We conclude that the fire at Grenfell Tower was the culmination of decades of failure by central government and other bodies in positions of responsibility in the construction industry to look carefully into the danger of incorporating combustible materials into the external walls of high-rise residential buildings and to act on the information available to them." ON GOVERNMENT, at 2.5: "In the years between the fire at Knowsley Heights in 1991 and the fire at Grenfell Tower in 2017 there were many opportunities for the government to identify the risks posed by the use of combustible cladding panels and insulation, particularly to high-rise buildings, and to take action in relation to them. Indeed, by 2016 the department was well aware of those risks, but failed to act on what it knew. In particular, it failed to heed the warning of the Environment and Transport Select Committee in December 1999 that it should not take a serious fire in which people were killed before steps were taken to minimise the risks posed by some external cladding systems." ON THE MANUFACTURERS, at 2.19: "One very significant reason why Grenfell Tower came to be clad in combustible materials was systematic dishonesty on the part of those who made and sold the rainscreen cladding panels and insulation products. They engaged in deliberate and sustained strategies to manipulate the testing processes, misrepresent test data and mislead the market. In the case of the principal insulation product used on Grenfell Tower, Celotex RS5000, the Building Research Establishment (BRE) was complicit in that strategy." At 2.20 the Inquiry finds that the certification bodies, the British Board of Agrément and Local Authority Building Control, "failed to ensure that the statements in their product certificates were accurate and based on test evidence", and that "UKAS, the body charged with oversight of the certification bodies, failed to apply proper standards of monitoring and supervision." ON THE TESTING HOUSE, at 2.18: there were weaknesses in BRE's conduct of BS 8414 tests and in its record-keeping "which exposed it to the risk of manipulation by unscrupulous product manufacturers, as happened in the case of the second test carried out for Celotex", and "Senior BRE staff gave advice to customers such as Kingspan and Celotex on the best way to satisfy the criteria for a system to be considered safe, thereby compromising its integrity and independence." ON THE INDIVIDUAL MANUFACTURERS: Arconic, from 2005 until after the fire, "deliberately concealed from the market the true extent of the danger of using Reynobond 55 PE in cassette form, particularly on high-rise buildings", having held test data from early 2005 showing the cassette form "reacted to fire in a very dangerous way and could not be classified in accordance with European standards", yet "persisted in telling the market that the panels had been classed B-s2, d0 without drawing any distinction between the cassette and riveted forms"; by summer 2011 "it was well aware" of the difference and "was determined to exploit what it saw as weak regulatory regimes in certain countries (including the UK)". Celotex "embarked on a dishonest scheme to mislead its customers and the wider market": in May 2014, "With the complicity of BRE", it tested a system "that contained two sets of fire-resistant magnesium oxide boards placed in critical positions to ensure that it passed", then obtained a test report "that omitted any reference to the magnesium oxide boards, thereby rendering it materially incomplete and misleading", and marketed the product on that test without disclosing the manipulation. Kingspan, "From 2005 until after this Inquiry had begun ... knowingly created a false market in insulation for use on buildings over 18 metres in height", a claim that was false "as it well knew". A statutory public inquiry: it makes findings of fact and recommendations and determines no civil or criminal liability.

carbon-class.title: Avoidable: the Commission’s Own Conclusions on the Securitization Pipeline, and the Two Dissents
participants: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The fee came at origination and travelled on. The Commission describes the standard: "Many mortgage lenders set the bar so low that lenders simply took eager borrowers’ qualifications on faith, often with a willful disregard for a borrower’s ability to pay." The loan was the product; whether it could be repaid was someone else’s exposure by the time it was sold.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The pipeline is the Commission’s own metaphor and its own finding: "We conclude collapsing mortgage-lending standards and the mortgage securitization pipeline lit and spread the flame of contagion and crisis." The report, it says, "catalogues the corrosion of mortgage-lending standards and the securitization pipeline that transported toxic mortgages from neighborhoods across America to investors around the globe."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was supplied by the ratings, and the Commission is blunt about their function: "The mortgage-related securities at the heart of the crisis could not have been marketed and sold without their seal of approval. Investors relied on them, often blindly. In some cases, they were obligated to use them, or regulatory capital standards were hinged on them ... This crisis could not have happened without the rating agencies." Its conclusion on them is that their failures "were essential cogs in the wheel of financial destruction".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: What the arrangement bought was regulatory room, and the Commission names who gave it: "the Federal Reserve neglected its mission ‘to ensure the safety and soundness of the nation’s banking and financial system and to protect the credit rights of consumers.’ It failed to build the retaining wall before it was too late. And the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Office of Thrift Supervision, caught up in turf wars, preempted state regulators from reining in abuses." The preemption is the windfall: it removed the one layer of supervision that was trying to act.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The Commission refuses the exculpatory account in its first conclusion — "We conclude this financial crisis was avoidable ... Theirs was a big miss, not a stumble" — and refuses the claim that nobody could have seen it: "Despite the expressed view of many on Wall Street and in Washington that the crisis could not have been foreseen or avoided, there were warning signs." But it was a divided body. Its report carries dissenting views by Keith Hennessey, Douglas Holtz-Eakin and Bill Thomas, and a separate dissent by Peter J. Wallison; the conclusions above are the majority’s. It determined no liability and brought no proceedings.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Originate-to-distribute mortgage finance, nationally chartered lenders able to preempt state consumer-protection enforcement, and capital rules that deferred to private credit ratings.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-crisis supervisory architecture — a consolidated consumer regulator, the abolition of the Office of Thrift Supervision, and rating-agency provisions — built on the Commission’s diagnosis but not on any finding of liability.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Loose underwriting produced volume; volume produced securities; ratings made the securities saleable and capital rules made them attractive to hold; demand for securities fed back as demand for loans, which pushed underwriting looser still. The supervisor that might have interrupted it had preempted the supervisors who were trying.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the crisis was a hundred-year storm nobody could have predicted — or, from the other direction, that it was a single conspiracy run from a few desks in New York.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Commission’s first conclusion rejects the storm: "We conclude this financial crisis was avoidable. The crisis was the result of human action and inaction, not of Mother Nature or computer models gone haywire ... Theirs was a big miss, not a stumble." And it rejects the idea that the signals were absent: "These trends were not secret." But its own account is not a conspiracy either; it is a list of systems failing in parallel — regulation, corporate governance, leverage, ethics, origination, derivatives, ratings — each with its own conclusion. The dossier should also carry what the report itself carries: the Commission split, and two sets of dissenting commissioners rejected the majority’s framing. A reader who takes "avoidable" as a settled national verdict is quoting a majority, not a unanimity.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A congressionally chartered commission concluding that the crisis was avoidable and that the warning signs existed. That collapsing mortgage-lending standards and the securitization pipeline "lit and spread the flame of contagion and crisis", with lenders taking borrowers’ qualifications "on faith, often with a willful disregard for a borrower’s ability to pay". That the Federal Reserve "neglected its mission" and "failed to build the retaining wall", and that the OCC and OTS, "caught up in turf wars, preempted state regulators from reining in abuses". That the rating agencies’ failures were "essential cogs in the wheel of financial destruction" and that the crisis "could not have happened without" them. And that the Commission reached these conclusions over the dissent of Hennessey, Holtz-Eakin and Thomas, and of Wallison separately.

citations.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, The Financial Crisis Inquiry Report: Final Report of the National Commission on the Causes of the Financial and Economic Crisis in the United States (January 2011)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. A TEXT CAUTION: the extraction drops numerals in a number of sentences in the conclusions (for example "nearly , mortgage-related securities"), so no figure is quoted from this document here and only sentences that survive extraction intact are reproduced. THE COMMISSION’S CONCLUSIONS, in its own enumerated form: "We conclude this financial crisis was avoidable. The crisis was the result of human action and inaction, not of Mother Nature or computer models gone haywire. The captains of finance and the public stewards of our financial system ignored warnings and failed to question, understand, and manage evolving risks within a system essential to the well-being of the American public. Theirs was a big miss, not a stumble. While the business cycle cannot be repealed, a crisis of this magnitude need not have occurred." It adds: "Despite the expressed view of many on Wall Street and in Washington that the crisis could not have been foreseen or avoided, there were warning signs." Further conclusions, each stated in the same form: "We conclude widespread failures in financial regulation and supervision"; "We conclude dramatic failures of corporate governance and risk management"; "We conclude a combination of excessive borrowing, risky investments, and lack" of transparency; "We conclude the government was ill prepared for the crisis, and its inconsistent" response added to uncertainty; "We conclude there was a systemic breakdown in accountability and ethics"; "We conclude collapsing mortgage-lending standards and the mortgage securitization pipeline lit and spread the flame of contagion and crisis"; "We conclude over-the-counter derivatives contributed significantly to this" crisis; and "We conclude the failures of credit rating agencies were essential cogs in the wheel of financial destruction." On origination: "Many mortgage lenders set the bar so low that lenders simply took eager borrowers’ qualifications on faith, often with a willful disregard for a borrower’s ability to pay." On whether this was visible at the time: "These trends were not secret. As irresponsible lending, including predatory and fraudulent practices, became more prevalent, the Federal Reserve and other regulators and authorities heard warnings from many quarters. Yet the Federal Reserve neglected its mission ‘to ensure the safety and soundness of the nation’s banking and financial system and to protect the credit rights of consumers.’ It failed to build the retaining wall before it was too late. And the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Office of Thrift Supervision, caught up in turf wars, preempted state regulators from reining in abuses." On ratings: "The mortgage-related securities at the heart of the crisis could not have been marketed and sold without their seal of approval ... This crisis could not have happened without the rating agencies." THE COMMISSION WAS DIVIDED, and the report says so on its own contents page: it carries DISSENTING VIEWS "By Keith Hennessey, Douglas Holtz-Eakin, and Bill Thomas" and, separately, "By Peter J. Wallison". The conclusions above are the majority’s. The Commission determined no liability and brought no proceedings.

carbon-class.title: Knowingly Allowed: Six Findings Against a Board That Witnessed and Chose to Ignore
