It also records that a 1990 report by India's National Environmental Engineering Research Institute concluded that "no contamination of soils and ground water was observed due to the impoundment of wastewater in solar evaporation ponds" while recommending remediation — a finding against the plaintiffs on pond contamination, recorded here rather than omitted. This opinion concerns the water claims; it is not authority on the gas-release settlement beyond noting that it barred those claims.

consent.title: War Is a Racket: The Profit Cap of 1934 and the Senate Committee That Reported It Unenforceable
participants: Senate Special Committee on Investigation of the Munitions Industry (Nye Committee)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Naval construction is let to private yards on bids the Navy is in no position to price. The evidence before the Senate munitions committee covers 1933 contracts worth $130,000,000 to the private shipbuilders, awarded by a department that takes the low bid and, in the committee's phrase, leaves the taxpayers "to hope and pray that the low one is somewhere within a few million dollars of being reasonable and proper".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The one instrument that could have priced the work is left unused. The committee finds that the Navy's failure "to turn the navy yards into effective yardsticks by which the charges of private shipyards could be measured and kept down has resulted in leaving the profits of the shipbuilders practically uncontrolled". The government yard that would have shown what a destroyer costs is not made to do it.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The buyer cannot see the price. The Navy "has never examined the underlying costs or profits of the private builders", "makes no pretense of doing this", has no staff for it, and the figures the committee studied "were all news to it"; enforcement of the profit limit is left "to the Treasury to do after 3 years, after a job is done". In the same season the Senate is weighing the word of the officer who called war a racket: on 5 March 1935 it debates Butler's own testimony to the Committee on Naval Affairs that at the waterworks of El Tejar outside Veracruz in 1914 his troops made a reconnaissance and "could find no enemy", against General Russell's sworn account of five or six hundred Mexicans and some twenty shots fired at him. The committee's chairman is Park Trammell, co-author of the profit cap.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The contracting form does the rest. The committee finds that the Navy's grant of adjusted-price contracts in 1933 with limits on the risk the Government assumed, and in 1934 "without any limitation on the Government burden for increased costs", "resulted, in effect, in cost-plus contracts" — and that these cost-plus contracts are "more profitable than the war-time contracts when only a 10-percent profit over cost was allowed". On the 1934 light cruiser, destroyer leader, destroyer and submarine contracts the Government "has assumed all the risk of increasing prices, and has lowered the risk for which the companies received 11.1-percent profit by an enormous amount".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The answer to war profiteering is a cap that the same Senate reports cannot be collected. The Vinson-Trammell Act of 27 March 1934 makes every naval vessel and aircraft contract conditional on the contractor's sworn report and on paying into the Treasury any profit "in excess of 10 per centum of the total contract price", and opens its books to the Navy, the Treasury "and/or ... a duly authorized committee of Congress". The munitions committee then reports that the cap "cannot be enforced without a huge police force of accountants", that interpretation disputes "similar to those which delayed the payment of war-time taxes by the companies for 12 years may confidently be expected", and that the Navy — which has "no responsibility for enforcing the act" and no reliable figures on private costs — is in a position to allow, and according to one company has allowed, increased overhead charges that "can invalidate the whole attempt by Congress to limit profits".

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The naval contracting of 1917-18 and the twelve-year fight over the wartime taxes owed on it, which the munitions committee names as the precedent for what the new cap would meet; and the wartime practice of allowing a fixed percentage profit over cost, which the committee uses as its comparison and finds was the less generous arrangement.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The statutory profit cap in place of enforcement. Vinson-Trammell writes a ceiling, a sworn report and an audit right into every naval contract, and assigns the Navy no duty to enforce any of it — leaving a Treasury computation three years after delivery as the whole machinery, on costs the buyer has never examined.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The yards keep the adjusted-price margin while the Government keeps the risk of rising costs; the cap is reckoned by a department that sees the numbers years later, on overheads the Navy may itself have allowed; and the profit the statute was written to recover is computed from books nobody has yet looked at.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Butler's significance is the 1933 plot he reported to a House committee — a coup story that either happened or did not — and that "war is a racket" is a slogan rather than a claim about contracts that can be checked.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The plot is a separate matter and is dossiered separately. The racket claim, unlike the plot, is testable on the Senate's own paper, and in 1935 the Senate tested it: its munitions committee reported that the shipbuilders' profits were "practically uncontrolled", that the Navy had never examined their costs and made "no pretense of doing this", that the 1933-34 adjusted-price contracts were "in effect" cost-plus and more profitable than wartime terms, and that Congress's own brand-new profit cap could not be enforced "without a huge police force of accountants".
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The Vinson-Trammell Act of 27 March 1934 (48 Stat. 503), conditioning naval contracts on a sworn report and on paying into the Treasury profit above 10 per centum of the total contract price, with books open to the Navy, the Treasury and any duly authorized committee of Congress; and the Senate munitions committee's own 1935 preliminary report on naval shipbuilding finding that cap unenforceable, the Navy incapable of pricing the work, and the contracts cost-plus in effect. Butler's own sworn testimony in the same window, debated in the Senate on 5 March 1935, is that a celebrated 1914 engagement at El Tejar had no enemy in it.

citations.title: An Act to establish the composition of the United States Navy ... and to authorize the construction of certain naval vessels (Vinson-Trammell Act), Act of March 27, 1934, ch. 95, 48 Stat. 503, Public No. 135, H.R. 6604 — United States Statutes at Large, volume 48
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from the downloaded govinfo granule (3 pages, running head "73d CONGRESS. SESS. II. CHS. 94, 95. MARCH 27, 1934"). Section 3 provides "That no contract shall be made by the Secretary of the Navy for the construction and/or manufacture of any complete naval vessel or aircraft, or any portion thereof ... unless the contractor agrees--" then (a) "To make a report, as hereinafter described, under oath, to the Secretary of the Navy upon the completion of the contract"; (b) "To pay into the Treasury profit, as hereinafter provided shall be determined by the Treasury Department, in excess of 10 per centum of the total contract price, such amount to become the property of the United States", collectible by the Secretary of the Treasury "under the usual methods employed under the internal revenue laws to collect Federal income taxes" if not voluntarily paid; (c) "To make no subdivisions of any contract or subcontract for the same article or articles for the purpose of evading the provisions of this Act", with any subdivision over $10,000 subject to the same conditions; (d) that the contractor's "manufacturing spaces and books of its own plant, affiliates, and subdivisions shall at all times be subject to inspection and audit by any person designated by the Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Treasury, and/or by a duly authorized committee of Congress"; and (e) that no subcontract be made unless the subcontractor assents to the same terms. The report must state the total contract price, the cost of performing the contract, the net income and the percentage the net income bears to the contract price, with a copy to the Secretary of the Treasury. The statute caps profit at 10 per centum of the contract price; it is the munitions committee, not the statute, that expresses the same cap as 11.1 percent of cost. The Act assigns the Navy no duty to enforce the cap.

citations.title: Munitions Industry: Naval Shipbuilding — Preliminary Report of the Special Committee on Investigation of the Munitions Industry pursuant to S. Res. 206 (73d Congress), Senate Committee Print, 74th Congress (Washington: U.S. Government Printing Office, 1935)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from the item's full text. A Senate committee print of the Nye Committee, GPO 1935, scanned from the Boston Public Library government documents collection. Under the heading "VII. ATTEMPTS TO LIMIT PROFITS" the committee finds "that the failure of the Navy Department to turn the navy yards into effective yardsticks by which the charges of private shipyards could be measured and kept down has resulted in leaving the profits of the shipbuilders practically uncontrolled"; "that the Vinson-Trammell bill of 1934 limiting profits to 11.1 percent of cost cannot be enforced without a huge police force of accountants and that disputes concerning its interpretation, similar to those which delayed the payment of war-time taxes by the companies for 12 years may confidently be expected"; and that the Navy's adjusted-price contracts of 1933 and 1934 "resulted, in effect, in cost-plus contracts", which it finds "more profitable than the war-time contracts when only a 10-percent profit over cost was allowed". On the 1934 light cruiser, destroyer leader, destroyer and submarine contracts it finds the Government "has assumed all the risk of increasing prices, and has lowered the risk for which the companies received 11.1-percent profit by an enormous amount". Elsewhere it records that "The Navy has never examined the underlying costs or profits of the private builders. It makes no pretense of doing this. It has no staff for it. The figures studied by the Munitions Committee were all news to it"; that the Navy "makes no attempt to examine the costs of the private companies to determine whether the profit limitation of 11.1 percent in the Vinson-Trammell Act is enforced or evaded. That is left to the Treasury to do after 3 years, after a job is done"; and that the evidence showed 1933 contracts worth $130,000,000 to the private shipbuilders. A "Chairman Butler" who appears in the hearing extracts is a shipbuilding officer, not Smedley Butler; the report contains no testimony by Smedley Butler, and two of the committee's hearings volumes contain no occurrence of "Smedley".

citations.title: Congressional Record — Senate, 5 March 1935, pp. 2921-2926 (74th Congress, 1st Session; bound volume 79, part 3)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from the downloaded govinfo bound-volume granule (43 pages). In a Senate debate on Marine Corps promotions, a Senator recounts the conflicting testimony on the 1914 "so-called 'battle of El Tejar'" near Veracruz: "Gen. Smedley Butler testified that he was present; that he rushed up there one Sunday morning; that he was met by General Lejeune; that after his troops had run a part of the distance they boarded a train and then went to the waterworks; that they made a reconnaissance in order to determine where the enemy which had been reported was to be found; and that they could find no enemy." Against that, "General Russell testified, as I recall, that there had been 500 or 600 Mexicans there; that he had been riding on his horse down the line; that he had been shot at about 20 times." The testimony referred to was given before the Committee on Naval Affairs, whose chairman is addressed in the debate as "the chairman of the committee [Mr. TRAMMELL]" — Senator Park Trammell, co-author of the 1934 profit cap. The debate also quotes General Lejeune's published reminiscences (Doran & Co., copyrighted 1930) describing the threatened attack on El Tejar as "one of the insoluble mysteries" and probably "a piece of bravado", and reproduces a letter of 2 March 1935 to Butler from a former bugler who swears "we did not find a single rebel that was supposed to attack us." This page concerns a valour and promotion dispute and Butler's credibility as a witness against the official account; it says nothing about war profits or the munitions inquiry, and is cited only for Butler's own testimony as the Senate recorded it. The OCR of this two-column page interleaves the columns, so passages were reassembled by reading, not transcribed mechanically.

consent.title: Dissolved Into Its Own Shareholders: The 1911 Decree, Six Months to Comply, and the Flag the Trust Asked For in 1914
participants: Standard Oil Company of New Jersey
U.S. Supreme Court (Chief Justice Edward D. White)
Circuit Court for the Eastern District of Missouri
William H. Libby (for Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The New Jersey holding company sits on the stocks of its subsidiaries and takes the return of the combination they make up. The Government sues under the Sherman Act of 1890 and the Circuit Court for the Eastern District of Missouri decrees that the combination be dissolved.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The remedy is not a sale to strangers. The fifth paragraph of the decree permits the distribution of the subsidiary stocks "among the shareholders of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey": the thing dissolved is handed, piece by piece, to the people who already owned it whole. The appellants' own complaint on appeal is not that the distribution was ordered but that the court presumed to limit how they carried it out.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The law itself is moved while the case is pending. Argued in March 1910, restored to the docket, reargued in January 1911 and decided on 15 May 1911, the case produces a Sherman Act read "in the light of reason", under which only unreasonable or undue restraints offend the statute. Justice Harlan, concurring in the affirmance, dissents from that reading in terms the record keeps: the Court, he writes, has "read into the act of Congress words which are not to be found there", and he warns that "illegitimate and unconstitutional practices get their first footing by silent approaches and slight deviations from legal modes of legal procedure".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The timetable is then relaxed at the trust's own request. The Court finds "the delay of thirty days allowed for executing the decree was too short and should be extended so as to embrace a period of at least six months", and strikes the injunction that would have stopped the New Jersey corporation and every subsidiary from carrying on interstate commerce until the stocks were transferred. Half a year to rearrange the succession, and not a day off the market while it happens.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: What remains of the prohibition is a rule against doing again what the decree had just done for them: paragraph 6 is construed as restraining the stockholders from "by any device whatever, recreating directly or indirectly the illegal combination which the decree dissolved", while expressly leaving them the power "to make normal and lawful contracts or agreements". Three years later the company writes to the Secretary of State asking the United States to obtain from the belligerent powers an exemption from seizure and inquiry for tankers moved to the American flag, citing the protection already given the six American steamers of the International Mercantile Marine Company — the flag applied for as an asset, and the precedent drawn from the shipping trust this atlas files at CC-1912-IMM.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Sherman Act of 1890, and the court-supervised reorganization practice of the 1890s railroads in which a judge's decree returns the property to its own owners in a new form — the receivership template, applied here to an antitrust remedy rather than an insolvency.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The rule of reason, and with it the dissolution that distributes instead of divesting: a remedy measured against a shareholder list, with a compliance window long enough to arrange the succession and no interruption of trade while it is arranged.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The subsidiary stocks pass to the holding company's own shareholders; the six-month extension and the struck injunction keep the business whole and trading throughout; and the surviving interest turns to the State Department for a flag the moment war threatens its fleet, citing a shipping trust's protection as the precedent.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That 1911 broke Standard Oil — that the Supreme Court ended the Rockefeller monopoly at the courthouse door and sent the successor companies out to compete with one another.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The decree's own fifth paragraph permitted the subsidiary stocks to be distributed among the shareholders of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey, so the ownership the decree dissolved was the ownership it handed the pieces to; and the Supreme Court then lengthened the time for doing it from thirty days to at least six months and struck the injunction that would have halted the subsidiaries' interstate commerce in the meantime. What the decree forbade afterwards was recreating the combination "by any device whatever" — while expressly preserving the stockholders' power to make normal and lawful contracts.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (1911), decided 15 May 1911: the Sherman Act read "in the light of reason"; the combination held an unreasonable restraint; the thirty-day compliance window extended to at least six months; the paragraph 7 trade injunction held wrongly awarded; paragraph 6 construed to bar recreating the combination while preserving normal contracting; and Harlan, concurring in the affirmance, dissenting from the rule of reason. Three years on, William H. Libby for the company asks the Secretary of State to obtain a belligerent-power exemption from seizure for its re-flagged tankers, on the precedent of the International Mercantile Marine Company's six American steamers.

citations.title: Standard Oil Company of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (1911)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read on CourtListener (the full report, headmatter through Harlan's separate opinion). Appeal from the Circuit Court for the Eastern District of Missouri; argued 14, 15, 16 March 1910; restored to the docket for reargument 11 April 1910; reargued 12, 13, 16, 17 January 1911; decided 15 May 1911. The syllabus states that the Anti-trust Act of 2 July 1890 "should be construed in the light of reason; and, as so construed, it prohibits all contracts and combination which amount to an unreasonable or undue restraint of trade in interstate commerce", and that the defendants' combination "is an unreasonable and undue restraint of trade in petroleum and its products". On the remedy the Court says: "We think that in view of the magnitude of the interests involved and their complexity that the delay of thirty days allowed for executing the decree was too short and should be extended so as to embrace a period of at least six months", and that the injunction provided for in paragraph 7 — against the New Jersey corporation and all the subsidiary companies carrying on interstate commerce until the dissolution was effected by transfer of the stocks — "should not have been awarded". It construes paragraph 6 "not as depriving the stockholders or corporations, after the dissolution of the combination, of the power to make normal and lawful contracts or agreements, but as restraining them from, by any device whatever, recreating directly or indirectly the illegal combination which the decree dissolved", and concludes "that the decree below was right and should be affirmed, except as to the minor matters concerning which we have indicated the decree should be modified." The appellants' assignment of errors records that "the court in s 5 permitted the distribution among the shareholders of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey of the stocks held by that company" and complains that it then limited the method of distribution. Justice Harlan, "while concurring in the general affirmance of the decree of the Circuit Court", dissents "from that part of the judgment of this court which directs the modification of the decree" and from the reading by which the Court "has now read into the act of Congress words which are not to be found there". The report does not state who held the successor stocks after distribution, and no post-decree ownership figure is taken from it.

citations.title: William H. Libby (for the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey) to the Secretary of State, New York, 18 August 1914, File No. 195.1/12 — Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1914, Supplement, The World War, Document 767
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on the Office of the Historian site. A letter written "In behalf of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey" about American-owned vessels under foreign flags, "for the registration of which as American vessels provision has just been made" — the Ship Registry Act of 18 August 1914. Libby states the understanding that vessels transferred to the American flag "would receive the same protection from the Government of the United States as has been accorded to vessels heretofore flying the American flag (for instance, the six American steamers of the International Mercantile Marine Company)", warns that if the good faith of a transfer were inquired into "in the prize courts of belligerent powers" the inquiry "would involve the seizure and detention of the vessel, the costs and delay of a judicial examination, perhaps in a distant place, and the loss of time and freight", and asks: "it has occurred to us that our Government might, without prejudicing in any way any other class of cases, secure the assent of the powers engaged in the present conflict to the exemption from seizure and inquiry of vessels transferred to the American flag which were actually owned in this country before the war began." The letter argues from the Declaration of London, which it notes "has not, we believe, acquired the force of a treaty". This document is a company request for diplomatic protection of its shipping; it records no reply, no instruction to any belligerent, and no use of force, and nothing is claimed here beyond the request itself.

consent.title: Mission Specialists: A Submersible Under No Flag, and Two Federal Boards That Called the Loss Preventable
participants: U.S. Coast Guard Marine Board of Investigation

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The fares are taken, and the people who pay them are given a job title. OceanGate carries its paying clients as "mission specialists" — in its own Project Execution Plan for the 2023 expedition, "guests who help fund OceanGate" who are assigned tasks aboard. A former operations technician, once a Coast Guard engineering technician himself, tells the chief executive "... you can't just change the title of a person when you're receiving compensation", and resigns citing "the legality of how it [OceanGate] was operating". The NTSB puts the purpose on the record: it notes "OceanGate's intent to avoid safety oversight by assigning tasks to those paying to ride".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The hull is never established as strong enough. The NTSB finds OceanGate's engineering process produced a carbon fibre composite pressure vessel "that contained multiple anomalies and failed to meet necessary strength and durability requirements", and that because the company did not adequately test it, it "was unaware of the pressure vessel's actual strength and durability, which was likely much lower than their target", including how storage condition and towing bore on the vessel's integrity.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Nothing is watching, and the one instrument that was is misread. The Titan flies no flag: it "was not registered in any US state, documented by the US National Vessel Documentation Center, nor inspected by any flag state", and its flag, port of registry, IMO number and classification society are all recorded as not applicable, with the title held by a US company and the operation run from The Bahamas. Its real-time monitoring system generated the data that would have condemned the hull, and the analysis was flawed, so "the company was unaware that the Titan was damaged and needed to be immediately removed from service after dive 80".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The arrangement holds because the rules do not reach it. At the time of the Coast Guard's 1993 guidance for passenger-carrying submersibles, vessels like the Titan — six or fewer passengers — were treated as "uninspected" rather than small passenger vessels, and that guidance was in any case voluntary; the operator never registered or documented the Titan in the United States, nor arranged Coast Guard inspection. The guidance it did not follow advised keeping operations within the depth at which rescue assistance is effective; the Titan dove to the Titanic, far beyond any available rescue, routinely with none standing by, as on the day it was lost.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Two federal boards report, and both say it did not have to happen — which is not the same as anyone answering for it. The NTSB's probable cause is OceanGate's inadequate engineering process, with voluntary guidance and small passenger vessel regulations "insufficient to ensure OceanGate adhered to established industry standards" as contributing. The Coast Guard board's chair says "This marine casualty and the loss of five lives was preventable", and its more than 300 pages add a toxic workplace culture, an inadequate domestic and international regulatory framework, and an ineffective whistleblower process under the Seaman's Protection Act, with 17 recommendations. The NTSB states expressly that it does not determine whether any conduct violated statutory or regulatory requirements; and the Coast Guard's recommendations were, when published, still with the Commandant awaiting a Final Action Memorandum — the gap each board identified left open by the documents that identified it.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The shape this atlas has tracked since 1912: a novel vessel no classification society has passed, a safety standard that is advisory rather than binding, and a class of passenger defined so as to fall outside the protective rule. Here it is the definition that does the work, not a liability cap — the people who paid were entered as participants in the mission.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The unflagged commercial submersible: title in one company, operation from another jurisdiction, no flag state, no class society, no certificate of inspection, and the paying passengers recorded as crew-adjacent "mission specialists" — a deep-ocean passenger operation standing entirely outside the regime written for passenger vessels.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The fares fund the expeditions, and the title given the people paying them is what keeps the oversight those fares would have triggered from attaching. The hull nobody certified is tested by diving it; the monitoring data that would have taken it out of service is read by the company that owns it; and the cost of the error falls on the five people inside.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Titan was lost to the unforgiving deep — a freak accident in water no rule could have made safe — or, in the other direction, that one reckless chief executive explains the whole of it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Neither survives the two reports. The hull was already damaged before the casualty dive: the NTSB found delamination after dive 80 and further damage of unknown origin after dive 82, and found that the company's own real-time monitoring data meant the Titan "needed to be immediately removed from service after dive 80" — so the failure was recorded in advance, not unforeseeable. And both boards found the framework itself insufficient, the Coast Guard board recommending that the Oceanographic Research Vessel designation be restricted for submersibles and that inspection requirements be extended to all submersibles on commercial or scientific dives — findings about a regime, not about one man's temperament.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: NTSB Marine Investigation Report MIR-25-36: probable cause OceanGate's inadequate engineering process, contributed to by insufficient voluntary guidance and small passenger vessel regulations and by the company's flawed reading of its own monitoring data; the Titan recorded as not registered in any US state, not documented by the National Vessel Documentation Center and not inspected by any flag state, with no IMO number and no classification society; the "mission specialist" framing taken from OceanGate's own Project Execution Plan, with the NTSB noting the company's "intent to avoid safety oversight by assigning tasks to those paying to ride"; and the US Coast Guard Marine Board of Investigation's report of 5 August 2025, more than 300 pages and 17 recommendations, whose chair called the loss of five lives preventable, and which remained under review by the Commandant pending a Final Action Memorandum.

citations.title: National Transportation Safety Board, Hull Failure and Implosion of Submersible Titan, North Atlantic Ocean, June 18, 2023 — Marine Investigation Report NTSB/MIR-25-36 (investigation DCA23FM036)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded and read (text extracted from the official PDF). Section 3.2 states: "The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of the hull failure and implosion of the submersible Titan was OceanGate's inadequate engineering process, which failed to establish the actual strength and durability of the Titan pressure vessel and resulted in the company operating a carbon fiber composite vessel that sustained delamination damage that was subsequently exacerbated by additional damage of unknown origin, resulting in a damaged internal structure that subsequently led to a local buckling failure of the pressure vessel. Contributing were US and international voluntary guidance and US small passenger vessel regulations that were insufficient to ensure OceanGate adhered to established industry standards. Also contributing was OceanGate's flawed analysis of their pressure vessel monitoring system data, which led to their continued operation of a damaged pressure vessel." The report records that Titan was owned by Cyclops II Inc and operated by OceanGate Expeditions, based in The Bahamas, both affiliates of OceanGate Inc; that "The Titan was not registered in any US state, documented by the US National Vessel Documentation Center, nor inspected by any flag state"; and in its vessel particulars table that flag, port of registry, official number, IMO number and classification society are all "N/A", with year built 2020. On the paying passengers it records that OceanGate referred to its clients as "mission specialists", described in the company's "Project Execution Plan" for the 2023 expedition as "guests who help fund OceanGate", and in a footnote states: "While the NTSB does not determine whether specific operator conduct violates statutory or regulatory requirements that may be the subject of enforcement by the US Coast Guard, we note OceanGate's intent to avoid safety oversight by assigning tasks to those paying to ride." It records a former operations technician's statement to the CEO that "... you can't just change the title of a person when you're receiving compensation", his resignation citing "the legality of how it [OceanGate] was operating", and his account that the CEO said "if the [US] Coast Guard became a problem ... he would buy himself a congressman and make it go away" — statements of a witness as the report records them, not findings of the Board. On the regulatory framework it records that at the time of NVIC 05-93 (July 1993) "submersibles carrying six or fewer passengers (like the Titan) were considered uninspected vessels--not small passenger vessels", that after the Passenger Vessel Safety Act of 1993 "the definition of a small passenger vessel changed to include any submersible carrying at least one passenger for hire", and that "OceanGate did not register or document the Titan in the United States, nor did they arrange to have it inspected by the US Coast Guard." The report determines probable cause; it does not determine liability.

citations.title: National Transportation Safety Board, investigation DCA23FM036 — Hull Failure and Implosion of Submersible Titan (investigation summary page)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in the browser. The Board's own summary: "On June 18, 2023, about 1047 local time, while diving to the wreck of the ocean liner Titanic in the North Atlantic Ocean, about 372 miles southeast of St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, the submersible Titan's pressure hull failed, and the vessel imploded. All five persons on board the vessel died." It states the damage sequence — damage after dive 80 "in the form of one or more delaminations", further damage of unknown origin after dive 82, and a local buckling failure on the casualty dive (dive 88) — and that "OceanGate's analysis of Titan pressure vessel real-time monitoring data was flawed, so the company was unaware that the Titan was damaged and needed to be immediately removed from service after dive 80." It records that had OceanGate followed NVIC 05-93 guidance for emergency response plans, emergency response assets would likely have been standing by and the Titan found sooner "even though a rescue was not possible in this case", and that despite OceanGate's failure to notify search and rescue assets, "the US Coast Guard's search and rescue coordination efforts were effective". It also states that "voluntary guidance and current US small passenger vessel regulations are not sufficiently tailored to current pressure vessel for human occupancy (PVHO) operations". It gives the Titan's value, with its launch and recovery system, as about $5.6 million CAD per a 2023 customs declaration. A summary page, not the full report; the probable-cause wording is taken from the report itself.

citations.title: U.S. Coast Guard, "Coast Guard Marine Board of Investigation releases report on Titan submersible", press release, 5 August 2025
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on the Coast Guard's official news site. Announces that the Marine Board of Investigation released its Report of Investigation on 5 August 2025 into the loss of the Titan, "which imploded during a June 2023 dive to the Titanic, killing five people", and that the "more than 300-page ROI" carries 17 safety recommendations. Quotes MBI chair Jason Neubauer: "This marine casualty and the loss of five lives was preventable," and his statement that the two-year investigation identified "multiple contributing factors" and that "There is a need for stronger oversight and clear options for operators who are exploring new concepts outside of the existing regulatory framework." States that "The board determined the primary contributing factors were OceanGate's inadequate design, certification, maintenance and inspection process for the Titan", with other factors including "a toxic workplace culture at OceanGate, an inadequate domestic and international regulatory framework for submersible operations and vessels of novel design, and an ineffective whistleblower process under the Seaman's Protection Act"; and that the board found OceanGate "failed to properly investigate and address known hull anomalies following its 2022 Titanic expedition", took no action on real-time monitoring data that "should have been analyzed and acted on", and did not conduct preventative maintenance or properly store the Titan over the extended off season. Recommendations listed include "restricting the Oceanographic Research Vessel designations for submersibles, expanding federal and international requirements to all submersibles conducting scientific or commercial dives and requiring Coast Guard documentation for all U.S. submersibles", and working with the International Maritime Organization "to define passenger submersibles". Records that "The Marine Board's report is now under review by the Commandant of the Coast Guard" and that a Final Action Memorandum will follow. The ROI PDF linked from this page is served from media.defense.gov, which returns 403 to scripted requests and triggers a download rather than rendering in a browser: the report itself was not read here, and nothing above is taken from it beyond what this press release states.

consent.title: The Pre-9/11 Put Options: 9.5 Million Transactions, One Bearish Adviser and a Newsletter Faxed on a Sunday
participants: Securities and Exchange Commission, Division of Enforcement
U.S. Attorney’s Office, Eastern District of New York
National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States (staff)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Money was made, and the record says who made it and why. A U.S. investment adviser registered with the SEC, running several hedge funds with $5.3 billion under management, bought 95 percent of the UAL put option volume on 6 September 2001 on a bearish view of the airline industry built on on-time departure figures and AMR’s own disclosed results. A New York hedge fund with $2 billion under management bought more than a third of the UAL puts purchased on 7 September. Subscribers to a California investment-advice newsletter, faxed and emailed on Sunday 9 September, bought AMR puts on the Monday. When the markets reopened on 17 September, AMR fell 40 percent and UAL fell 43 percent, and those positions paid.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What makes an option position look like foreknowledge is the leverage inside it. The Commission’s own staff footnote states the mechanism plainly: people trading illicitly on inside information "often have used options because they allow the trader to leverage an initial investment, so that a relatively small investment can generate huge profits." A high ratio of puts to calls is therefore "a potential indicator of insider trading" — and on 6 September the UAL put volume exceeded call volume by more than twenty times, while on 10 September AMR’s exceeded calls six to one. Those ratios are real. They are also, on the record, the only part of the story that was ever public.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The ratios were published; the account-level data that resolved them was not, and could not be. The fog in this episode runs the other way from the usual: the public could see the volume and never the buyer. Into that gap went the president of the German central bank, Ernst Welteke, whose statements that insider trading had occurred in airline and insurance shares and in gold and oil futures were never confirmed; his own country’s securities regulator said on 27 September 2001 that "there is no evidence that anyone who had knowledge of the attacks before they were committed used it to make financial transactions", and said the same again in December.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: There was no windfall to find, and the investigation that looked for one is on the record. From 12 September 2001 the SEC, with the FBI and a Brooklyn prosecutor assigned full time, analysed trading in 103 individual companies and 32 index or exchange-traded funds and examined more than 9.5 million securities transactions, with deliberate redundancy: Large Option Position Reports and Open Interest Distribution Reports that identify holders of large option positions whenever those positions were opened, direct canvasses of twenty of the largest broker-dealers, and the self-regulatory organisations’ own surveillance. The "profits left uncollected" claim was tested against the Options Clearing Corporation, which exercises profitable positions automatically unless a customer instructs otherwise and double-checks any such instruction with the broker: OCC staff recalled no such contact after 9/11.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: This is where the dossier departs from the pattern the atlas usually traces, and it departs from it because the documents do. There is no commission here that narrowed its terms of reference to protect an interest. There is a staff monograph that sets out its method, names the limits of its own authority — "they have not approved this text and it does not necessarily reflect their views" — and reaches a flat negative. What it does not do is name a single adviser, fund, trader or newsletter, or give a single account number; and the SEC memorandum it rests on, "Pre-September 11, 2001 Trading Review" of 15 May 2002, has never been published. A reader who wants to check the conclusion against the underlying data still cannot.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The surveillance architecture built into U.S. securities markets after 1934 and extended through the option-position reporting regime: a market in which, as the monograph puts it, no one can trade "without leaving a paper trail that the SEC can easily access through its regulatory powers".
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The terrorist-financing investigative apparatus stood up after 9/11, and with it the template for every later "trading on terror" claim: a published volume anomaly, an unpublished account-level resolution, and a regulator’s assurance in between.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The claim regenerates itself because the two halves of the evidence sit on opposite sides of a disclosure line. Option volumes and put/call ratios are public and permanent; the identity of the buyer and the rest of their book are not. Anyone can re-derive the anomaly at any time; no one outside the agencies can re-derive the answer.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That someone — al Qaeda, or insiders who were told — loaded up on puts against United and American in the days before 9/11 and made a killing, that some of the winnings were never even collected, and that the proof burned with the SEC’s files in World Trade Center 7.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Every element of it was tested and none survived. The 6 September UAL spike was 95 percent the work of one SEC-registered U.S. adviser running $5.3 billion, whose strategy also had it buying 115,000 AMR shares on 10 September — shares that fell hard when trading resumed; the 7 September UAL buyer was a $2 billion New York fund that held 29,000 UAL shares alongside the puts and came out $85,000 down; the 10 September AMR surge traced to a California newsletter faxed on the Sunday, with 26 of 28 interviewed purchasers citing it; the heavily reported AIG puts were a hedge against 4.2 million shares of AIG held at a low tax basis, on which the fund lost money overall; the offshore $5 million short-side profit belonged to a European speculator who had lost $8 million doing the same thing in the preceding six months. The uncollected-profits story fails on the Options Clearing Corporation’s own mechanics: profitable options exercise automatically unless the customer says otherwise, and the OCC recalled no one saying otherwise. And the WTC 7 argument fails on sequence and custody: the SEC opened this investigation on 12 September 2001 and ran it on exchange, self-regulatory-organisation, broker-dealer and clearing-house records, none of which were kept in that building.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: What the record supports is narrower than the rumour and narrower than a vindication. The volumes were real and anomalous on their face: UAL puts exceeding calls more than twenty to one on 6 September, AMR puts six to one on 10 September. An investigation of genuine scale followed — 103 companies, 32 funds, more than 9.5 million transactions, more than 40 SEC staff, the FBI and a full-time federal prosecutor — and resolved every profitable trade it found to a lawful strategy. The Commission’s own note 130 states the result: "the apparently suspicious consistently proved innocuous." Against that sits what is still not public: no trader, fund or newsletter is named anywhere in the documents, and the SEC memorandum the finding rests on has never been released. The honest ledger entry is that an exhaustive investigation found nothing, and that the public has been asked to take the finding on the word of the people who conducted it.

citations.title: National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States, Monograph on Terrorist Financing (Staff Report to the Commission, 2004) — Appendix B: Securities Trading, pp. 145–151
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the Commission's own site and read as extracted text. Appendix B opens: "This appendix describes the staff and U.S. government investigations into the issue of whether anyone with foreknowledge of the 9/11 attacks profited through securities trading, and explains the conclusion in the Commission's final report that extensive government investigation has revealed no evidence of such illicit trading." It records that "Almost since 9/11 itself, there have been consistent reports that massive 'insider trading' preceded the attacks" and that "The Commission has found no evidence to support these reports." On method: the SEC's chief of the Office of Market Surveillance opened an investigation into pre-9/11 trading on 12 September 2001; at a multi-agency meeting at FBI headquarters on 17 September the SEC agreed to lead it; the Department of Justice assigned a white-collar prosecutor from the U.S. Attorney's Office in Brooklyn full time, who relocated to Washington on 18 September. More than 40 SEC staff were involved at various times, working with the New York Stock Exchange, the American Stock Exchange, NASD Regulation and the Chicago Board Options Exchange; "the investigators analyzed trading in 103 individual companies and 32 index or exchange-traded funds and examined more than 9.5 million securities transactions." The SEC also obtained Large Option Position Reports and Open Interest Distribution Reports, "that identified the holders of substantial amounts of options without regard to when those options were purchased", contacted 20 of the largest broker-dealers directly and asked the Securities Industry Association to canvass its members. On the three trades most cited in the press: on 6 September the UAL put volume "exceeded the call option volume by more than 20 times", and "The SEC quickly discovered, however, that a single U.S. investment adviser had purchased 95 percent of the UAL put option volume for the day", an adviser "based in the United States, registered with the SEC, and managed several hedge funds with $5.3 billion under management", whose stated reasons included "recently released on-time departure figures" and "recently disclosed news by AMR reflecting poor business fundamentals", and which "also bought 115,000 shares of AMR on September 10" that "dropped significantly when the markets reopened"; the SEC referred the trade to the FBI anyway and the FBI "reached the same conclusion". On 10 September the AMR put volume "exceeded the call volume by a ratio of 6:1", and the SEC "traced much of the surge in volume to a California investment advice newsletter, distributed by email and fax on Sunday, September 9", interviewing 28 purchasers of whom 26 cited the newsletter, with another 27 purchasers listed as its subscribers. On 7 September a single trader bought "more than one-third of the total puts purchased that day" in UAL and was identified as "a well-established New York hedge fund with $2 billion under management" that also held 29,000 UAL shares and "actually lost $85,000 in value when the market reopened". A heavily reported AIG put purchase was found by the FBI to be a hedge of "a long position of 4.2 million shares in the AIG common stock" held at a very low tax basis, on which the fund "overall lost money as a result of the attacks". On the claim that profits went uncollected, the monograph records that officials at the SEC and the Options Clearing Corporation stated that "any profitable options positions are automatically exercised upon the expiration date unless the customer explicitly directed otherwise", that the OCC double-checks any such instruction with the broker, and that "The OCC personnel had no recollection of any such contacts after 9/11." It records that when the markets opened on 17 September "AMR fell 40 percent and UAL fell 43 percent." On the international side it records that a European regulator traced a $5 million offshore short-side profit to "an extremely wealthy European national who often speculated by taking short positions in the U.S. market" and who "had employed this strategy to lose $8 million in the six months preceding 9/11", and that on 27 September 2001 a spokesman for the German regulator BAWe declared that "there is no evidence that anyone who had knowledge of the attacks before they were committed used it to make financial transactions." WHAT THE DOCUMENT IS AND IS NOT: its own preface states "This is a study by Commission staff. While the Commissioners have been briefed on the work and have had the opportunity to review earlier drafts of some of this work, they have not approved this text and it does not necessarily reflect their views." It names no trader, adviser, hedge fund or newsletter, gives no account numbers, and says nothing whatever about World Trade Center 7 or about any record destroyed there.

citations.title: The 9/11 Commission Report (Final Report of the National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States) — note 130 to chapter 5, p. 499
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. Note 130 to chapter 5, printed at page 499, is the Commission's own statement on the question: "Highly publicized allegations of insider trading in advance of 9/11 generally rest on reports of unusual pre-9/11 trading activity in companies whose stock plummeted after the attacks. Some unusual trading did in fact occur, but each such trade proved to have an innocuous explanation. For example, the volume of put options — investments that pay off only when a stock drops in price — surged in the parent companies of United Airlines on September 6 and American Airlines on September 10 — highly suspicious trading on its face. Yet, further investigation has revealed that the trading had no connection with 9/11. A single U.S.-based institutional investor with no conceivable ties to al Qaeda purchased 95 percent of the UAL puts on September 6 as part of a trading strategy that also included buying 115,000 shares of American on September 10. Similarly, much of the seemingly suspicious trading in American on September 10 was traced to a specific U.S.-based options trading newsletter, faxed to its subscribers on Sunday, September 9, which recommended these trades. These examples typify the evidence examined by the investigation. The SEC and the FBI, aided by other agencies and the securities industry, devoted enormous resources to investigating this issue, including securing the cooperation of many foreign governments. These investigators have found that the apparently suspicious consistently proved innocuous." The note's own sourcing line cites interviews with Joseph Cella, an FBI briefing, and an SEC memorandum from the Division of Enforcement to the Chair and Commissioners titled "Pre-September 11, 2001 Trading Review", dated May 15, 2002. That memorandum is not public and was not read here; what is read here is the Commission's characterisation of it.

consent.title: A Disclosed Sale, a Sealed Warrant and a Closed File: the February 2020 Senate Stock Sales on the Court Record
participants: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Chief Judge Beryl A. Howell)
U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit
Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: On 13 February 2020 Senator Richard Burr and his wife sold stocks valued, on the mandatory Senate filings, at between $628,000 and $1.72 million. The market fell sharply soon afterwards as the pandemic became general knowledge. The sale is on the record because a statute requires it to be: the STOCK Act obliges the filing of a periodic transaction report within 30 days of notification and in no case later than 45 days after the trade.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The asymmetry at issue is structural rather than contrived. The Senator sat on the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions and, as the D.C. Circuit records, "had received briefings on the pandemic in his capacity as a Senator" shortly before those sales. Congress had legislated against exactly this in 2012, affirming that its own members "are not exempt from the insider trading prohibitions arising under the securities laws" and writing into the Securities Exchange Act a duty of trust and confidence owed to the Congress, the Government and the citizens of the United States.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog here was not in the market; it was over the investigation. A warrant to search the Senator’s cellphone issued under seal on 13 May 2020. For more than a year of litigation the Department of Justice would not confirm that any such warrant, or any investigation, existed — forcing the district court to reason about "hypothesized search warrant materials" and the court of appeals to do the same. What finally broke the silence came from a different agency: the SEC’s October 2021 application in the Southern District of New York to enforce a subpoena on the Senator’s brother-in-law disclosed the investigation, its parallel criminal track, and some of the underlying telephone records.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: No charge was ever brought. The Department closed its criminal review and told the Senator so in January 2021; his statement was four sentences long and ended "The case is now closed." The district court’s 2022 opinion describes the matter twice as a closed investigation "that resulted in no prosecution of former Senator Burr". What the trades were worth, against what the holdings would have been worth a month later, appears in no document read here.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment in this dossier is a sealing order, and it was partly undone in public by a judge. On remand, the Department acknowledged the warrant’s existence on 24 May 2022 and filed a heavily redacted version. Chief Judge Howell granted continued sealing for third-party privacy and investigative technique, and refused it for the rest: redactions "intended to preserve the due process interests of investigative targets against whom the probable cause allegations in the warrant were made without any criminal charges being brought must be disclosed", with named paragraphs of the supporting affidavit ordered opened by 5 September 2022. The mechanism the atlas usually finds closing over a case here partly reopened it — and only because a newspaper litigated for eighteen months.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Ethics in Government Act disclosure regime, as amended in 2012 by the STOCK Act — a self-imposed reporting duty on the legislature, enforced through publication rather than through an outside auditor.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A worked precedent on both halves of the problem: that the securities laws reach a sitting senator through a duty of trust and confidence owed to the citizens, and that search warrant materials in a closed, uncharged investigation of a public official are judicial records whose sealing must be justified line by line.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The same statute produces both the suspicion and the defence. Disclosure is what made the February 2020 sales visible at all; the absence of any charge is what the disclosure regime, having worked, leaves behind. Each side of the public argument now cites the half of that record it prefers.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That senators were briefed on the coming pandemic in January 2020, quietly dumped their portfolios before the public knew, and were protected from any consequence by their own institution.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The protection is the part that fails hardest. The sales are known because a law Congress passed about itself required them to be filed and published; the FBI obtained a warrant for a sitting senator’s cellphone within three months; the Securities and Exchange Commission ran a parallel civil investigation and went to federal court to compel testimony from a family member; and when the Department of Justice tried to keep the whole file dark, a federal judge ordered part of it opened over the Department’s objection. What did not happen is a charge: the criminal investigation closed in January 2021 with no prosecution. The timing also matters to the sweeping version of the claim — the trades that the court record actually concerns are dated 13 February 2020, not January, and the record read here concerns one senator. The filings of the other members named in 2020 coverage were not read, and nothing is asserted about them here.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Stocks worth between $628,000 and $1.72 million sold by Senator Burr and his wife on 13 February 2020, as disclosed under the STOCK Act. Pandemic briefings received shortly before, in his capacity as a member of the Senate HELP Committee. A sealed warrant for his cellphone granted on 13 May 2020, in an investigation the government later described as directed to "whether Senator Burr sold or purchased stock based on non-public information relating to the COVID-19 pandemic that he received by virtue of his position as a United States Senator". An SEC investigation running in parallel, disclosed in its own October 2021 filing, which also recorded telephone records among Burr, his brother-in-law Gerald Fauth and their brokers, and a declaration that prosecutors had told Fauth’s counsel his criminal investigation was closed. A Justice Department review closed in January 2021 without charges. And a court order of 29 August 2022 unsealing the parts of the warrant affidavit that make the probable-cause allegations, precisely because no charge was ever brought on them. What remains sealed is what the allegations rested on; what is settled is that no court was ever asked to decide whether they were true.

citations.title: In re Application of Los Angeles Times Communications LLC to Unseal Court Records, Misc. Action No. 21-16 (BAH) (D.D.C., Chief Judge Beryl A. Howell, Memorandum Opinion and Order, 29 August 2022)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full in a browser on CourtListener (the CourtListener API returns 401 to unauthenticated requests and the plain page returns an empty 202 to scripts). The opinion states that "On May 13, 2020, the government presented, and this Court granted under seal, a warrant to search the cellphone of Senator Burr as part of a now closed investigation into allegations of insider training and securities fraud, in violation of 15 U.S.C. § 78j(b) and 18 U.S.C. § 1348, respectively" (the typographical slip for "trading" is the court's). Quoting the government's own motion, it records that the government "sought to determine whether Senator Burr sold or purchased stock based on non-public information relating to the COVID-19 pandemic that he received by virtue of his position as a United States Senator, in violation of the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act ('STOCK Act'), codified at 15 U.S.C. §§ 78j(b), 78u-1(g)." It quotes the D.C. Circuit's factual summary that "On February 13, 2020, Senator Richard Burr and his wife sold stocks valued between $628,000 and $1.72 million, as disclosed in mandatory Senate filings", that the market then fell sharply, and that "shortly before those sales, Senator Burr had received briefings on the pandemic in his capacity as a Senator and member of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions". It records Senator Burr's January 2021 statement in full as reported: "Tonight, the Department of Justice informed me that it has concluded its review of my personal financial transactions conducted early last year. The case is now closed." It records that for over a year of litigation "DOJ never publicly recognized the existence of either the search warrant materials or any DOJ investigation into Senator Burr", that the district court had therefore to treat the warrant as "hypothesized", and that only on 24 May 2022, after the D.C. Circuit's remand, did DOJ notify the court that it "now acknowledges the existence of the Materials". The disposition: the government's motion for continued sealing was "GRANTED IN PART AND DENIED IN PART"; redactions protecting third-party privacy and law-enforcement techniques were retained, while "DOJ's proposed redactions intended to preserve the due process interests of investigative targets against whom the probable cause allegations in the warrant were made without any criminal charges being brought must be disclosed", with specified paragraphs of the supporting affidavit ordered unsealed by 5 September 2022. The opinion twice describes the matter as a "closed investigation that resulted in no prosecution of former Senator Burr". It makes no finding that any law was broken; it decides only what the public may see.

citations.title: In re Application of Los Angeles Times Communications LLC to Unseal Court Records, No. 21-5128, 28 F.4th 292 (D.C. Cir., argued 2 February 2022, decided 18 March 2022)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the court's own opinions server and read as extracted text. Opinion for the court by Circuit Judge Rogers. It opens the facts: "On February 13, 2020, Senator Richard Burr and his wife sold stocks valued between $628,000 and $1.72 million, as disclosed in mandatory Senate filings. Soon after, the stock market fell sharply as news about the COVID-19 pandemic spread. Because, shortly before those sales, Senator Burr had received briefings on the pandemic in his capacity as a Senator and member of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, the February 13 trades quickly garnered media scrutiny and public attention." It records the L.A. Times report of 13 May 2020 that a search warrant had been served and the Senator's cellphone seized, sourced to "a law enforcement official speaking on condition of anonymity", and that "Eight months later, Senator Burr issued a public statement noting that the investigation into the stock transactions had been closed." On the parallel civil matter it records that the SEC applied in the Southern District of New York for an order compelling compliance with an investigative subpoena issued to the Senator's brother-in-law Gerald Fauth (SEC v. Fauth, No. 1:21-mc-00787, filed 22 October 2021), that in its memorandum of law "the SEC disclosed that it was investigating stock trades by Senator Burr and Mr. Fauth, and that its investigation paralleled an investigation by the Justice Department", that the filing "also disclosed some of the underlying facts, including records of phone calls among Burr, Fauth, and their brokers", and that a declaration by Fauth's counsel "recounted a conversation in which Justice Department prosecutors stated that the criminal investigation of Fauth was closed." The court remanded for reconsideration of the common-law access analysis under United States v. Hubbard. It decided a question of public access only, reached no view on the merits of any allegation, and did not reach the First Amendment argument.

citations.title: Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act of 2012 (STOCK Act), Pub. L. 112-105, 126 Stat. 291 (4 April 2012) — sections 4 and 6
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. Section 4(a), "Affirmation of nonexemption", provides that "Members of Congress and employees of Congress are not exempt from the insider trading prohibitions arising under the securities laws, including section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder." Section 4(b) states that its purpose "is to affirm a duty arising from a relationship of trust and confidence owed by each Member of Congress and each employee of Congress", and amends section 21A of the Securities Exchange Act by adding subsection (g): each Member or employee of Congress "owes a duty arising from a relationship of trust and confidence to the Congress, the United States Government, and the citizens of the United States with respect to material, nonpublic information derived from such person's position as a Member of Congress or employee of Congress or gained from the performance of such person's official responsibilities." Section 6, "Prompt reporting of financial transactions", amends section 103 of the Ethics in Government Act of 1978 to require a report of a covered transaction "Not later than 30 days after receiving notification of any transaction required to be reported under section 102(a)(5)(B), but in no case later than 45 days after such transaction". Section 3 directs the ethics committees of both chambers to issue interpretive guidance clarifying that nonpublic information derived from the office may not be used "as a means for making a private profit". The Act creates the disclosure duty; it does not itself make any finding about any filer.

consent.title: Known at Ignalina in 1983: the Scram Defect Nobody Corrected, and the Announcement That Waited
participants: Chief Design Engineer for RBMK reactors
USSR State Committee for the Supervision of Safety in Industry and Nuclear Power (SCSSINP)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The saving here was made in advance and in kind, not in cash: a design change that was promised and never made. The positive scram effect — reactivity added, rather than removed, in the first moments of inserting the control and safety rods — was identified at the Ignalina RBMK plant in Lithuania in 1983. The Chief Design Engineer for RBMK reactors circulated the finding to the other RBMK stations and said design changes would be made to correct it. INSAG’s 1992 report records what followed: "he made no such changes, and the procedural measures he recommended for inclusion in plant operating instructions were not adopted."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: A second promise went the same way. After Ignalina the chief engineering organization told every RBMK plant that it intended to impose restrictions on withdrawing the control and safety rods completely from the core; "Such restrictions were never imposed and apparently the matter was forgotten." A 1975 event at the Leningrad plant had already shown that local reactivity feedback could damage a reactor. INSAG’s verdict on the pair of precursors: "It is a matter of great concern that this important information was not adequately reviewed and, where it was disseminated to designers, operators and regulators, its significance was not fully understood and it was essentially ignored."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog operated in two directions at once, and both are documented. Outward, toward the public: "the Soviet government delayed the public announcement that the accident had occurred. Information provision was selective and restrictive, particularly in the immediate aftermath of the accident", and reliable information "was initially unavailable to the affected people". The cost was measurable — countermeasures against radioiodine in milk were "only partially effective ... because of the lack of timely information about the accident and necessary responses, particularly for private farmers". Inward, toward the people sent to find out what had happened: the design flaw was not disclosed at the IAEA’s own post-accident review in 1986, and INSAG said so in 1992: "Certainly the account in INSAG-1 would have been different had the features of the control and safety rods been revealed at the Post-Accident Review Meeting in 1986."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: There is no commercial windfall in this record, and inventing one would be the easy, false move. What the documents show instead is a state that protected an industrial programme and its designers by controlling what the operators, the regulators, the public and finally the international review body were each allowed to know, and which was still protecting them a year after the reactor had destroyed itself.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment was the 1986 review itself, and its undoing is the reason the 1992 report exists. INSAG-7 is an official body publishing a correction to its own earlier findings once the withheld fact had surfaced — first acknowledged by Soviet experts at a Vienna conference in 1987, five years before the correction was printed. Its judgment is unusually direct for the genre: "It is reprehensible that such a deficiency had been known of for so long without its having been eliminated."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A nuclear programme whose designer, operator and regulator answered to the same state, and an information regime in which an industrial defect was a matter for the ministry rather than for the plants running the reactor.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The international convention, after 1986, that an accident at a nuclear plant is a matter of mandatory notification and assistance rather than of national discretion — and, in INSAG-7 itself, the precedent of a safety review body publicly reversing its own report when it learns it was not told everything.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Each layer of silence protected the one above it. The design organisation was spared the cost of a retrofit by not enforcing its own instruction; the operators were spared knowledge they would have had to act on; the public was spared an announcement; and the review that should have caught all of it was spared the one fact that would have changed its account.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Party elite knew what had happened at once and quietly evacuated their own families while ordinary Ukrainians were marched out under the fallout for the May Day parades.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: No document read for this dossier records any of it. The IAEA’s INSAG-7 is a report on reactor design, operation and regulation and says nothing about the evacuation of anyone. The Chernobyl Forum’s own report, which does cover the evacuation in detail, records no separate or earlier removal of officials, Party members or their families, and does not mention the May Day observances of 1 May 1986 at all. What it does record cuts across the simple version in both directions: the delay was real and the information regime was "selective and restrictive", and at the same time the authorities distributed stable iodine in Pripyat in the first hours — which "reduced the thyroid dose of the residents of Pripyat by a factor of 6 on average" — and evacuated about 50,000 people from the city within 40 hours. A dossier that asserted the nomenklatura evacuation would be asserting something it had not read.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The foreknowledge in this file is engineering foreknowledge, and it is documented to the year. The positive scram effect was identified at Ignalina in 1983; the Chief Design Engineer circulated it and promised design changes that were never made; the procedural measures he recommended were not adopted; the restrictions on full rod withdrawal were announced and never imposed. A 1975 Leningrad event had pointed the same way. The defect was not disclosed to the IAEA’s post-accident review in 1986 and was first acknowledged by Soviet experts in Vienna in 1987; INSAG published the correction in 1992 and called the delay reprehensible. On the public side: the announcement was delayed, information was selective and restrictive, the shortfall measurably reduced the effectiveness of countermeasures against radioiodine in milk, and the early secrecy is cited by the Forum as the reason official information on Chernobyl is still distrusted. Pripyat, about 50,000 people, was evacuated within 40 hours; more than 100,000 within a few weeks; 116,000 from the Exclusion Zone across the spring and summer of 1986; another 220,000 relocated in later years.

citations.title: International Atomic Energy Agency, The Chernobyl Accident: Updating of INSAG-1 — A Report by the International Nuclear Safety Advisory Group, Safety Series No. 75-INSAG-7 (Vienna, 1992)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the IAEA's own publications server and read as extracted text. INSAG-7 exists because INSAG-1, the 1986 post-accident review, was written without a fact the Soviet side held. On the positive scram effect — the insertion of reactivity caused by the design of the control and safety rods — the report records: "The existence of the positive scram effect was first acknowledged by Soviet experts at the Conference on Nuclear Power Performance and Safety in Vienna in 1987. The SCSSINP Commission report states that this phenomenon had been known of at the time of the accident and that it had first been identified at the Ignalina RBMK plant in the Lithuanian Republic in 1983 ... Although the Chief Design Engineer for RBMK reactors promulgated this information to other RBMK plants, and stated that design changes would be made to correct the problem, he made no such changes, and the procedural measures he recommended for inclusion in plant operating instructions were not adopted. Apparently, there was a widespread view that the conditions under which the positive scram effect would be important would never occur. However, they did appear in almost every detail in the course of the actions leading to the accident." It further records that after the Ignalina discovery the chief engineering organization "informed other organizations and all nuclear power plants with RBMK reactors that it intended to impose restrictions on the complete withdrawal of control and safety rods from the core. Such restrictions were never imposed and apparently the matter was forgotten." INSAG's own verdict on this: "it does not really matter whether a positive scram was the final step that caused the reactor's destruction. It only matters that such a deficiency existed and that it could have been the cause of the accident. It is reprehensible that such a deficiency had been known of for so long without its having been eliminated." On what the 1986 international review was told, it says plainly: "Certainly the account in INSAG-1 would have been different had the features of the control and safety rods been revealed at the Post-Accident Review Meeting in 1986." Its summary conclusion (4) records that the rod effect "was a result of faulty design of the rods, the nature of which had been discovered at the Ignalina nuclear power plant in 1983. However, no correction was made following this discovery at Ignalina, no compensatory measures were taken and any dissemination of information to operating organizations was not followed up." Section 5.4 adds the 1975 Leningrad event as a second ignored precursor and states: "It is a matter of great concern that this important information was not adequately reviewed and, where it was disseminated to designers, operators and regulators, its significance was not fully understood and it was essentially ignored." The report is about reactor design, operation and regulation. It says nothing about the evacuation of anyone, nothing about the May Day parades, and nothing about the movements of officials or their families.

citations.title: The Chernobyl Forum 2003–2005 (IAEA, WHO, UNDP, FAO, UNEP, UN-OCHA, UNSCEAR, World Bank, Belarus, the Russian Federation and Ukraine), Chernobyl's Legacy: Health, Environmental and Socio-Economic Impacts, second revised version
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the IAEA's own site and read as extracted text (parts of the PDF carry a font-encoding fault that garbles some passages; nothing garbled is quoted here). On what was and was not told: "Unfortunately, reliable information about the accident and the resulting dispersion of radioactive material was initially unavailable to the affected people in what was then the Soviet Union and remained inadequate for years following the accident." Among the report's findings on the social consequences: "Third, the Soviet government delayed the public announcement that the accident had occurred. Information provision was selective and restrictive, particularly in the immediate aftermath of the accident." And on its long shadow: "Overcoming mistrust of information provided on Chernobyl remains a major challenge, owing to the early secrecy with which Soviet authorities treated the accident". The same silence had a measurable radiological cost: agricultural countermeasures "were only partially effective in reducing radioiodine intake via milk because of the lack of timely information about the accident and necessary responses, particularly for private farmers." On the evacuation itself the report is specific, and records action as well as delay: "Pripyat was the largest city nearest to the Chernobyl nuclear plant and approximately 50 000 residents were evacuated within 40 hours after the accident", while the intake of stable iodine tablets in the first hours after the accident "reduced the thyroid dose of the residents of Pripyat by a factor of 6 on average" (the number of hours stated there falls inside a font-garbled run in this PDF and was not readable, so it is not given); "More than 100 000 people were evacuated within few weeks after the accident from the most contaminated areas"; 116 000 people were evacuated in the spring and summer of 1986 from the Exclusion Zone and "Another 220 000 people were relocated in subsequent years." WHAT IS NOT IN IT: no separate or earlier evacuation of officials, Party members or their families is recorded anywhere in this report, and the May Day observances of 1 May 1986 are not mentioned at all.

consent.title: Foreseeable Before 11 March: What the Diet Commission and the IAEA Each Found TEPCO and Its Regulator Knew
participants: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI)
Fukushima Nuclear Accident Independent Investigation Commission (NAIIC), National Diet of Japan

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was taken was the cost of the countermeasures that were not built. The Diet commission puts the motive on the record in the operator’s own terms: "From TEPCO’s perspective, new regulations would have interfered with plant operations and weakened their stance in potential lawsuits.
